Mr. Speaker, it is nice to see your smiling face again in this House.
As it is Small Business Week in Canada I am very pleased to have the honour of presenting to this House the government's third annual report on the state of small business in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I know that all hon. members share my strong admiration for the men and women who own and operate small and medium-sized businesses in Canada. The report I am tabling today is entitled From Best Practices to Competitiveness and it profiles these entrepreneurs and highlights many of the practices they have used to be successful.
The Government of Canada is committed to programs and policies which support the growth of the small business sector. I invite all hon. members to study the report I am tabling today in order to enhance their understanding of small business practices. I urge everyone to join me in congratulating the enormous accomplishments of small businesses in Canada.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, the simple explanation of this bill that I have introduced in the House of Commons is to restore the sections of the Criminal Code commonly known as the rape shield law.
Let me make this brief remark. This is my response to the outcry from women across Canada on the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada invalidating the rape shield law. This bill would allow us to use our constitutional power to reinstate the relevant provisions of the Criminal Code.
May I make one more comment, Mr. Speaker, and it is this. The women responsible for the "Take Back the Night" crusade offer a simple guide, yes means yes and no means no. It is a national shame that some of the judges in the Supreme Court of Canada do not recognize the social value of that simple rule. If we really intend to stop violence against women let us restore the rape shield law.

speechtext:
Agreed.
October 22, 1991

That this House take note of the Prime Minister's recently stated commitment to the principle of linking government aid to respect for human rights and, in light of documented violations of human rights in countries such as Mexico, China, Zaire, Indonesia, Iran, Kenya and others which currently receive Canadian financial support, that this House urge the government to discontinue immediately Canadian participation in the Canada-United States-Mexico free trade negotiations and to review immediately all international support programs to ensure that they meet the aid criteria as announced by the Prime Minister.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I will be sharing my time with my colleague from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca who will be focusing in particular on the situation in Mexico and the implications of human rights in Mexico on the North American free trade deal.
As I said, we welcome the words and declarations of the Prime Minister during the past week at Commonwealth meetings both in Gabon and in Zimbabwe when he said "that Canada will not subsidize repression and the stifling of freedom, that nothing in international relations is more important than respect for individual freedoms and human rights," and when the Prime Minister said here in Canada that "human rights form a very important component of foreign policy for Canada".
There is a huge gap between reality and rhetoric when it comes to this important principle. I would remind the House that it was four years ago that the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade, chaired by William Winegard, the member for Guelph, strongly recommended to the government in its unanimous report that in fact Canada should link clearly and explicitly its policy on human rights with its policy on aid.
In 1988 the government indicated that it was prepared to implement that particular principle. The excellent report of the standing committee in 1987 called for a comprehensive set of guiding principles for a CIDA policy unit to identify human rights abusers and to advise
Supply
on trends in each recipient country, for annual reports to be made public by this unit and sent for review to parliamentary committees and for a clear linkage between development and arms control. As the Canadian Council on International Co-operation has pointed out this must be a transparent and open process.
What has happened in those four years since the Prime Minister suddenly discovered the importance of human rights in international financial transactions? Just today the Canadian Council on Churches and the Interchurch Fund for International Development are releasing a major report on Canada's record on foreign aid. That report is a scathing indictment of the policies of the Conservative government on aid.
They say that CIDA is moving further and further away from the real development issues that face the poorest countries. They say that CIDA has moved to a single neo-conservative development strategy, that CIDA's present course is a betrayal of its best contributions of the past. They point out that Canada has not come close to reaching our 1970 target of .7 per cent of GNP. In fact in real terms we have cut back on foreign aid, that our aid budget ranks tenth among the 12 largest donors when it comes to social spending, when it comes to spending on real human needs, and that we have not moved nearly far enough on the question of tied aid.
This government has said that they intend to implement human rights considerations when it comes to aid and once again we welcome that. But it is also important that in looking at other financial assistance and financial transactions that similar human rights considerations must apply.
When we are talking, for example, about lines of credit to other countries surely we have to look at human rights considerations in those circumstances as well. Perhaps the most glaring example is Iran and the fact that our government is prepared to extend a $1 billion line of credit to the government of Iran at the same time that the United Nations Human Rights Commission has found that there are a significant number of executions, repression of human rights, gross violation of the rights of women and children, that the officially announced executions for the first seven months of 1991 were three times greater than the total for the same period in 1990, that there is widespread public flogging of women, that a

Supply
woman was just recently flogged 35 times with a metal cable by the revolutionary guards and is now being ordered back by the Canadian government to Iran.
This is the government to which this country is extending a $1 billion line of credit. It is shameful and obviously sheer hypocrisy when it comes to preaching human rights in international financial terms.
We can look as well at the situation in Kuwait where we just extended a $500 million line of credit, despite the fact that Middle East Watch, a very respected human rights group, has found that murder, torture, arbitrary detention and unlawful deportation have been the tools of a campaign of vengeance against Palestinians and others in Kuwait.
Where are the human rights considerations in extending lines of credit to Kuwait and to Iran? Surely we must look at the question of extension of lines of credit at this very sensitive point in Middle East peace negotiations to Israel as well when human rights concerns have been expressed with respect to the conditions in the occupied territory and when Israel insists on additional settlements in the occupied territories.
We must recognize that this standard cannot simply apply to ODA. It must apply as well to lines of credit.
Who does Iran buy its weapons from? One of its chief weapons suppliers is China. China is one of the chief weapons suppliers to Burma or to Myanmar which is ruled by a 19-member military junta described by Amnesty International as guilty of systematic torture and routine murder. It is a country in which state sanctioned brutality is a nation-wide phenomena.
China is responsible for selling arms to Burma, to Iran and other countries. As far as Canada is concerned, it is business as usual with China, despite the fact that Amnesty has documented that hundreds of thousands of people in China, including prisoners of conscience, are arbitrarily and in some cases illegally detained under the country's blatantly unfair system of administrative detention.
We know that in the wake of the Tiananmen Square massacre the police rounded up leaders of the pro-democracy movement and that as many as several thousand have been detained. The trials have been held behind closed doors, despite the call by Canada and other countries to open up those trials, to ensure that international observers can be present.
We recognize, of course, the progress that China has made in feeding its people despite tremendous adversity and in housing its people. Surely, Canada cannot remain silent on these abuses of human rights.
I note as well that Canada nominated China to the United Nations High Commission on Refugees, to an executive position there, as rapporteur despite the fact that we recognize China is a refugee producing country.
I could go down the list of other countries which are major recipients of Canada's foreign aid. Indonesia has been involved in the brutal suppression of the people of East Timor for some 15 years, with numerous killings, oppression, abuses of human rights. There has been the ruthless suppression of the rights of the people of East Timor, and yet Canada is actively involved in a financial sense in that country as well.
Kenya, where President Daniel arap Moi has suggested that he wants to hunt down like rats, those who have the audacity to oppose his dictatorial regime in that country. Kenya, a country in which prisoners of conscience have been held without charge or trial. In a number of cases, Canada provides $30 million a year to Kenya.

It is the same thing in Rwanda, dictatorship. Canada has subsidized the dictatorial regime in Rwanda, while the Prime Minister talks about respect for human rights. There is hypocrisy and a double standard, Mr. Speaker. Such double standards are quite unacceptable!
The same thing happens in Zaire. Canada gave a grant of some $70 million to the repressive Mobutu goveme-ment in Zaire. Where are the human rights standards, Mr. Speaker?

Is the Prime Minister in fact a bom again convert to this concept of linking human rights with financial aid as part of his campaign to become the Secretary General of the United Nations? We do not know.
We know he has tremendous support from his Conservative colleagues, but we have to ask ourselves: Why is there this last minute conversion to the principles of linking human rights with financial aid and financial support? Why is that? Why are they not practising what they preach? Why are they not practising what they preach in Central America, in Guatemala and in El

Salvador where the Central America monitoring group has documented very clearly the fact that we have bilateral government to government aid relations with those countries which are obviously guilty of profound human rights abuses? They are guilty of denial of rights to their own people.
We know as well about the concerns about the impact of structural adjustment policies in our aid as well.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, let us talk for a moment about the status of women. The Prime Minister in his speech in Harare, Zimbabwe, spoke about the importance of the Commonwealth setting the pace in ensuring the equality of women in all sectors of society. Yet Canada is selling 1,117 light armed vehicles to the fundamentalist regime in Saudi Arabia, a regime which has been denounced for its torture and ill treatment of detainees, a regime in which women are denied basic political and social rights.
Quite clearly there is a profound double standard in this government's approach to human rights. The Prime Minister, when he is outside the country, when he is in Zimbabwe, speaks about the importance of linkage of human rights and aid. We support that linkage. We have supported it since we joined in supporting the 1987 report. However, in closing, the time has come, Mr. Speaker, to match words to action. It is time to ensure that human rights are taken seriously by this government.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his very interesting survey of the violators of human rights with whom Canada has trade and aid relations.
I would like to ask the hon. member if he can comment further on the trade side of it since there is far more money involved both ways in trade. He has referred to tied aid, but I would like him to explain what the percentage is of Canada's ODA aid which is tied and what that tie means, not only for the profit of Canadians, but sometimes to the disadvantage of the country supposedly being aided.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the question from the hon. member because it does point out another glaring inconsistency in this government's policies with respect to aid.
The fact is that the government declared its commitment in 1988 to untying at least one-third of government aid, and that still leaves a very high proportion of tied aid. Yet that target is far from being met by this government.
Instead, we have a situation in which only 5 per cent of the aid which is accorded by Canada to needy countries goes to meet basic human priorities such as family planning, clean water, primary education and primary health care. In fact, the United Nations human development report of 1990 was very critical of the very, very small proportion of Canadian aid which is going to serve basic human needs. The OECD was critical of what it referred to as a significant decline in Canadian aid, and the United Nations in its human development report pointed out that much of Canadian aid was in fact misdirected.
I want to take this opportunity as well, Mr. Speaker, just to note that nine of the ten top recipients in the Commonwealth of Canadian aid-and I am not even speaking here of trade, but I am speaking specifically of aid-routinely held political prisoners in detention without trial, according to Amnesty International last year, and more than one-half of them tolerated torture and extrajudicial executions.
Yes, it is important to talk about aid, but we also need to have a trade policy, a policy with respect to lines of credit that reflect that commitment to fundamental human rights. It is not good enough to say we will extend lines of credit for hundreds of millions of dollars in Mexico, in Kuwait, in Iran when what that does is allow the governments of those countries to spend even more money on the military.
Pakistan, for example, spends three times as much money on the military as it does on basic human needs. It is time that Canada recognize that our country simply cannot allow it to be business as usual in these circumstances. We must stop, for example, welcoming with open arms Nicolai Ceausescu to this country. Some people have short memories. In 1985, he was welcomed with open arms. We have to promote business, we have to promote trade.

It is time we stopped this hypocrisy and recognize that Canada must have one human rights policy.
Mr. Speaker, on a personal note I want to say how pleased I am to see the chair being occupied by our Deputy Speaker who was unfortunately ill for some time but has now returned to this Chamber.
Hear, hear.

Under the calmness of the Deputy Speaker's chairpersonship I will make my comments to impress the House about the importance of this particular debate.
I will take just a couple of moments to congratulate my colleague, the member for Burnaby who has outlined clearly a continuation of a debate that took place in this House relative to the gulf war.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, the high statements made by the former minister of external affairs about ending the arms race, and the pious statements made some months ago in this House by the Prime Minister and the former minister of external affairs that we have to control the international arms race.
My colleague has outlined in his speech how we are contributing to the continuation of the international arms race, and the high sounding, high-falutin speeches of the Prime Minister and the former minister of external affairs turned out to be hollow and empty. It came as a shock and disappointment to me as a nouveau member of this Chamber, but what comes as even more of a shock to me is the repetition of the same kind of transparent statements taking place regarding the defence of human rights while at the same time acting differently as government. The same parallels exist: statements about actions on this way but actions taking place in reality in an another way.
I relate this whole debate to the question of our sitting at the table with the nations of Mexico and the United States. The issues of human rights, labour rights and environmental rights relative to the free trade discussions among the United States, Mexico and Canada were raised in the U.S. Congress and the U.S. Senate.
Last May I had the opportunity of appearing before a budget task force committee outlining my party's concern about the human rights aspects as well as the economic aspects.
President Bush was so concerned about the opposition in Congress and in the United States Senate that he was forced to set up a parallel study in the United States relative to the environmental issues, the labour issues and the human rights issues.
If this government is to be believed to be sincere, how can it sit at the table with the Government of Mexico, knowing in advance the catalogue of violence, torture and frankly murders that taken place in Mexico, catalogued by Amnesty International, and at the same time make pious statements about human rights relative to economic matters?
I want to refer to a recent column in The Winnipeg Free Press. It is not known as a social democratic organ or outlet. I want to quote just the first few paragraphs of a column written by Frances Russell. She says:
Like most giant corporations the Ford Motor Company has moved to the maquiladoras, the Mexican free trade zone along the U.S. border.
In 1987, the employees at Ford's Cuatilan plant earned $2.35 an hour, a generous salary compared to the average maquiladora manufacturing wage of 98 cents an hour.
Suddenly, Ford shut down the plant, laying off all of its employees.
Three months later, the company's doors reopened, but this time, the employees were offered only $8 a day. Their benefits and vacations were cut in half.
Workers demonstrated, which is their right in any civilized country. The consequence of that demonstration was that a blood bath followed. She continues:
Thugs attached to the Mexico's government labour organization, the CTM, stormed the plant, killing one person, shooting nine more and sending an additional 40 to hospital.
Subsequently, Ford president Harold Polling denied all knowledge of the incident to the United Auto Workers.
There is a catalogue outside Amnesty International of over 80 trade union activists who were murdered or who disappeared in Mexico over the last 36 months. We should contrast that statement to the response to the questions made by the then Minister for International Trade, now the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans in front of a committee just last year. Last October the Minister for International Affairs assured the external affairs and international trade committee that when it came to the North American free trade agreement "Canada is always
October 22, 1991

prepared to take a high moral plane". The plane left the ground without any facts. The high moral plane is ignoring the violation of labour rights, human rights and, as a matter of fact, organized thuggery under the approval of the Government of Mexico. Again I say it is documented.
Why is Canada at the table with the Prime Minister of this country making such statements as: "Canada will not subsidize repression and the stifling of freedom". It is a very bad taste in the mouth to have to repeat these words in light of what is going on in Mexico.
With deep disappointment I have to refer to the divisions inside the Liberal Party regarding this matter. I hate to bring this up again, but since the loss of the previous leader of the Liberal Party the Liberal Party is now back on the fence on this very important issue.
I quote from the October 16, 1991 issue of The Globe and Mail or The Globe and Flail as it is commonly known, where the hon. member for Willowdale, the Liberal industrial critic, said: "Canada needs to be involved in continental trade negotiations to protect our national interests. By participating Canada can renegotiate the Canada-U.S. pact". What a pile of nonsense. The fact is that this House, regardless of party, should stand and say that Canada as a nation will not sit at the table to negotiate a brand new trade agreement with one of the major violators of human rights.
How can the Canadian government and the Official Opposition suggest that these talks go on while violation after violation after violation of human rights is catalogued in Mexico? I quote the Prime Minister again: "Canada will not subsidize repression and the stifling of freedom".
I want to continue to quote the former minister of trade: "We should support the trade union organizations and shorter working hours". That is not what is happening in Mexico, and he was referring to Mexico. He said: "Workmen's compensation and all these things we have here in Canada, we want to see elsewhere. But I do not think unilaterally we can impose them on Mexico. Those are domestic matters for them to decide".

What position are we dealing with here? The Prime Minister lecturing other countries on human rights or the former minister of trade saying that we will not interfere in the internal matters of another country, particularly when those matters are so devastating to human beings and labour organizations.
You cannot have it both ways, regardless of the interpretation of the motivations of the Prime Minister. Should he indeed be seeking another job? The polls advise that would be the best and most prudent advice he could take. Nonetheless, one cannot have the idea of saying one thing about human rights here to promote one agenda, while at the same time another minister is saying: "We will not interfere with the internal matters of another country".
If I could say the word "hypocrisy", I would say it. But I know it is not parliamentary so I will not say it. Should it come from my mouth, I would withdraw it, Mr. Speaker.
Having said that, I want to say that this place is being measured by Canadians from coast to coast. It is being measured on the basis of seeing whether or not we really mean what we say in this Chamber, or as each week slips by do we say one thing and then something else? This conflicting statement between the minister and the Prime Minister is obvious.
The motto of this government is: "If we are going to give you money, we will tell you that you must behave yourself. But if we are going to make money out of you, we do not care what the hell you do". That is the blunt double standard that exists and I for one do not want any part of that. I beg the Liberal Party to end its confusion about this matter.
My last comment is: when I asked in committee that the all-party committee travel to Mexico to verify these matters as they were presented to the committee, with the support of the Liberal member from Winnipeg, that request was turned down by the committee. No one from the parliamentary committee has stepped a foot in Mexico to report back to this House about what is going on there before we continue these negotiations, no one. Blindly the committee was kept here in a cubby-hole downstairs, a comfortable cubby-hole nonetheless, with

Supply
no access whatsoever to talk to Mexicans in the trade union movement or Mexicans in the religious community about what is really going on. The agenda is dictated by money, money, money.
That is not morality. That is the word that I cannot use and I will not use it.

Mr. Speaker, first I want to congratulate the member from Burnaby for having the initiative to advance this debate on the floor of the House of Commons today. This very debate took place in my riding last Saturday morning. It started at 7.30 at the Albion restaurant on Queen Street. We never ended it, so I am happy that we are continuing it here today.
I do have a very specific question for the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca. About three years ago I had the opportunity of spending a couple of weeks in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. This is a country where human rights violations are quite public and quite dramatic. Hands are cut off and heads are cut off in a public forum when people are caught. Whether it is stealing or molesting women, one knows of the severe examples in Saudi Arabia. This was pretty shocking to me. I did not think that this kind of thing continued today. At the same time I discovered that through Bell Canada over the previous 10 years we basically set up its entire telephone network system. There were close to 40,000 Canadian jobs involved in putting this telephone infrastructure in place. Billions and billions of dollars went into manufacturing in every part of this country.
I am not supporting human rights violations but I want to be quite specific in my question. Do I understand the member correctly? Is he saying that that contract should have just been refused or turned down? If so, I would like to include that we just finished going through a Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto where our premier basically opened the Saudi Arabia exhibit and encouraged further trade ties to this same country where there is human rights oppression. I just need a bit of assistance on how dramatic he is proposing we should be.

I have always been impressed with that member's thoughtful and profound observations and questions. It is a very serious problem. Of course we need to expand our trade and a high moral plane is a desirable goal. We have to face reality on the basis of
issue by issue. However, I would like to point out that obvious violations demand action by a government.
Let me give some historical examples. During 1940, before the United States came into direct conflict with Nazi Germany and our Commonwealth was struggling to maintain its freedom, behind the united effort of all political parties in the Commonwealth it was discovered that the Texaco Oil Company was selling airplane fuel, high octane fuel through Spain to Nazi Germany. There was an international outcry and the United States government under then President Roosevelt tried to take an initiative to stop those sales, but the overwhelming sense was business as usual.
On reflection, had a moral stand been taken against that kind of activity in 1940, the Luftwaffe would have been handicapped earlier than the devastation of the Battle of Britain. These are documented facts.
What do you do? You make a decision on morality. What we are calling for in this imperfect world is an attempt to review every single one of these deals and potential deals on the basis of some sense of morality. We are not perfect human beings.
In the early 1970s I was confronted with a similar situation in trade with South Africa. As a government in British Columbia we unilaterally cancelled all importation of liquor products and wine in the B.C. liquor stores and made that our statement in any other contract with South Africa.
It cost us a tax politically and it cost us a tax financially, but we made that decision on a moral ground. On the same basis I am asking that as human beings we sit down with industry, with the Canadian people and ask: Is the high price for this deal in terms of moral standards greater than the economic benefits?
I do not know. I do not have a formula, but when I am given obvious information such as what exists in Mexico, it seems to me that there is no economic benefit from us backing away from the table and saying: Look, we will sit at the table with you when you clean up your act. Even the President of the United States has been forced to set up parallel investigations in response to Congress and the Senate.
This Chamber in a sense is no different from the Congress and the Senate in dealing with these moral problems. What frightens me and frankly angers me,

with no evil intent implied to other human beings, is that we cannot even get it straight from the government of the day where it stands.
On the one hand the Prime Minister lectures countries in Africa and on the other hand the former trade minister says: "We will not interfere". That is puzzling. It is not fair. It is not right. It is not decent.

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to rise to take part in this debate because it is a very serious one as the member for Broadview-Greenwood has pointed out.
It is serious first of all because victims of human rights abuses around the world want us to have a consistent policy that is sensitive to their needs. Their hope depends on it. Their lives depend on it. They are looking to Canada to have a consistent foreign policy, aid policy and human rights policy that will continue their hope.
Second, Canada's reputation is on the line on this issue. Over the years, regardless of which government was in office, Canada has established a reputation for being concerned about human rights issues around the world. Therefore this is a very serious motion.
I note with particular interest that the Prime Minister who has now generated this debate by his statements did not make his statement about human rights abuses here in Ottawa, in the House of Commons or in the parliamentary press gallery. He said it in the presence of the leaders of the world, where we are concerned about human rights issues.
I notice that the member for Burnaby said that the Prime Minister is a recent convert to human rights issues. This gadfly from Burnaby, who has taken a new interest in this subject since he has been appointed to this position, has had a very convenient lapse of memory.
The Prime Minister raised human rights issues seven years ago when he was in Korea where there is a right wing regime. He has gone to what would be called left wing regimes and raised human rights issues there. I want this member to know that the Prime Minister has been consistent wherever he has gone in raising human
Supply
rights issues, regardless of the kind of regime that was in office. He is not a recent convert. He has done it consistently. It was the Prime Minister's initiative that raised the whole matter of embargoes on South Africa.
It is just not true, as the member for Burnaby has said, that the Prime Minister is a recent convert and has suddenly discovered the issue of human rights. If we want to do justice to this debate the first thing we have to do is be honest, accurate, factual and non-partisan if he is really interested in it. While the motion is a very serious one, I am not too sure that it can be taken seriously because of the way it has been put.
The member for Burnaby has conveniently referred to one excerpt of the Winegard report of 1987 regarding Canada's foreign aid policy. I happened to sit on that committee, as did his colleague from Cowichan-Mal-ahat-The Islands, the former member Jim Manly. Now I notice with particular interest that in chapter 3, entitled Linking Aid and Human Rights, the committee recommends that verifiable reports of violations, not ideology or strategic interest, be the basis for unfavourable assessments of human rights observance.
With that in mind let us turn to the motion which the member has put forward. He says in part:
- in the light of documented violations of human rights in countries such as Mexico, China, Zaire, Indonesia, Iran, Kenya and others which currently receive Canadian financial support, that this House urge the government to discontinue immediately Canadian participation in the Canada-United States-Mexico free trade negotiations-
We know that New Democratic Party members are opposed to the North American free trade agreement. They were opposed to the United States-Canada Free Trade Agreement. That is an ideological position that they have taken. They are entitled to it, but why is it that they have taken an ideological position on free trade with Mexico? Why do they now want to inject human rights issues into that area?
I noticed with particular interest the good question put forward by my friend from Broadview-Greenwood regarding trade with Saudi Arabia. But the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca never did answer his question. The question very simply put is: Should Bell Canada install a telephone system in Saudi Arabia, a regime which is guilty of human rights abuses according to Canadian standards? It is a very simple question. Should

After agreeing that there are human rights issues in that country, the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca again took the high road in saying: "the Nazi regime in Germany, pre-war and during the war, got fuel from Texaco". Somehow there was a little bit of a non sequitur there, a little bit of a lapse. He never did come around to answering whether or not the premier of Ontario, of the same party of the member who put the motion forward, should have opened the Saudi Arabian pavilion at the CNE.
It is well and good to take a gadfly approach to human rights in aid and trade but surely we cannot afford to do that. Why should we, according to this motion, list the human rights abuses in Mexico, China, Zaire, Indonesia, Iran, Kenya and others and because of human rights abuses in Zaire cut off NAFTA? It seems to me that there is an ideological position which they have taken and now they want to superimpose human rights issues on that ideological position.
The second problem I have with the motion is that it is very erratic. New Democratic Party members want to take the high road on this issue, but they are very selective in their concern about human rights issues.
I was in Nicaragua some years ago leading a parliamentary delegation with the Interparliamentary Union. The member for Trinity-Spadina was with us and General Ortega was in command at the time in Nicaragua. He thought he had come to a kind of socialist heaven. I recognize that the Somoza regime had filled the penitentiary behind the hotel where we stayed with political prisoners. It was an oppressive regime.
But when General Ortega came in and took over he emptied that prison and simply refilled it with political prisoners of his choosing, people that he felt should be in prison. When mothers of missing persons wanted to take part in a parade, they were prevented from taking part because that would highlight the human rights abuses in Nicaragua. But all the time that those human rights abuses were taking place in Nicaragua, members of the New Democratic Party and the former member for New Westminster, Pauline Jewett, kept saying that we had to
increase aid. The member for Trinity-Spadina kept saying that we had to increase aid to Nicaragua. The former member for New Westminster kept asking why Canada did not open an embassy in Nicaragua to show good faith in the people of Nicaragua, to strengthen the administration and give them hope.
It strikes me that the members of that party have been strangely silent about the needs of the Nicaraguan people ever since there has been an election in that country.
If the member for Burnaby had included in his reference to the Winegard report the statement that verifiable reports of violations, not ideology or strategic interest, be the basis for unfavourable assessment of human rights observers, I think the motion would have been a little bit more believable.
We always need, in all of our programs, the opportunities for direct scrutiny to make sure that our motives, our operations and our principles are always square. We need that.
In that spirit I welcome the debate because Canada does have to re-evaluate its position. But I am surprised that when the member put forward the motion and made his speech and the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca talked about all the discrepancies that he saw they did not take time to notice the response of CIDA to the Winegard report that the member for Burnaby-Kings-way made. They never mentioned it.
In the introduction of that report we read that the government intends to ensure among other things that Canadian development assistance does not lend legitimacy to repressive regimes, that victims of human rights violations are not doubly penalized by being deprived of needed help in addition to being deprived of their fundamental rights, that there be a constructive approach to human rights rather than a punitive one, and that development assistance appropriately targeted can contribute substantially to the cause of both development and human rights.
In short those are some of the items that CIDA has responded to in that report. It goes on to say that when countries show progress toward a marked improvement in their respect for human rights, Canada will reflect this progress in its decisions about funding.

I could go on. There are several pages to the response by CIDA to this report, but suffice it to say that when it comes to overseas assistance, development assistance and human rights assistance, Canada cannot afford a gadfly approach. We need a systematic, studied, co-operative approach with other countries of like mind to make sure that our policies support our goals of human rights, not the repressive regimes but the people who need support.
I want to indicate some of the things Canada has done in working toward a human rights approach in a systematic way.
First of all, let me point out that we have to look at opportunities wherever they are and that no situation is hopeless. Canada must identify the prospects which best offer hope for change. We have to look for those opportunities. They are not necessarily what we read in the newspapers. Through all our contacts, through NGOs, through our embassies and through our consular officials we must look for those kinds of opportunities.
The Canadian practice is this: to speak out against abuses in an appropriate way and in an appropriate setting so that our message does not create the opposite effect from that sought and that we may avoid the ending impression of self-righteousness. No one's record is impeccable when it comes to human rights.
I see the member from Comox taking notes. I want to remind him of something he certainly does not remember because he was not there at the time: there was a day when Mennonites were excluded from Canada by law, prohibited from entry into Canada. It so happens that in today's world Mennonites are held in high esteem when it comes to monitoring human rights and development assistance. Between the years 1919 and 1922 by law of the Government of Canada Mennonites were prohibited from entering into Canada.
Canada's history is not impeccable. We have not always been right and we have to avoid any kind of self-righteousness on this cause.
Second, we must focus on the real problems of implementing human right's standards and strengthening the multilateral network of instruments and technical assistance. I say this in juxtaposition to a gadfly approach. It is easy enough to get up in the House of Commons and enumerate-God knows there are plenty of opportunities-human rights abuses all around the world, all too many of them. If we are going to be a
Supply
responsible administration, we have to work in a multilateral network of instruments and technical assistance and work together with other countries to make sure that we have a consistent policy.
Third, we have to co-operate for pragmatic changes. In discussions with new democracies we stress that we want to work with them as allies and partners to improve the situation in their region and to sustain reforms in their countries.
Fourth, we want to make sure that we have a longterm perspective. Human rights are partly a question of attitudes and changing attitudes takes time. Although sometimes changes can be spectacular, for example in South Africa and in eastern Europe, on a long-term basis we are progressing stage by stage.
Tailoring an appropriate Canadian policy response is the most difficult and sensitive part of human rights as a foreign policy issue. What we are seeking to do, in essence, is to take the policy instruments at our disposal and apply them in our relations with other states in such a way as to encourage or induce them into implementing internationally agreed standards of human rights.
The President of Mexico spoke in this Chamber not too long ago. I ask members to reflect on that speech. I ask them to ask themselves this question: Would it help the downtrodden, the poorest of the poor in Mexico, in Indonesia or in Saudi Arabia to quarantine Canada from every country in the world where there has been some human rights abuses? Should we quarantine and isolate Canada from the rest of the Third World, whether it be Mexico, El Salvador, Guatemala, Nicaragua or Zaire? Should we isolate ourselves totally until they meet our total criteria of human rights righteousness?
Again the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca never did come to grips with the reality that exists in the world, that there is no such thing as a perfect world. We have to live in concert with other nations.
I would like the members of that party to explain to the House how they reconcile their desire on the one hand to have harmonious international relations with all countries of the world, a kind of world of detente and peace, and at the same time isolate ourselves from that world. How do you bring together those two clashing concepts? They have never reconciled that. On the one hand they want us to trade, to get along with everyone and to give development assistance to everyone. On the

There are objectives that Canada has developed over the years, regardless of what government was in office, that we have to maintain. Throughout the course of this debate members from this side-the member for Halifax West, the member for Edmonton Northwest, the member for Kitchener, the member for Louis-Hebert and the member for Don Valley West-are going to take separate entities of this motion and are going to deal with them fully.
I hope that this party will begin to try to reconcile where it really stands on human rights issues, whether it wants to see Canada isolated from the rest of the world or it wants Canada to participate and share with the rest of the world some of the ideals that are part and parcel of our heritage.

question of the government in a fair and democratic election standing down while the next government took it. The end of the Contra war certainly changed the circumstances in Nicaragua. This government did have a hand in starving that regime out of existence with the United States.

I am sure the Liberal Party will support this motion that human rights are a priority. We agree with what the Prime Minister said. Let us put some of the other gross abuses behind us also. Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise today to participate in debate on the motion that was presented by the opposition today.
My colleague from Burnaby-Kingsway has spoken to the motion. I would like to say that at the conclusion of

my remarks today I would like to present an amendment to the motion on the floor today.
I would like to begin my remarks by saying that if the Prime Minister goes beyond the rhetoric of his words to actually substantive changes in our foreign policies with regard to the linking of human rights to aid, I know that many people in this country will be delighted and would thank him for the new directions that he is proposing.
It is not as if the government has not proposed a strict linkage of human rights to aid in the past. Unfortunately that linkage has not been seen. In fact, if the Prime Minister does not follow through his rhetoric with substantive changes to our policies then he will be subject to the charge of hypocrisy.
I would like to start by just reiterating what exactly it is that the Prime Minister has said. I quote from a newspaper article of last week where he says: "If you are asking me if Canada will shy away from tying its aid policies, we will not shy away at all". He goes on to say that human rights form a very important component of foreign policy for Canada. If that is so, then human rights in relation to foreign policy go beyond just aid and must also include trade and immigration issues.
He goes on to say that if we go to a specific policy of linking aid to human rights there is a risk of being accused of a colonial mentality dictating morality. Nonetheless, more and more Canadians are preoccupied by human rights in aid recipient countries. I believe that he is right in saying that, and I would support that as an issue. Human rights is a serious concern to many, many Canadians.
The motion before us today, however, refers in one instance specifically to the fact that the NDP is urging the government to discontinue immediately Canadian participation in the Canada-United States-Mexico free trade negotiations. Certainly the case of Mexico, I would say, is not clear. I think it is a difficult issue for us to address with regard to its human rights record. As well I would say that the human rights issues with regard to Mexico are not the only difficulties we encounter in the trilateral trade talks that are now taking place.
However, Amnesty International has outlined in its recent report which it published on September 18 very gross human rights abuses that have taken place in Mexico. It details those abuses very specifically saying, and I quote: "Torture is reported almost daily in Mexico
and despite the seriousness of the problem the Mexican authorities are doing little to put an effective stop to torture and ill treatment", the world-wide human rights organization said.
Yet we have to contrast that with a fact that I have taken from an article in a Mexico City newspaper dated September 19 which states: "Mexico's attorney general announced Wednesday his office would thoroughly investigate each allegation of torture in an extremely critical report released this week by Amnesty International. Attorney General Morales admitted that torture was still a problem in Mexico but said it was not condoned and was no longer widespread. Amnesty International will say that that is not so, but on the other hand Morales' acceptance of the Amnesty report represented a break from the recent past".
There are some indications that Mexico is indeed trying to deal with its human rights abuse issues. To corroborate that there was an article in The Gazette of October 20 which speaks to the case of a Norma Corona Sapien in Mexico, a Mexican woman who was murdered in May 1990. She was a human rights activist. She was apparently murdered by government security forces. The article outlines the fact that in Mexico they have now arrested a Gonzales Traveno.
We admit that it took an awfully long time for the Mexican authorities to get around to arresting anybody in this case, but I think it is important to acknowledge that they have pursued the case and have said that they will continue to pursue human rights abuse cases. Certainly this man who has been arrested is a high profile person in the security forces. The linkage there is very serious, one that we cannot underestimate and must watch. I would say that it is extremely important to look at that linkage, but we also must be very aware of improvements when they do take place and press constantly for greater improvements.
We are concerned about not only tying human rights issues to aid but also to trade. In today's newspapers there is one comment that I think bears recognition. A Toronto Star editorial today said: "While Mulroney's message deserves support, his methods also deserve close scrutiny. Will Canada throw its weight around when it has nothing to lose, such as with Haiti's enfeebled economy? What about the substantial aid allocated to Asian countries with dynamic economies such as

The latter suggestion is certainly what I would support, but I think that editorial expresses a lot of the concerns that we would have over what the Prime Minister is saying and what we will watch with regard to his own statements but more particularly his government's policies over the coming days, weeks and months.
Yesterday in the House of Commons the Prime Minister was questioned about his appearance last week before the Commonwealth Conference, linking human rights issues to aid and the importance of doing so. He was also questioned about giving a $1 billion line of credit the previous week to Iran, the worst human rights abuser in the world. So many people across Canada are very concerned about human rights abuses, not just at home but particularly internationally where the abuses are so gross and extreme. They have been calling for many years for more transparency with regard to how the government makes its decisions. Right now these decisions are made in cabinet. Not all government members understand how these decisions are arrived at. Certainly many of the decisions that are made such as extending the $1 billion line of credit to Iran through the Export Development Corporation two weeks ago affronts many Canadians. When we look at what the Government of Iran is doing,

there is not just human rights abuse. That country is spending the majority of its budget on military expenditures this year. I understand it is to the tune of $17 billion. Mr. Speaker, the member's amendment is quite a surprise. TTie Mexican free trade deal will probably affect Canada even more significantly than the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. It promises to devastate the economy of Canada. It points out that Mexico lacks an environmental policy and a social policy including health care. It is rife with political corruption.

Our aboriginal people have had to go before the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva which is a disgrace to our nation. They felt that they had to go to that forum in order to have their rights considerations heard.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate. It is a rare opportunity to look at Canada's record on human rights, foreign aid and international investment.
I would like to begin by quoting the Prime Minister: "Nothing in international relations is more important than respect for individual freedom and human rights". That was in his speech to the members of the Commonwealth just last week. A second quote: "Canada will not subsidize repression and the stifling of freedom". That was in his speech also at the same Commonwealth conference in the opening session. As I only have 10 minutes I am going to focus today on one country to give our viewers some idea of how what he said in Harare measures with what is actually happening.
I refer first of all to an Amnesty International report that was presented before the United Nations special committee on decolonization on August 7 of this year. This report is on East Timor and I wish to quote passages. Some of them are rather difficult reading.
Talking about East Timor: "It is a pattern of shortterm detention, torture and ill treatment of suspected political opponents described in previous reports that has accelerated in the past year. In Amnesty's view it appears to be part of a systemic strategy to silence real or suspected political opponents".
It goes on to say: "Many of those detained have reportedly been tortured or ill treated in custody. The forms of ill treatment and torture alleged include beatings with iron bars, batons, fists and lengths of cable and bamboo; burning with lighted cigarettes; sexual molestation and rape; slashing with razor blades; food deprivation; immersion for long periods in fetid water; death threats and electrocution".
"In view of the clear evidence that suspected political opponents of Indonesian rule in East Timor have been systematically ill treated and tortured while under interrogation, Amnesty International has concluded that the
Supply
safety of all those detained for questioning, however briefly, by members of the security forces must be considered at risk".
That report should be put next to an article from the Free Press by John Sorenson entitled "Canadian Role in Indonesia Opportunistic".
The history of East Timor is a sorry history. On December 7, 1975 Indonesia invaded that small island and subsequently annexed it. In the last 15 years, hundreds of thousands of Timorees have been slaughtered by Indonesian troops.
At the time of the invasion, Canada was one of the largest foreign investors in Indonesia. As such, Canada at that time under a Liberal government had an opportunity to exert some influence. However it did not. It had an opportunity to halt the genocide in East Timor but Canada did not.
Instead our ambassador at the time advised that Canada recognize the takeover as a fait accompli. This type of response fits with in a recent statement by the current minister of external affairs when she said that Canada considers, in response to a question from my colleague from Trinity-Spadina on September 18, that Indonesian sovereignty over East Timor is a fact, recognizing there has never been any history of independence, self-determination or self-government in that territory.
The ignorance displayed in that response is monumental.
The ambassador at the time also pointed out that if Canada recognized the annexation as a fait accompli, greater benefits to Canada, Canadian companies, and improved trading relations would result. In fact this proved to be astute judgment. The benefits to Canada which resulted from the decision not to criticize the Indonesian government are not as insubstantial and continue to accrue. Currently over 300 Canadian companies do business in Indonesia, which has been seen as an investor's paradise.
The Indonesian government has established this paradise by ignoring civil liberties, banning all unions, keeping the wages of most workers below one U.S. dollar a day, strictly controlling the media and maintaining an extensive security force.

Supply
Two-thirds of the population are undernourished and Indonesia's poor make up the cheapest labour force in Asia. A strict anti-subversive law and the activity of police death squads ensure that few protests are in paradise.
Canada has invested over $1 billion in Indonesia, with most of that money going to huge mining and smelting operations run by Inco, but also in manufacturing, oil, gas and financial services.
Since the invasion of East Timor, Canadian aid dollars have continued to flow through Indonesia. Indonesia is the third largest recipient of Canadian foreign aid dollars. This is the largest non-Commonwealth recipient of such assistance. Several Canadian universities have established lucrative, multi-million dollar contracts with CIDA and the Indonesian government to supply technical expertise. Put that record next to the Amnesty International report and we see the kind of thing we are talking about, the hypocrisy of not just this government but previous governments in dealing with this very important issue.
We have options. The New Democrats have options. As an opposition party we believe it is our responsibility not just to criticize bad legislation but to put forth alternatives, and that is where I want to end today. The idea of linking Canadian aid with the monitoring of human rights is not new. In 1987 the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade put forth an excellent report on overseas development assistance entitled "For Whose Benefit". It recommended linking development and human rights and called for a number of recommendations.
The NDP believes human rights and development can best be linked by increasing the quality of Canadian aid. For example, CIDA should increase funding through non-governmental channels. Credible NGOs and international NGOs are better able to direct Canadian funds to meet human priority needs. The most basic human rights are food and shelter. A 1990 UN development report shows Canada gives only 5 cents out of each aid dollar to meet human priority needs like family planning, clean water, primary education and primary health care.
If the Prime Minister is sincere about linking our development assistance to human rights, he must respond to the regret recently expressed by the OECD at the significant decline in Canadian aid and to the UN suggestion that much of this aid is misdirected.
In conclusion, I want to point out the kind of sorry history Canada has had on human rights and foreign aid and investment. It is not a recent occurrence; it is a long-standing occurrence. Consider what one international banker expressed to me when I was in New York on an external affairs trip examining international debt: "We don't care how our bills are paid as long as they are paid. We don't care about human rights abuses as long as our bills are paid". For Canada and for Canadians generally that is not an acceptable approach. We have to link human rights abuses with international aid. I urge the government not to repeat the sorry history of empty rhetoric but to put real substance behind the Prime Minister's statement and to turn around Canada's record on international investment and aid.

The particular point of the motion, including the particular point that would be removed by the Liberal amendment, is to ask the government to discontinue immediately Canadian participation in the Canada, United States and Mexico free trade negotiations.
Because of the principle of tying aid to human rights which the Prime Minister has announced and which has been discussed in this House and was the subject of a unanimous report in this House, it is proposed that we discontinue negotiating this trade treaty with the United States and Mexico. It goes on to say "review immediately all international support programs" and so on.
The main point of the motion is not to review support programs. That goes on all the time. The Liberal amendment which cuts out the Mexico part says "review". Of course as far as the review part is concerned it is like motherhood. The Liberals always review things and this House reviews things. So there is no problem about saying "review". The question is whether to

As for the NDP's position on this, I would point out that earlier this year the NDP government in Ontario did withdraw the entry placed by the previous Liberal government in ARMX, the arms bazaar that was to be held earlier this year but was cancelled. However, I want to acknowledge that there is no monopoly of human rights violations by any government, party, country, religion or social or political philosophy. Whichever one I belong to, I am involved in some of these human rights violations. I would rather first of all go back to what I think is the root of the problem.
There have been several centuries of conquests, massacres and thefts by the countries of the North Atlantic. Western Europe and North America, primarily western Europe, thus are the inheritors. Because of those centuries and the trade relations which after World War II nominally replaced relations of direct political rule over the colonies of Latin America, Africa, Asia and so on, the North Atlantic community is now economically dependent through its trade empires on the oppressive governments in these countries which we sometimes call the south or contemptuously call the Third World, mostly former European or U.S. colonies with Canada, of course, as a sort of minor partner not directly oppressing but engaging in trade relations based on the oppression.
For example, I regret Canada's participation in reneging on the regulation offered to Chinese students who chose to stay in Canada after the Tiananmen massacre. They were promised in a regulation from this government that they would be facilitated in bringing their spouses to join them in Canada. About 200 who made that application while that regulation was in effect have been denied the very thing that the Canadian government promised them. They are told they may have to wait three years now, three more years after these two years, to bring their spouses here. This, I presume, is because of Canada's interest in selling more telecommunications and other goods to China regardless of the fact

I think we can find other things for our people to make because God knows, and I speak advisedly, there is plenty of need among Canadians as consumers if they could get the wages to buy the products that Canadian factories are making. We do not have to sell everything abroad in competition with the United States.
I was embarrassed about six or seven years ago when, following Amnesty International and its information from its London research section, I phoned the High Commissioner of Singapore to complain that a certain member of Parliament of the opposition party had been held for years without charge in prison. I was told it was done according to law. I rashly said: "I think that is a bad law". He said: "That is the law that the British left us".
Now I find when dealing with countries, such as those in Africa that have been mentioned that there is a heritage of oppressive British laws. The law of detention without charge is used in Britain even now against its first and oldest colony, Ireland.
I object strongly to Canada rushing into a treaty with Mexico. This is not just a trade arrangement where we
are going to buy this or sell this. This is to be a permanent treaty with a country which has not recovered from the effects of the Spanish Conquest, the intervention of the United States and other western European or North American countries in recent history. It is struggling to be independent but it is still a dictatorship in many serious ways.
In recent years they have been forcing hundreds of thousands of peasants off their land to replace their subsistence agriculture with cash crops. They are exported to the profit of American multinationals and suit the taste of affluent Americans and Canadians. The peasants are crowding into the slums, lowering the wages, notwithstanding the new factories that are built there. Between 5 million and 10 million children under the age of 15 are obliged to work in those factories by poverty to prevent the starvation of themselves and their families.
Trade unionists and over 100 members of the main opposition party have been murdered with impunity. This is the country with which Canada wants to link not just for trade. Canadian workers will be obliged to compete with workers who are not allowed to have free trade unions. Mexican investors will have national rights in Canada to treat Canadians as they treat their fellow Mexican workers. Refugee claimants, including legitimate claimants in Canada, may be contrary to UN law reform through Mexico to the country from which they fled oppression. There is a deal under way in which Canada will seek to use Mexico as the dumping ground for refugee claimants from Latin America under our so-called safe Third World clause.
Therefore, I strongly urge this House to support the motion as originally presented to discontinue our treaty negotiations with Mexico. We must insist that Mexico first of all carry out the promises which are being violated right to this summer, violated by assassinations with impunity. We first of all must demand that they clean up that act before we place our Canadian workers into direct competition with the intimidated workers of Mexico.

By its own declaration it is underlining what is called the clear link between financial aid and human rights. The member for Burnaby- Kingsway made it clear that it was trying to establish this linkage in the course of his presentation.
But what members of the New Democratic Party and perhaps other members neglect is that there is also an equally clear and strong linkage between foreign aid and the relief of poverty and economic oppression. We also have to consider, in terms of economic aid internationally, not only the status of the nation but the status of the people within that nation.
I will not use that word "hypocrisy", but it might be pointed out that there is a contradiction in the position of New Democratic Party members who constantly focus attention on the plight of individuals, particularly those in a state of poverty, that they should throw this out and simply concentrate on the form of government and the administration of that government in those countries and neglect altogether for the purpose of focusing attention

on those kinds of generic human rights violations the plight of the people in the country.
I have always said that the whole basis of social programs is the economic ability to cany them out. If we reviewed all the nations of the world, it would be found that human rights violations on an individual basis are most evident in countries where there is a bankrupt national Treasury, where the assets of the nation are not being particularly applied.

I believe that the exponents of rhetoric are the members of the New Democratic Party. The purveyors of the reality include the Prime Minister and his government.
Let me take that as the theme of my remarks. If we are going to look for human rights violations across the world, we do not have to look very far. Indeed, as some members have rightly pointed out, we can start with our own country and our treatment of aboriginal people, our own history in the human rights field. We still have a lot of work to do.
Let me hasten to add, if any members of the New Democratic Party are listening, as was said by a civil rights leader in the United States: "I can talk the talk because I walked the walk".
I was involved in Nova Scotia as a legislative draftsman in the formulation of human rights legislation. I was involved as the person who established the legal aid program in Nova Scotia in the direct application of civil rights to individuals in those situations.
When we are talking about the kind of international concerns that exist today, I do not think we really need to look at Canada because all Canadians are the beneficiaries of a very strong human rights tradition, enforced in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Therefore, we are not talking about the kinds of instances which we would regard in Canada as violations of civil
and human rights. We are talking about much more serious situations.
Just the other day while reading the national press, I came across reports of two violations which would shock humanity. One came from the Republic of India, the largest unit within the Commonwealth of nations, where the practice of selling women as child brides is widespread.
The case that was pointed up that caused national and international tension was that of a young 10-year old female person who was apprehended on an international flight to Saudi Arabia. That resulted from virtual bride shopping within the rural villages of India and produced the situation in which a 10-year old girl was sold by her father to a resident of Saudi Arabia. That resident was taking the child back when the apprehension took place and has resulted in international concern being focused on this situation. The point is that it was readily admitted by Indian officials that the practice is widespread. They do not know if it can be stopped because it has roots in so-called religious traditions and other ethnic traditions and is not regarded by many people as being particularly wrong.
If we look at Brazil, there are seven million children on the streets of Brazil with no assistance whatsoever and no programs to deal with the problem from the Government of Brazil. Why? It is because the Government of Brazil does not have the economic ability to solve those kinds of problems.
Therefore anybody who would divorce economics of a country from a human rights situation is automatically going to deal in rhetoric and not in reality. I accuse the members of the New Democratic Party of utilizing that mask to create wrong impressions in this House of Commons and with the people of Canada. The rhetoric starts when you try to separate the economy from the status of the people, in terms of human rights.
We have had a long tradition in Canada of trying to keep open doors with other countries and not close off the opportunity to help those nations improve their situations for the benefit of the people.

Take a little example like Czechoslovakia. I happened to be in Czechoslovakia with a parliamentary delegation at the time the repression was still in force. I was proud to be there because Canada has, over the years, accepted refugees from Czechoslovakia. We have criticized the administration. The member from Toronto was there with me so he remembers all of this.
We gave aid and comfort to the dissidents in Czechoslovakia. We did not say: "Stay away from Czechoslovakia. They are repressing freedoms there". We went to Czechoslovakia. While the problems in Czechoslovakia were never like those in Brazil, India or many of the other countries that we mentioned in this debate, they were nonetheless problems of deprivation of human rights. We did not cut off the relationship. We hung in there with the then dissidents of Czechoslovakia. They are governing the country today.
