The NDP makes it impossible to deal with economic problems in Cape Breton and Nova Scotia and economic problems in northern Ontario, because it always says there is a simple solution, just as it says there is a simple solution to international trade.
"Stop it, stop it, stop it, if there is violation of human rights. Never mind, let the chips fall where they may". It does not work that way, and I cannot believe that given the intelligence and background of all the people in the New Democratic Party there is not somebody in that group who does not realize it. I hope and pray they will come forward.
This leads me to a point I wanted to mention. Those who are really interested in stopping violations of human rights in other nations through the instrument of withdrawal of external aid and trade to that nation should be looking for a competent monitoring body. What one would be looking for is a competent monitoring body, an officer within Canada who would say: Look, there is a
October 22, 1991

situation developing in any nation with which we are trading or are providing external aid that involves human rights violations and we should respond to that. Does anybody mention that?
The Prime Minister of Canada established by statute, by act of this body in 1988, the International Centre for Human Rights and Democratic Development. That centre is charged with the responsibility world-wide of monitoring human rights violations and trying to encourage better human rights practices and so on. We know who heads the centre. It is the Hon. Ed Broadbent who sat right there with those same people.
If members of the New Democratic Party were really concerned with what was happening in a particular place, Iran or whatever, and that we should exercise some influence over that situation as the Government of Canada by threatening to withdraw external aid or minimize trade relations, I would have thought they would call up Ed Broadbent and say: "Ed, get over there and find out what is going on. Bring us back a report. We will present the report to Parliament. It will be documented and every Conservative member and Liberal member will have to respond to the facts as presented".
We cannot respond to this rhetoric. We cannot respond to claims that the ideology of one place is different from ours, and if we want them to adopt our ideology then we have to put this pressure on them. One cannot respond to that kind of situation. One can only respond to facts, and one can only respond to facts that are so blatant and so obvious and so clear that they demand a response. We cannot respond to the practice in India of trading in child brides. We cannot withdraw our relationships with the Republic of India for those kinds of reasons. I think every member knows that.
Mr. Speaker, you say I have two minutes so I want to end on a positive note. I mentioned the monitoring. There are so many other things we could be directing our mind to. As I mentioned, bankrupt national treasuries are often behind human rights violations. Sometimes they do not have an adequate tax system. They do not tax the rich to help the poor in so many apparently deprived nations. We can help with that.
Supply
What we want to talk about is a positive approach. We want to talk about a long-term program. We cannot cut things off immediately if something goes wrong.
A second point beyond the long term is that we have to be concerned with a nation on a broad base. I have already indicated that. We just cannot focus on one item. We have to look at the welfare of the people, as well as at the status of the government. We should look for co-operation of the government and try to obtain it.
A positive approach and a positive foreign program have to have their roots in reality. I hope when I sit down that I will leave the NDP with that message. Let us talk about reality. We are politicians. We recognize rhetoric. Maybe its members do not recognize rhetoric out in the streets of Canada, but they certainly recognize it in this Chamber and should not use it.
As I said, they can take a message from the Prime Minister because the Prime Minister has stated the principle of good governance in relation to international and external aid, good governance within the recipient country. If they have good governance then everything will flow from that, including human rights.
What we have to do and what we have been trying to do is to assist those governments so that there will be good governance in the country, so that there will be a taxation system, an educational system, a health system and a social security system. When we have all those systems in place then, in my belief we have human rights established and we can deal with human rights like we now deal with them in Canada. I do not think too many nations around the world, 160 nations, have reached that plateau and it is our responsibility to help them.
I would like to say one more remark about trade because NDP members would have us think that we can reach out and stop an international nickel company from trading with a foreign nation that violates human rights without affecting workers in northern Ontario. What do they say about that? Would the member for Trinity- Spadina cut off trade and unemploy workers in northern Ontario? Yes, he would. He said: "Why?" It is because the member from British Columbia said we have to stand on principle. My principle is employment for Canadians,

Supply
not cutting them off because of some suspected violation.

Mr. Speaker, I would first like to comment on the remarks of the hon. member. I think they were a bit overzealous in terms of criticism of the NDP, which they always are, and I enjoy his speeches.
I would first say that I congratulate the Prime Minister on the remarks he made as every other member of the caucus does. The Prime Minister stood in Africa and said he was not prepared to provide aid or trade to nations with track records in human rights which do not warrant that. We applauded him. There is no doubt about it. But what we caution and what this motion cautions is that it is only empty rhetoric if there is no action. It is called into serious question along with Canada's credibility if there is not action. This motion proposes action.
It is ironic that the debate has centred on the Mexican trade agreement. We thought that our colleagues in the Liberal Party would support that. It is there and it is prominent. First it is an erosion of Canadian sovereignty, and it clearly is. It is going to compromise the Canadian economy.
An enormous number of Canadians are opposed to it. When we look at the motion to delete, that aspect of the motion, the trade agreement with Mexico is going to harm the economy of Canada. It is going to support a nation with no acceptable policy on the environment, no acceptable social policy, political corruption and extrajudicial execution of hundreds of trade unionists and members of the political opposition. That is what the Liberal motion supports. There is also a lack of any fair labour standards in that country. We are saying as Canadians that is the first and most critical thing facing this nation on the human rights issue and we can do something about it. We can say that we will not go to the table with that nation until its judicial system and its government's commitment to human rights matches this country's or shows significant progress.
The member for Nova Scotia stood up and said that we could not or should not do anything. The United States did something in response to its citizens' concerns. Certainly there are enough citizens' concerns in this country about the performance of the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party that we could start a parallel
process here. We could start a committee here in the House to look at the human rights record of Mexico and make suggestions to them about killing trade unionists and opposition political members. We could do that. We could set up a parallel process with a committee to look at the environment standards, the social policy and the lack of fair labour practices in Mexico.
We are asking for some fairness. I applaud the Prime Minister for his statements but for all our sakes do not make it empty rhetoric. Let us take some action. Let us take the focal point. I plead with the Liberals to withdraw this wrong-headed amendment where they say they are prepared to sit with the government at the Mexican trade talks. This is absolutely wrong. Let us start the parallel process in this House of Commons with our committees the way the Americans did.
Again, my last and parting remark: I applaud the Prime Minister and those statements. Those were worthy statements of which Canadians can be proud but they must be followed by action. Give us some action that we can be proud of.

Mr. Speaker, what is permeating this debate are those two fruitful words advanced by the member from Burnaby at the outset of the debate, that is rhetoric and reality.
I think that anyone who listens to this debate will recognize what is rhetoric and what is reality, because the old bogey of the free trade agreement is being brought before the House of Commons again. It is the ideological position of the New Democratic Party that is divorced from the realities of the world situation, divorced from the realities of trade and divorced from the reality that trade creates employment in Canada and that people in Canada are dependent for employment on selling our products abroad. The members of the New Democratic Party do not want to face up to those hard facts and keep them in mind when they are dealing with their ideological positions. I applaud the Liberal Party. There is some hope that sensible people in this country will get together and try to find sensible solutions to the real problems of our national economy and unemployment. If that involves exploring a trade agreement with Mexico and if that involves exploring, and I underline the words any trading arrangements with any country, then that is what we should do.

If down the line we find out that there are militating factors in relation to human rights, unstable government, and unfair demands then we can make our decision based on those facts, but we do not get the facts unless we examine the situation.
Let me ask the NDP in return: What are the other possibilities to a North American trading bloc? I am from Nova Scotia. They have virtually shut down a segment of our important fishing industry, the sealing, because people in Europe did not think we should be doing such a thing. They thought we should be getting our fur coats in some way other than the destruction of seals. That is how much Europeans care about employment in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. They will just shut it down if it suits their fancy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands - Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the member for Halifax West who has been in the Conservative caucus for several years and knows the Prime Minister well what he expects the Prime Minister's follow-up will be to his declarations at the Commonwealth. In terms of specific concrete actions, what can we expect from the Prime Minister on this?
Specifically could the member share with this House what positions the government has been taking in the opening rounds of the Canada-Mexico-U.S. trade talks with respect to the human rights positions of the Mexican government and the linkage between those two issues at those talks? Could he share, from his perspective, what his government has been doing to advance these causes in this forum?

Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member probably knows well that I am not privy to the negotiations between Canada and Mexico with respect to trade or quite frankly with any other matter. I can tell him that the Prime Minister has underlined time and time again the situation in Mexico.
I think the difference lies in the fact that the Prime Minister sees some hope for improvement through trading relations and the creation of wealth in Mexico. He believes that there is the possibility of substantial improvement in the welfare of the Mexican workers both with respect to day-to-day living and human rights.
Supply
I also offer to the member the fact that over a period of time the Prime Minister has underlined the linkage between aid, trade and human rights. I do not need any better evidence than the establishment of the centre that is now headed by Mr. Broadbent. That is tangible evidence that the Government of Canada under the Prime Minister has funded an organization with a duty and responsibility to monitor human rights legislation, report on it publicly and make recommendations with respect to it.
In relation to the Commonwealth, I think it is well expressed in an article by Ross Howard in Toronto's The Globe and Mail where the comment was made that with the 50-nation bloc all that was achieved was one small Canadian made candle in the dark in relation to human rights. I think the Prime Minister has made it clear that it was not a great impact on the Commonwealth leaders at the conference, but it did make a start. If we thought it was one small candle in the darkness of human rights, the Secretary-General of the Commonwealth said that the statement on human rights was a beacon of guidance on the issue of human rights.
Whatever we think, whatever the NDP thinks of the efforts made by the Prime Minister, they were cast as the beacon of guidance for the future by others.

Mr. Speaker, I too am delighted to stand here in the House today to debate the important motion that is before us. While I support the purpose of this motion to bring before the House the issue of linking government aid to respect for human rights, I cannot support its basic premise which is to discontinue immediately Canadian participation in the Canada-United States-Mexico free trade negotiations. It is for these reasons that I can quite readily support the amendment as put forward by my colleague, the member for Northumberland.
I want to address the issue of linkage shortly. First, I would like to say why Canada should be involved in the negotiations surrounding this North American Free Trade Agreement.
Canadian interests, by putting them forth while we can still make a difference, are of great importance. On a practical note, this means jobs. We must not forget that by being at the table we can also influence other factors such as extending the agreement to include other partners from the hemisphere to create a western hemispheric agreement.

October 22, 1991
Supply
The more partners involved, the better is the counterbalance to the power of the United States, the greater the market potential for Canadian products, and the faster we can help developing countries in this hemisphere create the wealth they need to provide decent lives for their people.
By participating at the table we can lobby to ensure that comprehensive adjustment programs are devised to protect Canadian workers from the possible adverse affects of this deal. We can also ensure the protection of Canada's existing social, cultural and regional development programs.
We can, through involvement in the negotiations, encompass other issues such as the environment. My personal favourite of course is human rights. I would much rather be sitting at the table now than crying over spilt milk later.
With respect to the phrasing of this motion today, we are not talking about aid in this particular case with Mexico. Nor are we talking about investing per se. We are talking about a trade deal and we are talking about participating at a table where negotiations are under way on an agreement that will have a profound effect on Canada, Mexico, the U.S. and indeed the world.
I think this motion, although it does have good elements to be sure, is mixing apples and oranges by insisting upon the withdrawal of Canada from these negotiations.
We can ensure through our participation that environmental standards in each of the countries involved continue to be or in some cases are made to be stringent. There is concern that the inevitable harmonization of environmental standards could bring it all down to the lowest common denominator.
I for one do not want Canada's environmental standards to be brought down to the level which exists in Mexico. Remember, this proposed agreement is still in the stage of negotiations. We can better deal with all of these issues including Mexico's human rights record while at the table. If we are not at the table we cannot have any influence.
One thing that is lacking in making this deal is the open consultation with the Canadian public. We in the Liberal opposition have been calling for such consultation so that the Canadian public could have a say in such a profound deal. This process could and should involve the debate on human rights.
Presently our clout with Mexico is limited in terms of affecting its human rights record through a linkage with aid. Canadian aid to Mexico is limited. We sent close to $2 million through the Industrial Co-operation Program in 1990-91, as well as $350,000 for local initiatives. That is a total of $2.5 million.
Earlier this summer I along with my caucus colleagues sponsored a symposium on international human rights which involved Canada's non-governmental organizations, intellectuals, church and human rights groups.
We had discussions specifically about the linkage of human rights to Canadian aid and trade. These front line people agree in principle with the Prime Minister's recently stated commitment to the tentative linkage in light of documented violations of human rights in various countries. However they believe that the government is not practising what it preaches. The Prime Minister told this House yesterday that his cabinet has been discussing linkage policy since 1987.
We have the government document from the same year called "Sharing Our Future". Yet as the Canadian human rights community points out, human rights records in recipient countries are not reflected in project approval.
Participants at our conference agreed overwhelmingly that there should be uniform criteria for rendering decisions with respect to how and if Canada should provide and conduct trade with certain countries, specifically those with questionable human rights records. That is why I have no trouble at all supporting the amendment of the member for Northumberland. I would like to reread that amendment:
That the government implement procedures which will guarantee coherency, transparency and accountability in relation to human rights considerations in all Canadian foreign affairs policies, including aid, trade and immigration.
It was felt that foreign aid was a tool which could be used in a relevant manner in bettering human rights records in certain countries. Participants at our symposium believe that there is no question that violations of human rights are more severe in developing nations. Governments of these nations are so busy trying to eke
October 22, 1991

out a method of survival that they have little time to worry about basic human rights.
Instead, they must deal with the social unrest caused by abject poverty, the social upheaval caused by policies of the governments of developing countries which as they struggle to improve their trade balance and a desperate effort to improve their balance of payments to international lending institutions multilaterally and donor countries bilaterally have a direct relationship to the massive move toward urbanization which leads to a further burden of populations in urban areas already ill-equipped to handle rampant over-population.
While this is not meant to excuse Mexico or any other government from the mistreatment of any individual or group, it does provide a relative description of the situation in Mexico.
Perhaps, as the symposium participants pointed out, an improved trade balance will have a direct and dramatic effect on Mexico's human rights record.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. I hate to interrupt the hon. member. She will have 12 minutes remaining after Question Period today, plus 10 minutes questions and comments.
It being one o'clock, I do now leave the Chair until two o'clock this day.
At one o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are delighted that their Royal Highnesses the Prince and Princess of Wales will visit Canada.
The monarchy has made a contribution to Canada's distinctness in North America and has played a key role
in stabilizing Canadian society. It should not be neglected in our current constitutional debate.
The Crown has protected Canadians from the expansionary and assimilationist United States and has protected minorities in Canada, a prime example being the Quebec Act of 1774.
The Crown permitted and encouraged the development of representative institutions to serve Canadians whose ancestors have come from all corners of the world and has acted as a court of last appeal for all.
I do not suggest that we return to our past, but I do urge Canadians to appreciate and perhaps be guided by our heritage. For over 200 years, the monarchy has given Canadians common purpose.
Today, as we search to redefine that purpose, we must not forget the legacy and role of the constitutional monarchy.

Mr. Speaker, in my province of Prince Edward Island there is close to
3,000	farming establishments. Almost 25 per cent of those farmers are dairy farmers.
I join with them today in calling on this government to maintain its commitment to supply management in this country. It must not waiver on any of the fundamental aspects of this system. Import restrictions, price adequacy and production discipline must be maintained if our dairy, poultry and egg farmers are to stay in business.
The livelihoods of many farmers depend on this. The welfare of their families is at stake. I dare say, there are many rural communities that would be hard pressed to survive if this government buckles at these GATT negotiations.
We must not trade away one of the most sophisticated marketing systems in the world. We must not diminish a system that has ensured ample quantities of high quality food to Canadian consumers at reasonable prices.
I call on this government to stand up for the farmers of this country.

October 22, 1991

Mr. Speaker, this year's theme for Small Business Week, from October 20 to October 26, is about entrepreneurships as a national resource.
The purpose of Small Business Week is to emphasize the contribution made by small businesses to the economy and give entrepreneurs an opportunity to meet, exchange information and learn how to improve their business management skills.
Owners of small businesses have injected about $64 billion into the Canadian economy in the form of wages and have created two million jobs during the past ten years.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw your attention to the substantial contribution of small business to the economy in the riding of Drummond, where leadership and entrepreneurship are second nature.
Thanks to the involvement, know how, creativity and co-operation of its business community, Drummondville was named Quebec's industrial city of the year by the association of Quebec manufacturers. The purpose of government's Economic Renewal Program is to create a favourable climate for small business, and thanks to the Free Trade Agreement, Canadian entrepreneurs can take advantage of new business opportunities.

Mr. Speaker, Haiti is a country that has just come through decades of oppression under the cruel dictatorship of the Duvali-er families and continues today to experience the cruelties of the vicious Tontons Macoutes and now the illegal government forces.
A year ago Haitians had the privilege of being able to democratically elect their own leader but as we know have just experienced the cruel withdrawal of that leader from power. Canada, with the OAS, has publicly supported the return of the democratically elected President Aristide to power in Haiti. The people of Haiti are
hour by hour, day by day, threatened by the Haitian military. They demand the return of President Aristide. They need our help.
What is Canada is doing today to guarantee the return of President Aristide? Haitians who have been able to clandestinely make contact with the outside world speak of the murder, terror and persecution of those not in power in Haiti. Will this government assure us today that the trade embargoes against Haiti will be increased immediately to pressure a speedy return of Aristide to Haiti and that we will support his return with an international monitoring team.

Mr. Speaker, October 21 to 25 has been designated as National Infection Control Week. The Community and Hospital Infection Control Association, known as CHICA-Canada, in conjunction with local health care facilities and community agencies will be promoting infection control and the role of the infection control practitioner.
A few patients acquire infections as a result of hospitalization. These are known as nosocomial infections, but for those who do become infected there can be a prolonged hospitalization stay and chronic health care problems.
Economically nosocomial infections may cost Canadians as much as $1 billion annually in terms of cost of treatment and loss of work due to a prolonged hospital stay. Many of these infections are preventable.
Throughout this week health care facilities across Canada will again be conducting special Infection Control Week activities to raise our awareness.

Mr. Speaker, the politics of green have caught up with the Government of Alberta and sadly Canada's wildlife is the victim.
Alberta wildlife officers are now under order to kill all wild elk that come in contact with elk held at tuberculosis stricken game farms across the province. This bizarre shoot-to-kill policy is supposed to halt the flow of TB
October 22, 1991

from the game farms into the wild populations. What a policy. Protect the sick by killing the healthy.
The image of Alberta government sharpshooters surrounding the 26 quarantined Alberta game farms to slaughter Canada's proud wild elk population is truly sickening. Warnings of the spread of disease from the penned elk have been on the desks of federal and provincial ministers for many months. Who knows whether tuberculosis or other domestic diseases have not already been transmitted from the disease ridden stock under quarantine? In the greedy rush for the big bucks the Getty government has placed at risk elk and other ungulates of western Canada.
What's next? The slaughter of the elk in Banff and other national parks to protect the profits of a handful of greedy breeders raising wild animals for slaughter and body parts?

Mr. Speaker, an advertisement in the New York Times describes Quebec as the worst possible place for aboriginal people on the North American continent. In response to those lies, I have some statistics from Statistics Canada. Indians are over-represented in the prison population across Canada, except in Quebec, where they are underrepresented. Quebec has fewer Indian families living below the poverty line, and the gap between aboriginal people and the rest of the population is smaller in Quebec. Ninety-one per cent of aboriginal people in Quebec speak their own language, while in Ontario only 50 per cent do so. Quebec also has the lowest suicide rate among aboriginal people. In Quebec, the number of homes without central heating, among aboriginal people, is much lower than in the rest of Canada. Canadian politicians should stop this hypocrisy, and aboriginal leaders should tell the truth instead of letting themselves be used by the federalists against Quebec.
Let us hope that the new government in Saskatchewan will be able to improve the situation of aboriginal people in a province that was headed by an NDP government for
a long time and that has the sad distinction of having the worst record for the way it treats aboriginal people.

Mr. Speaker, like the member for Oxford, I am pleased to inform members that this week, October 21 to 25, has been dedicated National Infection Control Week in recognition of the many health care workers who have worked to assure the application of effective infection control measures to prevent the transmission of infectious diseases in health care agencies and community-based institutions.
The purpose of this week is to focus public and professional attention on the seriousness of hospital acquired and community infections and on the measures that can be taken to reduce them.
I am particularly proud to applaud the efforts of the Community and Hospital Infection Control Association for their efforts in sponsoring and organizing this week across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, economic union has proved beneficial for Canadians, but we should not take it for granted. We cannot maintain or improve our situation by marking time while the rest of the world marches on. We must constantly work on developing our prosperity by improving our competitive position on international markets.
If we achieve our ultimate goal, which is to reduce the national debt, we will contribute to our future prosperity. However, every level of government and every sector of our economy can and must do more to meet the challenges that will face us in the future.
No more status quo. We must make a concerted effort to ensure that our economic union leads to productive growth and creates jobs.
Mr. Speaker, we must reduce barriers to the exchange of goods, services, people and capital within this country. We must eliminate overlap and duplication in government services, so as to provide for maximum efficiency and effectiveness.

October 22, 1991
Mr. Speaker, these are major challenges that cannot be met without the participation of each and everyone of us.

Mr. Speaker, the minister of immigration announced on October 4, 1991 that the refugee backlog clearance program would be completed by December 1992 and within "its original budget of $179 million". There are at least two things wrong with this announcement.
First, when announced in December 1988 the deadline for completing the backlog was September 1991. Now we are told by the present minister that this date has not been met and that in fact cases within the backlog and in particular in Ontario, where most cases are, will not be completed until December 1992. This is a difference of 15 months.
This may not seem like a long time for the minister but for the tens of thousands of refugee claimants trapped in the backlog it is like a decade.
Tune in tomorrow when I will discuss the second major error.

Mr. Speaker, this government recently distributed to all Canadian households a brochure entitled "A Personal Message to All Canadians-An Invitation to Help Build A new Canada".
Several days later, on the floor of the House of Commons, the hon. member for Shefford criticized this message and launched some cheap shots at the principal originators of this important document, the Prime Minister and the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs, the Hon. Joe Clark.
A Granby daily, La voix de I'Est, in an editorial under the headline "Joe Clark was right, whatever Jean La-pierre says", said that Mr. Clark was to be commended for his message to Canadians and especially to Quebecers.
Subsequently, editorial writer Valere Audy, who has known Mr. Lapierre for some time, severely criticized the attitude taken by the hon. member for Shefford. Mr. Audy writes: "The M.P. for Shefford can keep this up if he wishes, but except for a few people who are prepared to laugh at his jokes, his audience is dwindling rapidly. In other words, Mr. Lapierre, when you make fun of others, there comes a time when the joke is on you!"

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my sad duty to inform the House today that Dominion Textile's Fiberworld plant, located in Hawkesbury, in my riding, has closed its doors. Mr. Speaker, 86 hard-working constituents will swell the overflowing ranks of job seekers.
Two years ago, imported carpets accounted for only 10 per cent of our market; today this share has risen to 35 per cent. Fiberworld is thus unable to compete with the Americans. Our Canadian dollar, which was worth 75 cents U.S. less than two years ago, now trades at 88.7 cents. Fiberworld is no longer competitive with its American counterpart. The most outrageous part is that Canada will now import carpet canvas from an American subsidiary of Dominion Textile called Waynetex. The government must devalue our overvalued currency. I also reiterate the appeal for the federal government to set up an economic development program for eastern Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to draw to the attention of the House the dismal condition of our country's mining industry. In many communities all across Canada mines have been closed, workers have been laid off, and entire towns and surrounding areas have suffered. We all recognize there is a life cycle to a mine. But many jobs in communities can be saved by positive action.
I call upon the government to establish a national mining reserve fund, a special fund created by a percentage of mining revenue. This fund would be used to assist mining communities prior to any possible closure. Mo-
October 22, 1991

neys obtained could be used to further exploration that may uncover new resources which would extend the life of a mining operation. The fund could also be used to build infrastructure that would attract businesses to mining communities, and money could be used to help laid off workers.
A national mining reserve fund would be an ideal vehicle to provide more stability for mining companies, mining communities and miners. The ad hoc approach of the past must be replaced. The federal government needs to be involved in an ongoing process to assist mining in Canada and to provide more security for those living in mining communities.

subtopic: NATIONAL HOMEMAKER AND HOME SUPPORT WORKER WEEK
NATIONAL HOMEMAKER AND HOME SUPPORT WORKER WEEK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, October 20 to 27 National Homemaker and Home Support Worker Week will be celebrated across the country. This will be a time to recognize the outstanding work done by home support agencies. Congratulations to our government for supporting Home Support Canada, the organization representing such agencies.
Home care helps people to remain independent and allows them to receive any necessary care in their own homes. Continued support funds research into such significant areas as services to persons with AIDS and persons with Alzheimer's.
Home care provides a multitude of invaluable services such as snow shovelling, meal preparation and child care. So let us take the week to commend the homemakers in our communities for their important contributions.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. The name of the Prime Minister is now on an official list of names under consideration by the Security Council for the job of Secretary-General of the United Nations.

Hear, hear.
Oral Questions

I can understand some Tories being very happy about that. But this has very serious implications for the Prime Minister and his government and for the international reputation of Canada.
Canadians have the right to know this: Does the Prime Minister want to be Secretary-General of the United Nations? If not-
I do have to remind the hon. Leader of the Official Opposition, who is a very experienced parliamentarian, that that seems to me a personal question and I think it is out of order.
It is a serious question and we want to know-
I did not suggest it was not a serious one. I think it is a personal one and I think it is out of order.
We want to know why, if he does not want to be the Secretary-General of the United Nations, the Prime Minister let his name be put on such a list.

Mr. Speaker, I did not put my name on any list, but I would tell my hon. friend that he should not lose any sleep over this.
The thing that I look forward to perhaps most in the world is meeting him in an election campaign in 1993.
Hear, hear.
Mr. Speaker, I have to tell the Prime Minister that I am delighted. There are millions of Canadians who are disappointed because he is not leaving. One Canadian is very happy, and that is me.
Hear, hear.
I was afraid he would chicken out and I am happy that he did not. Now we can come back and ask the Prime Minister this, if he does not intend to go there.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, does the Prime Minister subscribe to the proposition of his finance minister, who said yesterday that 1.5 million unemployed was the normal level in Canada and that he could do nothing to change the situation. Now that the Prime Minister says that he

October 22, 1991
Oral Questions
wants to take care of problems in Canada, instead of going around the world distributing his C.V. to everyone, will he soon present policies to put people back to work in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not say that the Government of Canada could do nothing.
The Government of Canada is doing everything to get Canada's economic and fiscal house in order. The fundamentals are right. Every think tank and objective organization in Canada and throughout the world recognizes that we are on the right track in containing inflation, bringing inflation down, regulating inflationary expectations, bringing about price stability and bringing about durable growth.
I think even the hon. Leader of the Opposition recognizes that there is restructuring and adjustment that must take place in the Canadian economy. That will provide a little more lead time in terms of being translated into jobs.
The fact of the matter is we should accept these serious challenges as a challenge. It is going to require not only governments, but it is going to require business, labour and everyone working together in co-operation to improve our competitiveness and our productivity so that we can take advantage of the opportunities in a globalized world.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can see that the members on the other side are disappointed that the Prime Minister is not leaving-
Oh, oh.

-and disappointed too by the answer of the Minister of Finance.
The minister is asking for more time. We have been in a recession for almost two years. It is the longest recession we ever had in Canada.
We want to know from him when he will do the right thing and put the workers of Canada back into jobs so that there will be money for the fishermen and the
farmers in Canada. We are fed up with hearing statistics that mean nothing for them.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statements of the hon. Leader of the Opposition are categorically false.
This has not been the longest recession. As a matter of fact, the recession which he was very familiar with lasted 16 months. This one lasted 12 months. We have recovered one quarter earlier than that which was expected.
Interest rates are down. They are the lowest they have been in 13 years. They are continuing to go down and not go up. Inflation is going down and not going up. We have one of the lowest inflation fates on record. Unemployment is going down. It is not going up. The trade balance is going up. It is not going down. All the indicators are pointed in the right direction and that will be translated into jobs.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
Canada's prolonged unemployment crisis, a crisis the Minister of Finance acknowledges, is having a catastrophic effect on young Canadians. Canada's youth has to live with the harsh reality of a national unemployment rate of 17 per cent and in some regions of 25 per cent.
What immediate action will the minister take to solve this extremely serious crisis facing young Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, young Canadians are looking at their future and their current situation and are asking their governments at all levels not to do as the previous government did and tiy to throw money at a problem by bankrupting the country. That is what the youth are saying.
We have in place under the Canadian Jobs Strategy initiatives throughout Canada that require cash disbursements by our department of over $3 billion a year.
If the hon. member is not aware of the multitude of programs in place in every province, I would be more than pleased to give him time after Question Period and brief him.
October 22, 1991

Mr. Speaker, a supplementary to the same minister.
I gather from the minister's response that 17 per cent youth unemployment is indeed part of the jobs, jobs, jobs strategy he is talking about.
At a time when this government is talking about prosperity through competitiveness and while our global competitors are busy training, educating and offering employment opportunities for their youth, can Canada as a nation really afford to have 400,000 young people standing in the unemployment lines of this nation? Is this the new way to global competitiveness?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it takes some gall for a Liberal to stand up in this House and complain about the youth and about unemployed Canadians being out there without help. We tried to pass Bill C-21 and I remember the Grits opposing that bill, where we activated $800 million more to train Canadians in order to be ready for the global economy that he does not understand.
Mr. Speaker-
Hear, hear.
Mr. Speaker, that spontaneous outburst from my caucus obviously was out of respect for the premier elect of Saskatchewan, Mr. Romanow. We are happy to see that.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
The government continues to talk about economic recovery and by the government's standards, perhaps it is a recovery. But hundreds of thousands of Canadians who have no work do not see this recovery. We have thousands of farmers who are no longer farming. Thousands of fishermen are no longer fishing. Factories lay idle and empty while unemployment and welfare offices are full.
Today we hear that the finance minister has said that it will be two years before he can see these people back working.
I want to ask the Prime Minister if it is this government's policy to do nothing for the 1.5 million unemployed in this country, and say that there is a recovery. There is no recovery. There is just more unemployment.
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just to advise the hon. member, last month 65,000 new jobs were created and the unemployment rate went down, from 10.6 per cent to 10.2 per cent. I think that is going in the right direction.
The Gross Domestic Product is increasing. Housing starts are on the increase. As I said, the key to job creation is bringing interest rates down. Interest rates have come down by well over 500 basis points, or 5.5 percentage points. That is creating and stimulating new investment and new opportunities for job creation. I might say that interest rate is the lowest rate in 13 years. Inflation is going down and prices are coming down, which adds to our ability to compete more effectively internationally.
The merchandise trade balance is up. Housing starts are up. Business confidence is up. As I indicated to other hon. members, there is a certain degree of lag time before that is translated into jobs.

I wish to ask a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. A million and a half people are jobless and that is reality for many Canadians. Often children live in poverty because their parents lack work. When the Minister of Finance is faced with this reality, he says that he can do nothing for two years because price stability must be maintained. I want to reassure the Prime Minister that price stability will be maintained. His fiscal policies have knocked consumers out. Will the Prime Minister finnally tell his minister to implement a job creation program?

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance already indicated that nearly 75,000 new jobs were created, that interest rates were going down, that inflation was down and that everything was in place for quite a solid, lasting economic recovery. The real gross domestic product increased 0.2 per cent in July, the real production of goods increased, the volume of exports rose 3.5 per cent in July, housing starts jumped 6.9 per cent in September,
75,000	new jobs were created since the recovery began, including 37,000 in the manufacturing sector alone, and

October 22, 1991
Oral Questions
unemployment fell 0.4 per cent in a month. Although it is not a miracle, I think that the Leader of the New Democratic Party should admit that the policies advocated and pursued by the Minister of Finance are in the national interest and producing real gains for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Prime Minister.
Clearly what is happening with the fiscal policies of this government is that we are continuing to see more people unemployed. We had a debate two weeks ago on the prices in the farming industry. Everywhere you look, people are seeking jobs. That is the criteria this government should be looking at.
The Atlantic premiers are meeting because they have been told that they can expect $160 million less in transfer payments. As the Prime Minister well knows, that reduction would have a devastating effect on the people of the Atlantic who have suffered very badly from the decline in the fisheries and other economic factors primarily created by this government.
In the past, the federal government has had a supplementary expenditure for transfer payments. I want to ask the Prime Minister, if the premiers of the Atlantic provinces request this, in order to address the very serious problems they have, will his government consider their request.
Just a moment. That is a completely hypothetical question. The minister may want to deal with it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to advise the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party that there is nothing unusual here. The equalization program is enshrined in legislation and there is a formula that is enshrined within that legislation. These adjustments occur at least two times a year. This normal adjustment process has occurred over the last number of years. As a matter of fact, in the last two years there have been incremental increases as a result of the new economic and financial data coming in.
Is the hon. member suggesting that we should readjust the figures and contravene the legislation? If that were
to happen, then the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, which under this review are going to get more money, would be getting less money.
I think what the hon. member has to recognize is that we are governed here by a legislative measure. I should advise her as well that the issue of equalization and the whole issue of fiscal transfers is under review by the federal and provincial governments. If there are any inconsistencies or problems with the existing program, we will review that and hopefully provide the necessary corrective action in the next bit of legislative that will come down the pipe.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister of Canada and it is in regard to the future of de Havilland.
Given that the European consortium will not pursue majority ownership any longer, and that without a new arrangement Boeing can possibly close and wind down its operations in Downsview, when will the federal government, rather than passing the buck continuously to the provincial government, act in the national interest and commit itself strongly and immediately to saving the thousands of jobs at stake at de Havilland, which only happens to be the leading aerospace manufacturer in our country and the single largest industrial employer in all of metropolitan Toronto.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are very much aware of the position of de Havilland and its importance to the economy of metropolitan Toronto, of Ontario and indeed of all of Canada.
We have been working with the province of Ontario, with the Boeing company and with ANA. We have made representations to the European Community. We have been very much involved in trying to find ways to allow this company to continue in a successful way.
I would caution the hon. member from drawing too hard and fast conclusions from things that he reads in the media. These discussions are continuing and I would hope would have some successful conclusion.

Mr. Speaker, Canadian taxpayers have invested nearly $1 billion in the Augmenter and STOL wing technologies, making de Havilland the world leader.
However, in the United States Lockheed needs this technology in order to rebuild its C-130 Hercules aircraft and Boeing needs this technology in order to build military transports.
Will the minister tell us what guarantees he has that these technologies will not be stolen from Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has asked a fairly complex question. If he had given me notice I would be able to give him a specific answer. But if he wants to provide me with the information that is behind that question I would be happy to get him a specific answer.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Yesterday in the House the Prime Minister seemed personally touched by the case of the Iranian woman who was being held under house arrest by his government following her torture in Iran.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether, having had a chance to review the case, he is now willing to personally take up her case and ensure that she and her family will not be sent back to Iran where she faces torture and her family faces a threat to life and limb?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, without at all commenting on the premise of the hon. member's question, which I really ask myself what the purpose of it is, I can advise the House that, as I indicated yesterday I have completed my review of this case and all the aspects of it.
Some information which was not before the Refugee Determination Board having been brought to my attention I have, following representations on the part of colleagues and members of this House, indicated and directed to officials of my department to process this family for admission to Canada.

Hear, hear.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I for one am very happy that this happened and I am sorry that the issue had to be brought up on the floor of the House of Commons.
I for one, Mr. Speaker, personally intervened with the minister last week to bring to his attention the new information.
I want to ask my question now of the Prime Minister. Given that this particular case has been resolved in a positive way, and for that I thank the government, will the Prime Minister advise the Immigration Appeal Board that in future similar cases involving flogging will be dealt with in a positive manner so that no other woman will face the possibility that this woman faced?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I noted and took care to note that the decision that I have made to process this family for admission to Canada is based on information I have received.
The immigration refugee board, to which the hon. member refers, is an independent board set up by this Parliament. It operates without political intervention. Surely she is not suggesting that this minister or this government intervene in an independent process.
As for her larger issue, I do not think that it would be proper for me at this time to speculate on decisions which the board has to make. If the Liberal Party wants to suggest an amendment to the Immigration Act on the definition of what is a convention refugee let them do that.

Mr. Speaker, we too welcome the decision of the minister on humanitarian grounds to allow this family to remain in Canada.
I want to ask a question of the Prime Minister which touches directly, however, on the situation of human rights in Iran. Yesterday when I asked the Prime Minister about the extension of a $1 billion line of credit to Iran, the Prime Minister said that his human rights policy only applied to the extension of aid.
I want to remind the Prime Minister that the former Secretary of State for External Affairs, now the Minister for Constitutional Affairs, said in a letter last year: "The Export Development Corporation takes direction from the Government of Canada on matters relating to

October 22, 1991
Oral Questions
human rights abuses. The government can direct the EDC not to support exports to a certain country because of that country's human rights record".
In view of the clear contradiction between the Prime Minister's statement yesterday and the minister's letter, I want to ask the Prime Minister if he stands by the earlier assurance that the EDC will take direction on human rights and, if so, will this government stop this $1 billion line of credit to Iran, a country which flogs, tortures, detains, and executes its own citizens.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to draw a distinction for the hon. member between aid and EDC credit. EDC credit is made on commercial terms in the case of the arrangements with Iran. It is not aid. In no way is it considered to be aid.
We have on a number of occasions expressed our concerns to the Iranian authorities about their treatment of individuals. I did it personally when I was in Iran about a month ago. The Secretary of State for External Affairs did it when the deputy foreign minister for Iran was here earlier this year. This concern is something we have kept in front of the authorities in Iran and we will continue to do so.

Mr. Speaker, the minister states that these considerations are based solely on commercial factors, yet his colleague the former Secretary of State for External Affairs said that human rights considerations should be a part of EDC financing.

My supplementary question is for the Prime Minister. For 30 years, the American government has imposed a total embargo on Cuba, including food and medicine. At this session of the United Nations General Assembly, many countries will propose the elimination of this destructive embargo.
Given the policies of the Canadian government, which never imposed such an embargo and which supports the admission of Cuba to the OAS, will Canada support a resolution asking the United States to lift this embargo against Cuba?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is not a specific question to which I can give a precise answer, but I believe the position of the Government of Canada in dealing with Cuba has been quite clear. In dealing with Cuba, we have taken a different position from that of the United States in our relationships with Cuba and I think that the concerns that have been expressed by the hon. member have been reflected in the policies carried out by the Government of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the four premiers from the Atlantic provinces are meeting on Wednesday to discuss an attack by this government on the equalization payments to the four Atlantic provinces. They are not meeting, as the Minister of Finance would have us believe, to have a tea party.
Does the Minister of Finance realize that the equalization payments to the three maritime provinces for this year are practically the same as they were last year, according to his department, and the equalization payments to the province of Newfoundland are actually less this year than they were last year.
How can this government be so cruel as to now suggest a further $116 million cut? Why this Atlantic attack?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all may I advise the hon. member that equalization payments are not being slashed. They are being increased by $250 million to $8.3 billion. Unless the hon. member wants me to unilaterally change the formula, there is nothing I can do about it. This formula is enshrined in legislation. It is implemented on the basis of financial and economic data that flows in and these adjustments are made on a regular basis.

Mr. Speaker, the utilization payments to the four Atlantic provinces are being cut. Not only are they being cut, but the Atlantic provinces have been asked, and they are doing it, to pay back equalization money that they
October 22, 1991

received years ago because of an audit done by the Department of Finance in March 1990.
I ask the Minister of Finance: How can the government of Canada forgive loans to foreign banks and to foreign countries while demanding money back in equalization payments from the four Atlantic provinces? Why this double whammy to eastern Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1988-89 when this same adjustment was implemented, the adjustment ended up in an additional $1 billion directed to the provinces from the federal government. Does the hon. member want us to cancel that too?
For 1989-90, after the review was taken, as a result of the regular review based upon the formula and using the financial and economic data that flows in, there was an increase of $720 million. Does he want me to collect that back from the provinces?
You cannot have your cake and eat it. A formula is in place and it has to be honoured.

Mr. Speaker, my question concerns the fisheries aid package and it is for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans who yesterday accused members of Parliament of rumour-mongering that the package was inadequate.
Since that statement, I have received over 100 telephone calls in my offices from people who are very angry and very distressed by that statement. They are reaffirming that there is not enough money, there are not enough programs and the ones that are there are coming on stream too late to be worth while.
I am going to ask the minister again to consult with his job creation colleague and tell us why he cannot put more teeth in this program.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, all I can do is repeat to this House and to hon. members that we have in this program sufficient funds for the volume of people who have been identified. Assessments however, and this may explain perhaps his number of phone calls, are
Oral Questions
taking longer than we expected given the numbers involved. That is a reality out there.
We have begun the job of identifying specific amounts of money and negotiating contracts. This is being done as we speak. As the minister said yesterday, all people who qualify will be able to take advantage of that special program.

Mr. Speaker, the minister is not listening. If you boil that $57 million package down, it works out to somewhere in the vicinity of $25 million for job creation. That is for 10,000 people. The Fishermens Union suggested $100 million might be more appropriate. In the minister's own figures that works out to $2,500 per person.
The minister may consider that as more than adequate. He may even consider it generous, as he said yesterday. Certainly the Newfoundlanders and the Atlantic Canadians who are receiving at that end do not consider it adequate, neither do I nor my colleagues. It simply is not good enough.
I want to ask the minister one more time: When will he get serious and come clean with Newfoundlanders and tell them how he is going to provide a reasonable solution to this devastating and demoralizing problem?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are not Liberals, we cannot predict the future. However, it is estimated that 4,300 fishermen and 6,000 plant workers have been unable to acquire sufficient weeks of insured earnings to qualify for UI. It is this money that the hon. member refers to which will create some 45,600 job weeks of work for those people.
Maybe we could raise taxes and or increase the deficit to give more, but I think that this package will help the fishermen in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the right hon. Prime Minister.
President Bush has now recommended to Congress that the largest unspoiled wilderness in the United States be opened for the development of gas and oil. These lands are known as the Arctic National Wildlife

October 22, 1991
Oral Questions
Refuge. Since the drilling would take place in Alaska on the coastal calving grounds of the porcupine caribou herd, a decision posing a direct threat to the 200,000 caribou that spend most of their life cycle in Canada, will the Prime Minister contact President Bush and express the deeply-held Canadian view that we support wilderness designation for the 1002 lands.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this issue has been ongoing for a certain number of years. In fact, the Government of Canada has been making representations to different representatives in the United States Congress and with the administration on this issue. In fact, we have been working in close co-operation with the governments of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories and with native people on this issue.
Last week, no later than Thursday, there was some positive developments when the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee I understand voted 12 to 4 in favour of designating that area as an Arctic national wildlife refuge, as a wilderness. That is a positive development. We intend to pursue this issue very vigorously.

Mr. Speaker, the more important vote on this issue is going to take place on the floor of the whole Senate later this week, and even the members of the Senate there are encouraging Canada's Prime Minister to get in touch with President Bush if Canada is serious about drilling not proceeding on the 1002 lands.
I will direct my supplementary to the Minister of the Environment. Earlier today the all-party Standing Committee on Environment passed a resolution calling on the Prime Minister to call President Bush. All parties in this House for many years have unanimously held the view that there should be wilderness designation for the 1002 lands.
Since the minister has offered to lead an all-party delegation to Washington to talk to the Congress in the next short period of time about this, will the Minister of the Environment at least rise today and call upon his Prime Minister to call President Bush as this is a key executive decision-making ingredient to protect Canada's porcupine caribou herd?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada has made a series of representations on this very important issue to
the American government at the executive level. No later than the week of September 16, for example, our embassy in Washington was instrumental in putting together a lobbying effort on this very specific issue. We have been very active at every level and we intend to pursue this issue, to be very vigilant, and to do anything in our power to ensure that this area be designated a wilderness area.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. For several months, Via executives in their ivory tower in Montreal have been trying everything to abolish rail service in Abitibi and Champlain, with the complicity of CN President Ron Lawless.
Is the Minister of Transport prepared to make a decision this year on the future of rail services in remote regions, including Senneterre and Amos in Abitibi and Parent in Champlain County?

Mr. Speaker, it is quite obvious that both the President of Via and the Minister of Transport are concerned about this issue of rail services to remote regions. We are concluding a study on the costs of maintaining these centres and should be able to make a decision in a few weeks.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Yesterday, the Canadian dollar reached 88.77 cents, its highest level in 13 years. Since every cent increase in the value of the dollar costs nearly $1.3 billion in exports, can the minister tell us why he is pursuing policies that are disastrous for the Canadian economy and guarantee very high unemployment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated in the House before, the Government of Canada does not have a set target for the value of the dollar, nor does it have a range, nor does the Bank of Canada have a range
October 22, 1991

or target for the valuation of the dollar. It is essentially set in the marketplace, and based upon a whole number of factors, including the capital flows, the need for capital, the need for capital to invest in meeting fiscal deficits, with respect also to inflation and the economic fortunes.
I should indicate to the hon. member that notwithstanding the value of the dollar which he suggests is too high, the trade figures indicate that Canadian companies are competing. Our merchandise trade balance is increasing, particularly our trade balance with the United States, which again demonstrates the effectiveness of the free trade agreement.
As was pointed out in The Financial Post this morning, Canada cannot devalue its way to prosperity.

Mr. Speaker, a supplementary to the same minister.
The government has added to the problem of high unemployment in the forestry sector with its high dollar policy. In that sector every one cent increase in the dollar translates into a loss of $100 million in exports.
What new and specific measures will the minister implement to assist the forestry sector in regaining its competitive edge and when can the forestry sector expect relief from this devastating high dollar policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is true that there are very serious competitive pressures in the marketplace, not only from the current value of the dollar.
I remind the hon. member that for the last 40 years, the average value of the Canadian dollar vis-a-vis the American dollar was 92.6 cents. So, in historical terms it is not high. I know that it is high relative to recent trends, but the fact of the matter is that the value of the dollar does reflect a certain strength and stability in the Canadian economy and it provides the way in which we can continue to get the fundamentals right, that is bringing inflationary pressures down, bringing interest rates down. That will increase the opportunity to compete more effectively, bring down the cost of living and bring down prices.
Oral Questions POVERTY

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
The Canada Assistance Plan was established over two decades ago by a Liberal government to help Canada's poor maintain an adequate standard of living. Parliament defined "adequate" to mean that all Canadians should have food, shelter and clothing.
Given the number of Canadians who go to food banks every day, how does this minister define adequate for these people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to say that what we do in terms of the Canada Assistance Plan is done with the provinces and in conjunction with the capacity that the provinces have to put money in the system. If my friend would would like me to say that we are ready to put in $1 billion, $2 billion or $3 billion more, I have to say that we do not have those resources.
As the Minister of Finance has said, we are trying to improve the economy to have the capacity to put in more and more.
I would say that if we can do more for poor people and for those in need in terms of services, we will do it. The member will agree that the resources have to be there. Maybe his party created the plan, but it created the deficit and the debt that came with the plan.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Prime Minister.
Yesterday, several colleagues stood up and asked questions about food banks across this country. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance are fond of responding that national economic policies are helping Canada's poor. In Winnipeg we now have 36,000 people looking for jobs, and several thousand aboriginal youth who can no longer find jobs or training. We have thousands of people using the food banks to the point

October 22, 1991
Oral Questions
where they are no longer able to feed people each month. These macro policies are not working.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister what specific plans he can present to the people of Winnipeg to help provide for them in the future.
This government has done nothing but take away things such as the Core Area Initiative and needs federal government intervention.

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what we said yesterday about Montreal and Toronto is true for Winnipeg.
With all the help that foods banks provide, I believe everybody in the House and in the country would like to do without them.
Second, he knows too that in order to be reasonable we have to provide as much as we can to have an economy which will produce jobs and let people work. We were talking about young people before. Now we are talking about everybody in the country.
The first move to deal with that is to give people the capacity to work. As simple as it is, when you work, you do not normally need food banks.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General.
Very seldom in the lives of those of us who have been elected to office do we have an opportunity to correct an injustice of the past. I am putting my question to the minister in that light.
I think the time has come to correct an injustice. Leslie James Bennett was forced to resign as deputy chief of the RCMP, counterespionage section in 1972. He was accused of being a mole for the KGB and has proved to be totally innocent. His pension today is $4,500 a year and he is living in exile in Australia.
Will the minister review the file of Mr. Bennett with a view to a full exoneration and a reinstatement with full pension rights?

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with my hon. friend who makes the point that when we have an opportunity to correct unfortunate cases from the past we should do so.
My hon. friend was good enough to give me notice of his question. I have taken the opportunity to review the file with my staff and I find myself in a position of referring to the answer given to one of my predecessors in this House, the Hon. Francis Fox on November 24, 1977.
"Mr. Bennett left the RCMP on a medical discharge and in spite of rumours to the contrary, he was not paid off and nor ordered to get out of the country." I have nothing more to add at this point.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
I believe the middle income earners have gradually been burdened with an unfair proportion of total personal income taxes. Will the minister be reviewing this problem with the idea of reducing tax rates or perhaps eliminating the surtax which was brought in in 1985 and now generates over $1.5 billion in taxes.
Clearly such a measure could give our sluggish economy a boost and help alleviate the unfair tax burden on middle income Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly appreciate the hon. member's question, but I think that he would be the first to acknowledge the tremendous overhang of debt that Canadians face. The cost of servicing that debt consumes about $43 billion annually and takes 35 cents out of every taxpayer's dollar that we collect. It really restricts our ability to bring about any tax cuts.
What we are endeavouring to do, as the hon. member I know is aware and supportive of, is the ongoing attempt to reduce the deficit, bring our fiscal house in order, bring down interest rates and bring down an inflation rate.
The fact that we have brought interest rates down by over 5 per cent has translated into reductions of payments on a monthly basis on $100,000 mortgage. It
October 22, 1991

reduces monthly payments by roughly $320 per month. I think that is a good break for middle income people.

Mr. Speaker, I have a single question. My question is for the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister on April 6, 1984 in commenting on the then suggested appointment of the Minister of Finance of the day to the OECD as Secretary-General said: "Canadians have had it up to here with the hypocrisy of people who inflict unemployment on Canadians and then go off to cushy jobs".
My question is straightforward. Does the Prime Minister consider being Secretary-General of the United Nations a cushy job?
I do not think that question is in order.

I wish to draw to members' attention the presence in the gallery of a parliamentary delegation from the United Kingdom Branch of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association led by the Hon. Robert Boscawen, M.C., Member of Parliament.
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this debate and to add some thoughts to this whole question of human rights and

Canada's aid policy and to respond to the concerns of the hon. member opposite.
There are few development issues quite as complex or as sensitive as this one. It is an issue for which there are no easy answers, no fast solutions and no quick fixes. It is a matter that at times calls for delicacy and careful diplomacy. At other times more forceful measures are required.
I believe that Canada's policy on human rights and aid reflects a balanced and judicious approach, one that emphasizes progress rather than postering and one that is concerned first of all with helping to promote human rights through the development process.
