speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, our approach emphasizes support for the victims of human rights abuses while maintaining pressure on oppressive governments where required. TTiis means that we do take human rights records into account in determining the nature and size of our aid programs in the developing world.
This does not mean that we automatically terminate assistance to the countries that do not have spotless records. We do not expect miracles. We do look for trends that indicate improving or worsening human rights situations.
It is true that in some cases assistance may be reduced or denied where systematic gross or continuous violations of human rights occur.
We do not think it wise or fair to punish the victims of oppression doubly by withholding much needed development assistance. Instead we look for the best means of delivering our aid to the people who really need it.

Supply
In many cases that means channelling our aid through non-governmental organizations or community and grassroots organizations, through the very groups that work with the poor, the disadvantaged and often with those bearing the full brunt of human rights abuses.
We work through them because very often they are in the best position to ensure that our aid reaches those in need. I could refer to the example just five years ago where, with the toppling of the Marcos regime in the Philippines, there was a re-evaluation of our aid program which up to that point had been delivered by non-governmental organizations. I will have something to say about that shortly.
This seems to me to be a far more reasoned and, I would argue, far more compassionate response. To cut off all aid without looking for alternative means of reaching the poor seems to me to be ill considered, counterproductive and harmful.
There are many ways to reflect this concern for human rights and democracy in our aid program. For example, personnel within the Canadian International Development Agency are trained on human rights issues. Our government has established the International Centre for Human Rights and Democratic Development headed by the Hon. Edward Broadbent to support research and provide guidance on this issue.
Canada has always been a forceful advocate of human rights in the international arena, in the UN, as well as within the Commonwealth and La Francophonie. Canada is continuing to move forward on the issue. We are refining our policy and exploring new avenues that broaden our conception of human rights to encompass the notion of democratic development. We are doing this because we recognize that development, democracy and human rights are closely linked and interdependent.
Development does not depend simply on economic and technical co-operation. It ultimately depends as well on economic and political pluralism, on grassroots participation. In a word it depends on democracy.
Democratic systems with their emphasis on free and open participation in the political and economic life of society and their respect for human rights are clearly best suited to creating an environment where human potential can be developed and put to full and productive
use. For that reason CIDA is continuing to develop its thinking and activities on the theme of democratization and human rights.
Although CIDA's policy essentially remains that defined in the releases Sharing Our Future and To Benefit a Better World, the mechanisms for its implementation are rapidly changing. This enables Canada to maintain its position as a leader in defending human rights and democratic development.
We must show imagination. We must do much more to encourage and help our partners gradually to lay the foundations for a truly democratic society: elements such as an independent judiciary, freedom of the press, opinion and association, the establishment of the rule of law, a multi-party system and so on.
Even so lasting democracy cannot simply be built on a legal or institutional framework. For democracy to flourish and prosper many other elements are needed including a pluralistic and participatory society where a wide variety of organizations, institutions and enterprises are all free to express their views and pursue their interests. There must be a democratic culture that accepts compromise, the free exchange of ideas and the peaceful settlement of political competition.
There must be good governance because the legitimacy of a democratic process depends to a large extent on fair, open, competent and honest public administration.
Finally there must be progress toward economic and social development so that citizens have the means and ability to participate in the civic and political life of their societies.
There is a whole range of constructive activities that can be undertaken to build the foundations for democracy around the world. Let me now turn to some of those activities. Some are very direct, for example providing assistance to electoral processes. In the past two years Canada has been involved in electoral competitions in Namibia, Nicaragua, Benin and Malaysia.
Our association and assistance have taken many forms ranging from the provision of ballot boxes, paper and ink, to providing training for polling officers, electoral observers, jurists and legislators. In the case of Namibia, we sent election observers as well as 100 RCMP officers to
October 22, 1991

help ensure stability during that country's difficult transition to democracy.
Strengthening the institutions of government or international organizations is also important. As I have noted, we have created here in Canada the International Institution for Human Rights and Democratic Development as a new mechanism to further promote human rights and democratic concerns. We have carried this institution strengthening over into the international arena where we have put forward a number of proposals that would build respect for human rights and democracy right into the framework of a number of multilateral institutions.
For example, the Prime Minister recently announced that at the coming November summit of La Francopho-nie, he intended to propose the creation of a secretariat to support democratization within that organization's Agence de co-operation culturelle et technique. Canada has also suggested that a human rights information unit be established within La Francophonie. Similar initiatives are also planned for the Commonwealth and the Organization of American States has adopted Canada's proposal to create a unit for democratic development within its secretariat.
Within our aid program we have made decisions on aid funding that directly reflect our commitment to support the democratic and social stability that makes democracy possible. For example, Canada decided in 1986 to establish a major bilateral program in the Philippines in support of President Aquino's re-establishment of a democratic government in that country. In this case the program was subsequently developed very specifically to include two major components, one focusing on community development and the balance directed to broader economic support for central government needs. Our increased support is a clear sign of our commitment to help the people and the Government of the Philippines as they promote democratic development.
I had the great good fortune to have had a hand in this operation. In May 1986 I led on behalf of the then Secretary of State for External Affairs, who was governor of the Asian Development Bank, our delegation to the annual meeting of that bank. Shortly after I agreed to do so, there was the election of February 1986 in
Supply
which the Marcos regime was defeated and President Aquino succeeded in part through people power. I was asked then by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister for External Relations to extend my visit in the Philippines and visit the areas where our aid was being delivered by non-governmental organizations, the Asissi Foundation and many others.
I spent 10 days travelling the country, visiting Cebu and Negros provinces and had an opportunity to meet not only government leaders, who were the fresh new leaders of democracy, such as Governor Daniel Lacson of Negros Occidental, but also church leaders, community development leaders and co-operative leaders.
Because the co-operative movement in the Philippines is doing very well and is very strong, the Bayawan Fisheries Co-operative in Negros Oriental is succeeding largely due to our efforts. Not only was there economic success but there was also success leading towards democratization and freedom of economic action.
While I am on the topic, I should also mention the great value of mission administered funds which are available at the discretion of our local ambassador. The example that I saw was the remarkable infusion of a very small number of dollars into a convenience store on the edge of Smokey Mountain.
Now Madam Speaker perhaps you have visited Smokey Mountain. It is a heap of garbage as tall as Parliament Hill. There are approximately 6,000 to 10,000 individuals living off that heap of garbage, ferreting around for valuables that can be sold and in some cases searching for discarded food.
Those people are the poorest of the poor in the Philippines. What happened there was that those living in that area had no store to go to not even a convenience store or any grocery store nearby. The nearest one was two or three miles away and it was run by the loan sharks. These poor people were in hock to the loan sharks.
What happened was that our mission administered fund under the direction of our then ambassador, Hon. Russ Davidson, offered something in the way of $150 Canadian in terms of capital to capitalize a convenience store on the edge of Smokey Mountain. That freed not only the people from the loan sharks but freed up a

October 22, 1991
Supply
beginning of a market economy for those very poor people.
I had an opportunity to see some follow-up to the five-point program which I was able to recommend to President Aquino and our government. I saw it consummated when I met the other day with Mr. Robert Dowling, a resident of Alberta and a former minister of tourism in the Alberta provincial government. He was on his way under the auspices of CESO, the Canadian Executive Service Overseas to Negros Occidental to advise Governor Lacson and the government of that province on developing a tourism industry in what is a very, very desirable tourist destination.
You see that our aid projects and programs themselves contribute in a very fundamental way to building the foundations of democracy throughout the developing world.
For example, the programs we support in the field of human resource development are essential parts of our strategy to support human rights and democratic development. Literacy and education are basic to forming the human capabilities that are most crucial to democratic life.
Human resource development, as the sponsor of today's debate knows, is a priority of side's work and programs like these account for a significant portion of Canada's development co-operation. Moreover women in development, another priority of side's work, makes a crucial contribution in this area. The programs Canada supports here help women throughout the Third World develop the personal capacity and the collective means to participate in the economic and political life of their societies.
CIDA has had a women in development policy since 1984. All of its bilateral projects must be evaluated for their impact on women. It also supports a wide range of projects that are especially designed to benefit women whether by providing them with credit to establish private enterprises or through support for groups that defend the most basic rights of women.
For example, we provide support to the Asia-Pacific Forum on Women and the Forum on Women, Law and Development, which is working to promote greater respect for women's rights.
Support for NGOs and community development organizations is also fundamental. Here again Canada is a leader, challenging a larger share of its aid through NGOs than any other major aid agency. NGOs connect individuals to the political process and are often in the front lines in defending citizens against abusive governments.
Just as importantly they serve as schools for democracy, teaching their members the value of free expression, compromise and civic life, all crucial qualities that can be carried over into the wider political arena.
In short they build the foundations for a culture of democracy that allows free and open systems to take root and flourish. Often NGO programming makes a very direct contribution to democratization. CIDA's program in the Philippines is a very good example. The government of that country has made it clear that it views NGOs as an important force for development and for democracy. I think one of the reasons for that is that President Aquino herself had a background in working for NGOs. Its mid-term development plan for 1987 to 1992 set out a policy for what it called "people powered development" which encouraged NGOs to promote the welfare of the nation.
CIDA has responded with a number of programs to help NGOs and co-operatives that are involved in poverty alleviation and community development. One of the goals of this programming has been to reinforce the capabilities of NGOs to influence the Philippine government policy on poverty alleviation issues, as well as providing them with direct input into the planning and orientation of the CIDA program.
Similarly Canadian NGOs are veiy active in the community level throughout Indonesia where they are playing an important role in empowering people to take charge of their lives.
Clearly there are a lot of positive things that the aid program can do to promote democracy, but if we are to encourage greater respect for human rights and democracy we need judgment, patience and understanding. That is why we have opted for a constructive rather than a punitive approach to human rights. We need these qualities because democracies and respect for human rights are not created overnight nor is the path to democracy direct, continuous and free of trouble. We must exercise careful judgment in responding to tenta-
October 22, 1991

tive initiatives or setbacks for democracy. To act hastily and terminate aid may simply nip democracy in the bud.
We must recognize that many factors go into creating and nurturing democracy. If development is essential for democracy, and I believe it is, then we must expect that the state of democracy throughout the developing world will to some extent reflect the differing levels of social and economic progress.
If we do not take these factors into account we may end up punishing the poor and therefore less open countries in favour of the wealthier nations. This in effect would amount to punishing those who are already the worst off.
Moreover we must always remember that our system of democracy is not perfect and may not be suitable for every society. Our democracies are not perfect nor are they the final immutable product of all human striving. We must therefore be prepared to accept that other countries will adopt other systems of democratic rule that reflect very much their own history and culture. We cannot impose carbon copies of our systems on to other societies.
It will require patience, understanding and careful nurturing if democracy is to take root throughout the world. Nonetheless I believe that however bleak the situation is in many countries the prospects for democracy have never been better. A vast wave of democracy is surging around the world sweeping aside decades old military regimes and one-party states. In its wake are a host of fledgling democracies and literally thousands of popular organizations that together give expression to a collective desire for greater freedom and self-reliance.
Canada is supporting that movement, but we are not doing it through empty gestures or moralistic and indulgent rhetoric. We are supporting democracy and human rights through a balanced and pragmatic mix of programs, policies and diplomacy. Our approach places a premium on helping those who need help the most. It is a positive and a practical approach and in an imperfect world the one that works best of all.
Years from now the 1990s may well be recorded by future historians as the decade of democratization. We can help in this process but only by making hard choices and difficult decisions. Our government is making those decisions. I believe that if Canada continues along its
Supply
present course, future generations of Canadians will be able to look back with pride on the record of this government and this country and our collective contribution to human rights and democracy.

Madam Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to this debate and I have followed the Prime Minister's remarks, particularly those made in the context of the Commonwealth.
I wonder whether the Prime Minister took the opportunity to discuss human rights on a broader basis rather than just simply linking it to development with other members of the Commonwealth, particularly with countries like India where there is a widespread abuse of human rights in the Punjab.
Amnesty International has said in a report that serious human rights violations in the Punjab have persisted under three governments. They have set the stage for the widespread abuse by passing the grossly unfair 1987 Terrorist and Disruptive Activities Act and letting extreme violations like torture and killings go unpunished. Suspected government opponents are routinely tortured in police stations and detention centres. Hundreds of Sikhs are killed in fake shoot-outs staged by police called "encounters". Well over 10,000 Sikhs are being held in the state without any chance of getting a trial under laws which members of the UN Human Rights Committee recently called disturbing and completely unacceptable.
Amnesty International said people are often picked up by police, tortured or disappear on the slightest suspicion that they have ties with the armed Sikh secessionist groups.
The New Democratic Party and I condemn this type of abuse of human rights in the Punjab. We are wondering whether the Prime Minister raised it with the Prime Minister of India at the Commonwealth Conference. I note that the Prime Minister of India was the first member of the Commonwealth to dissociate himself with the linkage of aid and human rights when the Prime Minister raised it.
I would like to ask the member if he feels that the appropriate venue, as I feel it is, for the Prime Minister to raise these matters is the Commonwealth. Does he

October 22, 1991
Supply
not feel that he should have spoken out on all types of violations of human rights, not just linking it to aid?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's question. It is a pertinent question since the Prime Minister has just returned from the Commonwealth Conference.
I do not believe that the Prime Minister confined his observations on human rights to the linkage with aid, nor has he historically over the past seven years. One will find when one examines this country's record in its dealings with South Africa, for example, that it is a very rigorous approach. It has been a graduated approach and only with the movement toward democratization that has occurred recently in South Africa has consideration been given by Commonwealth members, with a great deal of leadership from Canada, to the relaxation of some of the so-called people sanctions.
There are 25 countries in the Commonwealth that have declined to subscribe to a code of human rights behaviour. I do not know if India is one of those.
I listened with care to the comments the hon. member made about the situation in Punjab. I am aware of a number of the situations he describes.
I am afraid I do not know whether the Prime Minister in his bilateral meeting with the Prime Minister of India did discuss these instances, but I will undertake to relay the hon. member's question to the Prime Minister. It may be a question he may wish to put to the Prime Minister on some occasion.
I believe that the Prime Minister sincerely and very profoundly has human rights as a personal cause and that he does not see it within the narrow confines, although the very important confines, of linkage to aid.

Madam Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the member opposite and his speech on aid and trade.
Recently the Prime Minister announced a review of all international support programs to ensure that they meet the aid criteria. It is still unclear to us on this side of the House what exactly the policy of the government is with respect to the linkage question. We in opposition, in fact all Canadians, have been asking for clarification on this point.
At a recent symposium here in Ottawa, NGOs put forth recommendations for a clearly defined criteria in determining aid and trade linkage issues. In other words, coherency. They agreed that there should be transparency in the development of foreign policies so that all Canadians could have input and that the government could be held accountable for its decisions.
I think we are curious, for instance, as to why Canada treats Myanmar, China and Indonesia one way and South Africa and Haiti in another. Those at the symposium expressed repeated frustration over the lack of consistency and transparency with the government in terms of the foreign policy development. They would like the government to live up to its own rhetoric on its behalf. If there is going to be a policy, it has to make sure that the policy is even right across the board.
These NGOs suggested strongly that the government take a holistic approach to its own foreign policy to involve in the process the NGOs.
I know the previous speaker mentioned that there was a good relationship between the NGOs and the government, as well as church organizations and human rights groups. These people wish to be involved and in fact do not believe that they are presently involved to an adequate extent.
They say consultation, consistency and conviction has got to be more prevalent with regard to the government's approach. I guess I would like the previous speaker to respond to whether Canada is isolating itself from some countries as opposed to others, or are we being more free with our policies with some countries? I have mentioned a couple of them with regard to high economic growth.
Take a country like Haiti where we do not seem to be dealing economically. I am wondering if he could comment with regard to the government's appropriate action and a rational approach to developing a foreign policy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the questions of the hon. member opposite.
With regard to coherency, transparency and input from NGOs into our aid policy, I do not think there are any countries that have a better relationship between their aid policy and the formulators thereof under non-governmental organizations.
October 22, 1991

There may be times when the input is not followed to the letter, but consultation is constant. It is thorough and cordial, and it will continue that way.
The hon. member referred to Myanmar and Indonesia as two examples by implication where Canadian aid is continuing in the face of repressive regimes. There is no doubt that the regime in Myanmar is repressive.
Perhaps the hon. member did not hear the Prime Minister's response in Question Period yesterday when he confirmed that the Petro-Canada International Assistance Corporation program in Myanmar has been terminated for the veiy reason of the human rights abuses in that country.
In addition, I did refer in my speech to Indonesia and a number of programs whose purpose is in power and that in itself is, I think, salutary. Indonesia is not nearly as repressive a regime as Myanmar, God forbid. It is not a pluralist party state and the military is intimately involved in the administration of the government.
With reference to Haiti, I believe if the hon. member checks she will find that there are a number of NGO funded programs aided by CIDA within Haiti. A number of them are properly targeted.
I take her point about a holistic approach and I believe that that is exactly the kind of approach that is being followed.

Madam Speaker, the motion proposed by our colleague from the New Democratic Party would have Canada terminate immediately its assistance to some countries which are listed in the resolution.
I have a copy only of a draft resolution in front of me and I think that draft perhaps indicates the difficulty in this type of approach to foreign aid and trade. More specifically, the listing that was proposed by our colleagues from the New Democratic Party have been changed.
They cited among the other countries Gabon as a violator of human rights. Then Gabon was crossed out and Zaire was added. I do not offer that comment facetiously but rather as an indication of the difficulties in determining what I think is a misdirected exercise those countries which by some criterion are less than
Supply
admirable practitioners of human rights and those which are not. I suppose all of us could be tempted to identify from our own particular points of view those countries that we think are violators and those countries that are not, but it always seems to me that in this sort of discussion that our energies would be better directed in two ways. One would be to attempt to promote the international criterion widely accepted, globally accepted if that were possible, but widely accepted criteria for human rights. Then you have a measure, then you have something that you can say: "Well, Indonesia and Iran do not measure up, but some other countries do".
The second thing that I think the energy should be directed toward in this sort of exercise is to ask ourselves this, and I say this quite seriously to our colleague in the New Democratic Party. Our international institutions are based essentially on a 19th century idea of the sovereignty of nation states. The United Nations is founded on the principle that the collectivity of the United Nations cannot intervene in the sovereign affairs of a nation state.
Yet, the sources of conflict today are increasingly at the sub-national level. They are within nations rather than between nations.
To what extent are we reshaping, modifying and improving our international institutions, and I speak not only of the United Nations family, but of a variety, a galaxy of international institutions. To what degree are we asking ourselves how those institutions can be improved so as to deal more effectively with sub-national disputes and by implication to deal with the questions of human rights, because almost invariably ethnic divisions within a nation state, or what I have called sub-national disputes, involve human rights problems?
I would urge my friends from the New Democratic Party, when they are considering this sort of an initiative, to ask themselves whether their time and energy would not be better directed to considering how Canada could contribute to a strengthening on the one hand of international criteria of what constitutes human rights, and on the other hand, to consider how our international institutions might be improved so as to enable them to deal more effectively with that growing source of inter-

October 22, 1991
Supply
national dispute, that is the ethnic and sub-national difficulties that we see in many countries of the world.
The second part of this resolution before us today urges the government to discontinue immediately Canadian participation in the Canada-United States-Mexico free trade negotiations in light of documented violations of human rights in Mexico.
Let us leave aside the question of what degree there are violations of human rights in Mexico, but let us think for a moment about the broader question. Is it likely that Canada will be able to contribute to the improvement of human rights in countries which, in our view, may violate human rights by terminating aid and trade with them? Do we think that is an effective sanction against their practices? Does history suggest-most recently I suppose in the case of Iraq and the gulf war-that economic sanctions of the sort envisaged here are the most effective way to bring about internal change in a country and to enhance the human rights in that country?
I think you will be able to infer that I have some real misgivings about this approach to our international relations.
I do not deny for a moment, and I cede to no one in my wish to see the evaluation of human rights be a feature of international relations, but whether those human rights are advanced by terminating aid and, as this resolutions says, terminating immediately Canadian participation in the Canada-United States-Mexico free trade negotiations, it seems to me an entirely different question.
Let me deal for a few minutes with the question of the negotiations with the United States and Mexico with a North American free trade area. In calling for the immediate termination of the negotiations, it strikes me that the New Democratic Party is once again setting itself on a course of protectionism. It is setting itself on that familiar and timid course of trade policy which is to attempt to develop autarky in Canada presumably and eschew the opportunities to develop greater trade relations elsewhere in the world.
Certainly for our part on this side of the House we seek to give further substance to Canada's long-standing commitment to freer trade, and I mean that in a broad, global sense, and to deny the sort of protectionism that
seems to me implicit in the resolution that is before us today.
My party on this side of the House has urged co-operation among labour, business and government in Canada as a means of achieving a united front in the face of global competitive challenges. I have to regret that the government of the day does not seem capable of making any progress in bringing forward its ideas on how to enhance Canada's international competitiveness but, leaving that aside, in promoting our interests in multilateral free trade we have argued on this side of the House that the factors extending beyond the more traditional definitions of trade policy, such as environmental protection, labour standards and human rights concerns should also receive recognition.
We have certainly emphasized that continuing consultations with Parliament and with the people of Canada have to be prominent features of trade policy, again a commitment that this government seems incapable of giving substance to.
The talks involving Canada, Mexico and the United States were in effect triggered by the United States and Mexico. They were not a Canadian priority. By no stretch of the imagination could they be seen as a Canadian priority, but certainly once the two other countries in North America had embarked upon such discussions, it would have been impracticable for Canada to stay out of those negotiations.
The question however remains of how the government of the day has chosen to commit itself to those discussions. I deplore that in entering the negotiations the government has at no time set forward in a clear and cogent manner the reasons why it followed the U.S. initiative, the Mexican initiative, to attempt to create a North American Free Trade Agreement.
The Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade-its distinguished chairman is with us today and I say this is an all-party report-noted and I quote: "We were frankly amazed by the lack of detailed economic analysis of the cost and benefits of a North American free trade area".
Exactly so, we have not had from the government any clear indication of what it is that it is pursuing in the negotiations, what Canadian goals it is trying to achieve, what Canadian values it is attempting to express in those negotiations. Myriad questions remain unanswered
October 22, 1991

about the trade negotiations with Mexico and the United States.
Has the government embarked upon the talks with the goal of enhancing Canadian export opportunities in a growing market? Is that a quite clearly defined goal, the principal goal or the only goal? Is the government attempting to, on the other hand, multilateralize Canada's bilateral trading relationship with the United States? Does it see the continental relationship which it helped to create as rather restrictive and now embraces the Mexico opportunity to, as I said, multilateralize Canada's bilateral trading relationship with the United States?
Did the government, when it announced its intention to participate, regard the possible formation of a North American free trade area as an insurance against a possible failure of the Uruguay round of the GATT? That is something we should know in a few weeks time.
Did it base itself on a more negative or at least the passive belief that Canada, having entered into a free trade agreement with the United States, had no choice but to participate? I think the answer is probably yes. That remains the government's basic position.
At the negotiating table have we embarked upon policy initiatives to attempt to protect our vested interests in the existing Canada-U.S. trade agreement, or does the government see this negotiation with Mexico as an opportunity to reopen some of the issues which have been a matter of concern and debate within our country?
Specifically on the question of subsidies, does the government see the Mexican talks as offering an opportunity to ensure not only guaranteed access to the U.S. and Mexican markets but a commitment from both those governments to limit, reduce or eliminate subsidies, an area which has not yet been tackled in the bilateral agreement with the United States?
The government's failure, it seems to me, to articulate its position clearly in these talks has contributed to the sort of resolution that we get today which, as I suggested earlier, seems to me to be an example of muddled thinking but one which, at the least, can be justified to some degree by the fact that the government has never
Supply
been clear on what exactly it is attempting to do within the proposed trilateral agreement.
At the same time that the government has failed to offer Canadians a clear explanation of its policy initiative. We have not had any indication from the government that it is prepared to undertake the adjustment assistance which is a necessary corollary of both the bilateral free trade agreement with the United States and the proposed trilateral agreement involving Mexico.
Any comprehensive adjustment assistance program for Canadians who are affected by these two trade agreements should, in my view, recognize the uneven impact on Canadians of moving toward freer trade.
I would cede to no one in my advocacy of multilateral free trade. I doubt very much that the government has fulfilled any of the requirements with regard to adjustment assistance that would make such an opening an effective opportunity for all Canadians.
Let me say that on our part, our approach to the Mexican talks has been predicated on a number of principles. We would seek, if we were directly involved in the negotiations ourselves, the following points.
We think that the agreement should be a truly comprehensive trilateral agreement which would both further multilateralize our trading relations and mitigate, to put it at its least, the unsatisfactory bilateral nature of the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement.
Second would be the negotiation of trilateral provisions so as to ensure that Canada is not asked to cede more than Mexico is prepared to contemplate.
Third would be an agreement which could be extended to Canada's trading partners elsewhere in the western hemisphere and potentially to Europe and to the Pacific region.
Fourth, we believe that an essential part of any approach to liberalized trade must be a comprehensive adjustment program for Canadian labour and for Canadian industry to be undertaken prior to the conclusion of the agreement.
Fifth, we would seek commitment from the government to uphold Canada's social, cultural, and regional development programs and an explicit statement of Canada's minimal position prior to the upcoming subsidies negotiations.

Supply
Sixth and finally, we would look for provisions in a trilateral agreement for the protection of environmental and social standards including labour.
That represents our approach to the current Mexico-Canada-U.S. trade talks, but I want to turn to a moment in conclusion to a somewhat wider issue concerning how we trade with the world, an opportunity that I want to develop a little as a result of the initiative taken today by the New Democratic Party.
Members of the House will remember that my party opposed the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement in 1988, not simply because of flaws in the agreement itself-and there were certainly a number of those-but more fundamentally because of the threat such a bilateral agreement can pose to Canadian independence. By entering into a bilateral free trade agreement with the Unites States to the relative exclusion of the rest of the world, Canada in our view would become further dependent on the U.S. market while diminishing its historic counterbalances overseas.
This, in short, was the road to continentalism and away from internationalism, a road which in my view a strong, independent Canada travelled at its peril.
The central question is how Canada can reduce its dependency on the United States within the context of the existing bilateral free trade agreement. Is there a way for Canada to avoid on the one hand continentalism and on the other a retrograde slide into protectionism as represented as I said just a moment ago by the approach adopted by the New Democratic Party?
What we have suggested is that the most effective and certainly the boldest way of achieving such a goal is to continue to expand Canada's open trading relations beyond the United States and beyond the continent. That is to say Canada should seek to become the first truly global outward oriented trading economy in North America.

Madam Speaker, I listened with interest to my colleague- from Etobicoke North and his comments with respect to this opposition motion by the New Democratic Party and the points he made
I might add that I am also a little confused by this New Democratic statement today. One would wonder why it would not have included in its list of countries that have violated human rights a country that should stand foremost in our minds today: Iraq.
The hon. member who posed this motion missed Iraq and Romania with the dictatorial regimes that they once had. You would think they would come at the top of the list because all of us in this Chamber and around the world did not have any difficulty noticing what those individual leaders and regimes did to the very fragile part of the economy and ecology of those countries, as well as what they did to human dignity.
The same member who proposed this motion recently asked that special consideration be given to Iraq and yet by this motion supports the Prime Minister in opposing aid to any country that has great human rights violations. If that is not the greatest contradiction of policy that I have heard in the last little while, it really poses some very difficult questions for me to understand what the point of view is of the New Democratic Party.
I will not comment on the fact that I cannot ask a question directly of the member, but to the previous speaker who had some difficulty with it. Regarding tremendous violations, and one that we are so familiar with which happened so recently, does he believe that we should not rethink the situation as we have done with South Africa because of a human rights violations and the lack of democracy?
There are a lot of other countries listed here that clearly have dictatorial regimes, very evidently very hard on any individuals who oppose them. Should this government or other governments not consider some aid sanctions under those circumstances? Would he not agree that unless some very severe situations should turn around in those countries and regimes we should demonstrate publicly, openly and in this House some restrictions of aid? I did not say total trade, but I talked about aid. I would like him to comment on that.

Madam Speaker, my colleague from the government side of the House has asked, as it were, for a comment on the policies of the New Democratic Party. I would only say to him that they are like the peace of God: they passeth all understanding.
October 22, 1991

On the substance of his question as to whether there are instances where Canada should pursue unilateral economic sanctions, there may be. I would hope that in every instance before contemplating such a step we would consult with our friends in the OECD and in the United Nations on such matters and attempt to evolve, as we did successfully in the case of Iraq, a system of economic sanctions that might, if given more time, have been more effective. That question is somewhat academic now.
It does not undermine the fact that the consultations and co-operative effort are, I think, a better way to go in almost any instance than to pursue a wholly unilateral approach. I think one gets into this terribly difficult question of arbitrarily deciding who is good and who is bad, who is reprehensible and who is to be rewarded. I think that sort of approach is more effective if it is carried out on a multilateral basis.

Madam Speaker, perhaps I could ask the hon. member for Etobicoke North some questions about his comments on trade policy generally. He used his intervention in this debate to discuss some of the issues on trade and particularly his attitude toward a free trade agreement with Mexico.
I take it, and I hope I am correct in this, that he is the spokesperson for his party on issues of international trade and therefore his comments on the issue of the free trade agreement and discussions with Mexico are an authoritative statement of his party's position. I just want to be sure that I understood the general drift of his remarks.
As I understood it, he sees no problem whatever with Canada entering into a free trade agreement with the United States and Mexico, but what he had instead were some-
Oh, oh.

We hear the other wing of the Liberal Party apparently objecting to this characterization of things. I will rely on the member for Etobicoke North to explain himself rather than his erstwhile friends to my far right.
Supply
As I understood his position, he essentially agrees in principle, if I may put it that way, with a free trade agreement.
He would have us participate in the discussions. His concerns are rather that the government is, if I can put it in the vernacular, screwing up the idea rather than with the idea in itself. I think I should explain to him that our party's position is very clear and unequivocal. We do not favour a free trade agreement with Mexico and we are strongly opposed to participation in those negotiations.
I would like to hear him just clearly put on record so there can be no misunderstanding his party's position with respect to the free trade agreement discussions with Mexico.

Madam Speaker, I would refer the hon. member for Victoria to the sixth report of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade dated December 12,1990 where the position of the Official Opposition is set forward quite clearly and in some detail.
My hon. friend spoke about my erstwhile friends to the right. They are not erstwhile friends. I am proud to say they are present friends and they will be future friends, so I would not accept for a moment that they are erstwhile.
Indeed, I would also recommend to the hon. member for Victoria who seems to take an interest in these matters that on this complex question we eschew the simplistic and protectionist approach of the New Democratic Party. It is in no way our policy to attempt to circle the wagons and not equip Canada to compete effectively with the challenges of a global marketplace.
If the hon. member does not know, then I think he should know that the very same questions which are being posed to Canadians by the negotiations with Mexico and indeed to a substantial degree by the agreement with the United States, flawed though I think it is, are the same questions in essence that will be posed to Canadians in the years ahead by the growing economies of Asia, by the resurgence of Europe 1992.
These are the same questions of how Canadians compete. How can they compete better? How can they equip themselves to compete? These are questions which lamentably this government has not addressed. It

October 22, 1991
Supply
has not addressed them. It is a signal failure of their whole approach to free trade with the United States and now negotiations with Mexico, but which for my part, our party is committed to.
When we form the next government, I can assure the hon. member for Victoria that we shall commit ourselves to a program of assistance which will ensure that every Canadian benefits equitably and fully from the advantages of a freer global trading economy.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Suzanne Duplessis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for External Relations and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to respond to the motion tabled in the House this morning by the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway, a motion that to my mind needs considerable clarification.
I would like to start by extending my warmest congratulations to the Prime Minister on his vigorous and impressive statement on human rights during the recent Commonwealth Conference of heads of government held in' Harare. It was a splendid opportunity to announce Canada's carefully considered position on human rights issues and their impact on the process of determining Canadian channels and levels of assistance.
First of all, issues as important as human rights cannot and must not be avoided just because they are delicate matters and may lead to disagreement between governments.
Second, the profound and sustained commitment of our fellow Canadians to respect for these fundamental rights was reflected in the past few days, more clearly than ever before, in the past few days in the various media that shape and reflect public opinion. This positive reaction to the Canadian government's initiative makes it incumbent upon us to persevere in our efforts to improve our record, to strengthen our commitment and to intensify our dialogue. We have learned, from history and experience, that the advancement of respect for human rights and establishing democratic institutions based on participation by the people went hand in hand with economic development. We are also aware that in many countries, the tradition of respect for the law is a fragile one.
However, that is where we must start, either to discourage corruption, to ensure a harmonious change of government, to safeguard the yield on production and investment, or for a host of other reasons.
It was the fragile nature of respect for these fundamental rights that inspired the government to found the International Centre for Human Rights and Democratic Development, located in Montreal. The purpose of this centre is to foster a broader understanding for the need for reforms that make respect for human rights an integral part of the day-to-day concerns of societies, their institutions or agencies and their respective governments.
It is not an easy task. We have seen a tendency among certain countries to co-operate with their neighbours in hiding from the international community the extent of human rights violations committed in their respective territories. However, such strategies, used by countries who vote as a block to cover up the real situation, are doomed.
Canada will continue to use its influence on a bilateral level and join countries that uphold the same principles, in order to exert pressure that will not be limited to mere reprimands of a moral nature.
Nevertheless, we are glad to see that national and international institutions have created a number of mechanisms that embody our respect for human rights. Unfortunately, Madam Speaker, much remains to be done because we must improve these mechanisms and define new kinds of rights.
We must be aware of the various dimensions of human rights and today's and tomorrow's imperatives, because world peace and security are based on respect for these rights, and economic and social development will not be viable without that respect.
For instance, in many societies, women have traditionally been disadvantaged. That is why the defence of women's rights has always been an urgent priority for Canada. Our country is generally recognized in the international community as a leader in this important field. Thus integrating women in development is a priority of the Canadian official development assistance strategy.
October 22, 1991

On another level, Canada was one of the first donor countries to be concerned about the fate of the most vulnerable groups in the application of structural adjustment policies by developing countries.
CIDA is now busy working with its partners in developing countries on economic reform and structural adjustment policies that will considerably improve rather than worsen the condition of the weakest social groups, especially women and children.
This work is even more important since the United Nations General Assembly adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child. We know the leading role that Canada played at the World Summit for Children in New York last year, under the co-chairmanship of the Prime Minister of Canada.
Our country is an ardent defender of children in the international community.
We committed about $350 million through CIDA last year to initiatives that directly or indirectly benefit children in developing countries, in such fields as health, education, the environment, improving the role of women in development or in other key areas like food aid or AIDS prevention.
Support for child vaccination programs is a large part of Canada's aid for health in developing countries. You will recall that in 1985, the Prime Minister of Canada launched the first phase of the Canadian international immunization program. Nineteen national organizations and six international agencies took part in it.
Under this program, Canada committed a total of $43 million over five years. This international effort helped save the lives of over 8 million children in the world. We recently began the second phase of this worldwide immunization program which will extend vaccination coverage for the most dangerous childhood diseases. These major commitments will contribute significantly to the improvement of opportunity and living conditions for the world's children. Is the right to life, Madam Speaker, not the first human right?
In these times of profound and rapid changes, in this world where peoples freed from the colonial yoke found their most legitimate aspirations reflected in the precepts of the United Nations Charter, we must think
Supply
collectively on what must be done to prevent a setback in hopes for progress in respect for human dignity.
In 1987, when we published the Canadian official development assistance strategy in Sharing Our Future, the Government of Canada undertook to tie its international development policies to respect for human rights. We set up a system on which to base our assessments and judgments. These appraisals are essential because every situation is difficult and comparisons are quite misleading.
In countries where human rights are systematically violated and where there is no guarantee that Canadian aid reaches its destination, the channels and levels of government-to-govemment assistance are reconsidered. Aid is then concentrated on our development partners who work directly at the grass roots, like non-governmental organizations that can transmit this aid directly to the poor in needy regions.
In the case of Zaire, Madam Speaker, mentioned in the motion by the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway, CIDA's aid program is targeted mainly at rural areas. It is delivered on the basis of partnership, thus meeting constraints and operational difficulties. Much of the cooperation program is now inoperative since many cooperants were evacuated from Kinshasa, Butembo and Goma.
Of the 71 Canadians, including dependants, in Zaire as part of the bilateral cooperation program, 61 were evacuated, Madam Speaker. The ten remaining provide a minimum essential service.
For the time being, we aim to provide the essential in emergency humanitarian assistance through the Red Cross or other religious or charitable organizations represented in Kinshasa.
It must be understood, Madam Speaker, that any money sent by CIDA never goes to the government itself. Only discussions are held between governments to establish the country's needs and the money is then paid to the agencies that do the work.
The people of Zaire, already among the poorest in the world, were hard hit by the events of September, which will lead to more misery with the destruction of many businesses and factories that provided employment and with the havoc in the food supply system.

October 22, 1991
Supply
Madam Speaker, withdrawing aid would amount to penalizing these disadvantaged groups twice for a political situation for which they are not responsible. Although it wishes to ensure that Canadian development aid does not contribute to the legitimacy of repressive regimes, the government must also ensure that victims of human rights violations are not doubly penalized by being deprived of the aid they need, in addition to being deprived of their most fundamental rights.
If a constructive instead of a punitive approach is taken to the issue of human rights, development assistance, if granted with discernment, can contribute very substantially not only to development but also to the cause of human rights. In fact, that is one of the points the Prime Minister made in his statement at the Commonwealth Conference.
Incidentally, Madam Speaker, perhaps I may remind honourable members that the next Sommet de la Franco-phonie will be held in Paris instead of Zaire, because Canada wanted to protest against the abuses committed by the present regime. In fact, at the Chaillot Summit, our Prime Minister intends to suggest setting up a unit for human rights and democracy within the Francophonie, whose mission would be to prepare elections, observe the electoral process and train staff. Five elections of this kind will take place next year, and Canada is determined to support the process.
Developing an appropriate Canadian response is the most difficult and delicate aspect of promoting human rights as part of our foreign policy. In our relations with other countries, we use the mechanisms at our disposal to encourage or persuade these countries to apply internationally accepted standards.
We must understand, as was pointed out by the Prime Minister, that our aid program complements other mechanisms used by the government to implement its foreign policy, such as the expression of criticism through multilateral agencies for the protection of human rights, and putting restrictions on official relations, trade and sales of military and other equipment.
Promoting human rights and democracy can be supported in a host of ways. CIDA is actively involved in developing ways to support this process through NGOs,
involved in education, health, technical assistance and other areas. We also support the activities of regional and multilateral agencies such as the Organization of American States, the Commonwealth and the Franco-phonie.
There are a variety of positive approaches and it is the duty of us all to support as best we can the worthy efforts of the grass-roots in developing countries. It is also our responsibility to support the government in its efforts to convince the international community to consolidate the economic development and human rights agendas. This way, not only do we promote justice, but at the same time we give human societies a greater chance of enjoying real economic and social development.
The Canadian foreign policy continues to be based upon the promotion and protection of human rights and basic freedoms. Both at the bilateral and multilateral level, Canada has worked very hard and with dedication to promote the implementation of international standards regarding these rights.
It was clear from the Prime Minister's statements in Harare that this government is firmly determined to see these factors fully integrated in Canadian foreign relations and that development assistance programs reaffirm human dignity.
Madam Speaker, I fully support this approach and, in closing, I would like to remind you that on December 1st we will be celebrating the 43d anniversary of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights which states, and I quote:
Recognition of the inherent dignity and of the equal and
inalienable rights of all members of the human family is the
foundation of freedom, justice and peace in the world.

Madam Speaker, I listened intently to the hon. member's comments and I know of her deep concern for humanitarian aid, whether it is in our own country or internationally, and so I welcomed her comments. But she ended by referring to the remarks made by our Prime Minister in Harare. Of course, every time our Prime Minister speaks when he is out of the country he just adds to the confusion.
Canadians, especially the NGOs and the receiving countries, do not know where they stand as far as aid and trade with Canada.
October 22, 1991

I was pleased that yesterday the Prime Minister, in response to questions from the opposition, did at least clarify the difference between providing, as he called it, aid versus commercial transactions, aid giving and granting capacity of Canada in regard to the international community. That is what it is limited to. He tried to clarify his remarks by referring to aid versus commercial transactions and trade.
I would like to ask the member what her interpretation would be of the Prime Minister's remarks in regard to the plight of the children in Iraq.
Last week we had a delegation make representations to members of Parliament about the plight of the children in Iraq who had to be operated on literally in the streets during the war. They showed us videos of a child's hand being cut off, of other children being affected by the bombs and the shrapnel still in their bodies. Because of the sanctions, they do not have the hospital equipment, the bandages and the medicine to operate on these children. One hospital was shown as not having any windows. They cannot operate on these children because the dust will blow through the windows and there will be infection and these children will die.
There is an international appeal right now to help the children of Iraq. The Speaker received an invitation from a committee of the European Parliament to send a Canadian parliamentary delegation to see for ourselves what these children are facing and how we as Canadians can help.
Taking into account the Prime Minister's remarks when he was out of the country and yesterday during Question Period, what is her interpretation? Would her party be in full support to help the children of Iraq or, because of the human rights violations in Iraq, we would not help these children in Iraq?

Madam Speaker, I would like to return the favour to the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park, who is also very concerned by development and anything that goes on in this world.
Supply
His question concerning those children suffering in Irak touches me very deeply, as a mother and as a former teacher. One cannot be insensitive when one hears about children suffering in some part of the world. On the other hand, madam Speaker, if Saddam Hussein, the president of Iraq wants to make amend, if he shows good faith-and we will soon know the outcome of the mission that went to Iraq-and if he does not continue to build an arsenal of nuclear, bacteriological and chemical weapons, I imagine that the countries of the world will show compassion and might lift the embargo if, in the first place, good will is shown on the part of Saddam Hussein.

Madam Speaker, it is interesting. I think the House has indicated its support of the Prime Minister's statement in tying, aid, trade and human rights together.
This party is asking that it take concrete action so that it is not hollow rhetoric, that in fact it gives meaning to the government's program. That is what our resolution tried to do today. It lists a number of actions that would be supportable by many sides of the House.
It also points out that Mexico is a major violator of human rights. In addition to that, we are being asked by this government and the United States to join in a negotiation to a treaty in which Canadian sovereignty would be reduced in this treaty and which our standards for social programs, health care and labour rights would be reduced, and generally our economy would be reduced. We are being asked to join in this.
Our motion today asks that that negotiation be discontinued because of Mexico's human rights violations. More than 100 members of the opposition party have been killed; hundreds of trade unionists killed.
The Liberal Party today opted out of that and said: "No, we support that and we want to continue those negotiations".
Through you, Madam Speaker, may I ask the previous member if she supports that initiative of the Liberal Party to continue those negotiations with Mexico in light of the human rights violations there. Does she support the fact that the Liberal Party wants to continue those

October 22, 1991
Supply
negotiations in light of those human rights violations toward a Canada-U.S.-Mexico trade agreement.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all, I would like to remind the hon. member for the New Democratic Party that the government's approach to human rights is intended to be positive and constructive, not punitive. Canadian aid must not aid and abet repressive regimes.
I happen to know that the New Democratic Party objected to free trade with the United States, and now that we are discussing free trade with Mexico, it is objecting again.
The hon. member claims that Canada's sovereignty will be diminished by free trade with Canada and Mexico. I don't think Canada's sovereignty is affected by the Free Trade Agreement.
Regarding the intent of our policies at External Affairs on human rights violations, the government has made it clear it does not want to be punitive. Madam Speaker, if we isolate ourselves and refuse to talk to other countries, how can we exert a positive influence and be able to change things?
I want to make it clear to my colleague in the New Democratic Party that I support the Free Trade Agreement with Canada, United States and Mexico, as I did when this extremely important issue was before the House. Today, Madam Speaker, the economies of our various countries are so intertwined that we suffer the consequences of a decision made halfway around the world.
Madam Speaker, it is important for Canadian businesses to have a big market, to be able to invest and to have access to markets that are much larger and more substantial that our own.
Today, our industries seem to be adjusting to the situation, and we will see that the agreement will be a very beneficial one for Canada. Personally, I was not aware there were human rights violations in Mexico or that they were as substantial as the hon. member claimed. I will be glad to check this, but I think that if we maintain economic ties, it is a way to be able subsequently to exert some kind of influence and be in a position to protect the people of these countries, since they suffer most as a result of these human rights violations.

Madam Speaker, I have to say just by way of opening that the hypocrisy of the government on this issue is absolutely breathtaking.
We have just listened to the minister go on with this long explanation about how devoted the government is to human rights in other countries and to progressive policies in official development assistance when this minister has presided over the persistent dismantling of the programs that this country has supported for years and years and years, the increasing commercialization for Canadian benefit of official development assistance and the complete ignoring of reports from this House of Commons committees on the issue of human rights development.
In 1987 the Standing Committee on External Affairs produced a report "For Whose Benefit". That was the name of the report. It recommended a human rights unit be established in the Policy Branch of CIDA to co-ordinate human rights policy with External Affairs, that CIDA develop an appropriate human rights country classifications system and that an annual ODA human rights review be tabled in Parliament.
What has happened over the last four years? Zilch. Nothing has happened. The minister has been completely negligent in the way in which he has responded to the report of the standing committee with respect to human rights.
She has presided equally over a change of programs to favour business; the merging of the Special Programs Branch with the Business Co-operations Branch, severe cutbacks of assistance and aid to reputable NGOs, non-governmental organizations such as CUSO, Crossroads and Canada World Youth.
The minister has no business standing up in this House and proclaiming the government's virtue with respect to human rights. This government has set this country's reputation back over the last eight years.
The Prime Minister said in his remarks in Harare that Canada will not subsidize repression and the stifling of freedom. He said: "We shall increasingly be channelling our development assistance to those countries which so respect the fundamental rights and freedoms". Yet in Mexico, 5 million to 10 million children under the age of 14 are working in Middle Ages conditions.
October 22, 1991

This government sits down at the table with that government and negotiates a free trade agreement, the result of which will be that Canadian workers will be asked to compete with those who are working under primitive working conditions with no rights whatsoever. The ultimate long-term effect will be to take from Canadian workers the rights that they presently enjoy. That will be the equalization effect of a free trade agreement with Mexico that is permitted to continue to violate the basic rights of human beings under the UN charter.
There is only one approach to trade agreements with Mexico and with other countries in the world. It is to say as a precondition there must be an agreement to have a social charter with that country ensuring that employment rights, human rights, environmental rights are maintained and developed in those countries to a standard that meets international standards, standards to which Canada can adhere. Only at that point can Canada consider free trade agreements with those countries. Only then will Canadian workers be protected from the impact of an attempt to compete with those who suffer as they do in Mexico.
The motion before the House calls on the House to take note of the Prime Minister's recent statements and calls on the government to discontinue immediately the current negotiations with Mexico and to review all international support programs to ensure they meet the eight criteria announced by the Prime Minister.
Any discussion of this motion has to begin with an analysis of the extent of the problem involving human rights violations around the world. First of all, it should be seen that generally there is a rise in violations around the world.
Second, eveiy country on the globe, including Canada, is guilty at one level or another of significant human rights violations. In our case, we see the condition on reserves across Canada and the treatment of our native people. We had the example even in this House a couple of weeks ago of a government driving through legislation forcing its employees back to work, counter to the provisions in my respectful submission of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which requires all Canadians to have equality and respect of the law, including, I submit, the law giving employees in Canada the right to free
Supply
collective bargaining and the right to strike, except in exceptional circumstances.
Third, it is necessary to note that problems with human rights violations do not simply involve people languishing in far-flung jails. The violations occur in a myriad of ways, and the violations of human rights that are occurring around the world are not merely the product of foreign feuds or tinpot dictators in local countries with which we have no connection. The reality is that we in the west are co-conspirators in the violation of human rights that is occurring increasingly in every comer of the globe. We export the means of repression and violation. Now the methodology of torture, as documented by Amnesty International, has taken on even more horrific tones in the latter part of this century.
There is documentation suggesting that the U.S. government, for example, has trained those who use the most modern methods of torture against their own citizens, torture which is becoming more deadly and more efficient.
The violations of human rights that are occurring around the globe are often generally in the interests of the countries of the west, including Canada, and we along with the United States, which has been particularly active and aggressive in this, have in fact encouraged regimes which are repressive, maintained regimes which are oppressive and actively supported them.
We have often given indirect assistance through our propping up of multinational corporations and our use of the products of multinational corporations, our integration in the international economic system, while we stand by and watch those same corporations locally sustain repressive regimes.
We see the expansion of the U.S. military all around the world. We see it from our part of the world particularly in the Pacific, and the dumping of toxic wastes in other countries, the use of other countries essentially as U.S. military bases.
Finally, we have supported consistently policies which bring Third World countries into environmental, economic and social degradation, all of which is as significant a violation of human rights as a violation of the individual right to security of person. The UN human rights charter itself has sustained the proposition that

Supply
social, economic and environmental rights are equally a matter of concern as are other human rights. Our government, as demonstrated by its persistent refusal to respond to every urging to change its policies in respect of development assistance, is a co-conspirator in the deprivation of human rights around the world. We see the practical effect on Canadians of these policies because as human rights sink around the world, as people are deprived of their employment rights, the rights to organize, the rights to bargain, the right to reasonable working conditions, the right to strike around the world, as these rights are deprived of people they put other countries in an intense competitive position vis-a-vis Canada.
How are we going to change it? First, we must change the international economic social environmental policies and structures. Second, we have to change Canadian official development assistance policies as outlined, for example, by Canadian churches in a submission today, as outlined in the resolution before the House and as outlined by the Standing Committee on External Affairs. We have to deal with the worst cases and those worst cases have been outlined: Iraq and Iran, China over Tibet, Indonesia over East Timor, Kenya and South Africa over its violations through the use of RENAMO in Mozambique. We have to support the agencies of the United Nations and the Commonwealth that are seeking to deal with human rights violations.
We must support Amnesty International and other similar organizations, and we must not participate in free trade negotiations with Mexico which will lead to the violation of rights of the people in those countries and the violation of rights of Canadians.

Madam Speaker, once again I want to say what a positive thing it is that we have had this debate here today, but I want to go back to the member for Halifax about his comments this morning when we have to separate, and understand the difference between rhetoric and reality.
Earlier today I asked the member from Spadina, if he realized that about 70 per cent of our manufacturing jobs in this country were related to exports that involve countries that in some way, shape or form were involved in human rights violations, and the member for Spadina was quite direct. He would just say: "Listen, we would cut off all of those contracts".
Does the member for Victoria share that view? Everyone in this House is supportive of the fact that we develop plans and approaches to eliminate human rights violations. Even the New Democratic Party earlier today complimented the Prime Minister on his initiative of recent days. I think we have to give him the benefit of the doubt that his words are absolutely sincere and he will back them up with action.
I want to ask the member what he will say to the Canadian Labour Congress, Premier Rae, Premier Har-court and Premier Romanow who are involved in the national economy of this country and who are concerned about jobs and agricultural exports. I just do not see it as black and white as the member for Spadina. I would like to hear what the member for Victoria says.

Madam Speaker, I, too, agree that of course it is not a matter of black and white. As I said in my speech, all countries including Canada violate human rights in one fashion or another and no one is perfect and no country is perfect.
It should be understood that there are choices that we make as a country. Our official development assistance for example is limited. We would like to see more of it, but it is limited and we are forced to make choices. For example, we had before the external affairs committee people from Mozambique who are pleading for money. The government just recently agreed to give $1 million extra aid, but that country needs far more if it is going to stand on its feet and it is going to survive and the people in that country are going to survive. We are providing assistance to South Africa, to Namibia, countries which have the potential for doing the right thing, programs which are very good.
With those potentials, why then is the government providing Export Development Corporation assistance to Mexico with the human rights record that it has? How come Petro-Canada is entering into agreements with Burma? How come Canada is giving a $500 million line of credit to Kuwait after the treatment that that country metes out to Palestinians? How come Canada is entering into agreements to provide military equipment to Saudi Arabia, given the record of that country in respect of the rights of women? How come Canada is giving $30 million of foreign aid to Kenya when Kenya is financing RENAMO in Mozambique? How come Canada is supporting Iran, Rwanda, China, Zaire, Indonesia? We have choices
October 22, 1991

and we should make those choices, as the Prime Minister says.
The Prime Minister was quite correct and the Prime Minister I am sure if he comes to the vote on this, if it should get to a vote, will have to vote in favour of this motion because this motion puts into words the sentiment that the Prime Minister offered in Harare. What we would like to see is the government put action behind the words of the Prime Minister in southern Africa.
