speechtext: There was only, as the hon. member knows, five minutes of questions and comments as the hon. member's colleagues are sharing their 20 minute period. There was only five minutes and that five minute period had expired, so we are resuming debate.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to join in this debate and perhaps attempt to move from the general that has exercised the attention of the House for some considerable time today and bring it down to one specific. Before doing so I would like to briefly review the terms of the motion which urges the House to "take note of the Prime Minister's recently stated commitment to the principle of linking government aid to respect for human rights" and then urges the government "to review immediately all international support programs to ensure that they meet the aid criteria as announced by the Prime Minister".
An excellent suggestion. The one instance I would like to offer where justice cries that this be done, one of many as my hon. colleague noted, but a very important one, is in the sad country of Burma, now subject to renaming by its despotic military rulers as Myanmar. Consistency demands that the fine words of the Prime Minister be matched with equitable actions by the government.
In this instance those equitable actions require that the government vote its 80.5 per cent share in Petro-Canada to compel the company to cease its commercial
Supply
activities in Burma. The reason for this is simple. The outlaw regime currently governing Burma has committed among the worst human rights atrocities to be found in that unhappy corner of the world and cannot any longer be permitted to escape the censure of enlightened world opinion.
This is not a debatable point. Amnesty International in its 1991 report notes and I quote: "More than 350 prisoners of conscience and possible prisoners of conscience were known to be among thousands of people believed held for political reasons. Many were detained without charge or trial but others were sentenced after unfair trials by military tribunals. Torture and ill treatment of prisoners were reportedly common".
The same report continues elsewhere: "By the end of 1990 the actual number of people held for political reasons was thought to be in the thousands".
This is to say nothing of the routine torture that some of those prisoners undergo.
It is, for example, for her brave resistance to the despotic regime that Madam Aung San Suu Kyi has been awarded this year's Nobel Peace Prize for her, as the citation says, non-violent struggle for democracy and human rights within Burma against the military government now ruling.
The Canadian government, to its credit, acknowledges its concerns for human rights in Burma. The then Secretary of State for External Affairs, the right hon. member for Yellowhead, issued a news release on October 5, 1990 expressing the government's grave concern that members of the National League for Democracy continued to be detained by the interim government. That is a direct quote from his news release, which went on to call for the release of all political prisoners.
The Canadian government acknowledged the seriousness of the situation as well when it instructed the Petro-Canada International Assistance Corporation, the international development arm of the Petro-Canada Crown corporation, to withdraw from its oil exploration assistance activities in Burma. This withdrawal took place even before at least some of the PCIAC activities

October 22, 1991
Supply
were taken over by CIDA after the February 1991 budget.
However, and this is the situation that compels me to speak today, Petro-Canada, which has been Canada's flagship energy company now subject to privatization and now being sold to private investors, is still active in Burma and the Canadian government is doing nothing about it.
Let me quote from the June 18, 1991 Petro-Canada prospectus. Page 19 states: "Since 1988 Petro-Canada has substantially increased its international exploration activities, particularly in areas such as Myanmar", that is Burma. "In Myanmar Petro-Canada operates one offshore block in which it has a 70 per cent interest and participates in another in which it has a 30 per cent interest. In 1990 more than 620 miles, which is to say
1,000	kilometres, of seismic data were gathered and drilling is planned for both blocks in 1991".
Page 36 of the same prospectus reads: "In each of the countries in which Petro-Canada is active the petroleum exploration and production rights held by the company are issued by the central government in that country either directly or through its national oil company. After according Petro-Canada a percentage of production to cover its exploration, development and operating costs, the agreements generally provide for sharing the balance of production between Petro-Canada and the government or national oil company".
What that means is that Petro-Canada, our company, is aiding the military dictatorship of Burma in the development of those resources.
There is more. I quote from the Edmonton Journal of May 25, 1990, an article from the Canadian Press date-lined Calgary: "'Petro-Canada paid $6 million in cash to the military dictatorship of Burma for the right to mount a drilling program there', the Crown corporation said Wednesday. Petro-Canada spokesman Sheilah O'Brien said Wednesday the national oil corporation turned its cash over to Burmese authorities as a 'signing bonus.' The payment, which goes to Burma's military regime was required to close a deal for rights to prospect for oil and natural gas on a concession or land area".
That is blood money. That is blood money being paid by what was our national oil company. More recently it has been revealed that Petro-Canada is training in its
Calgary office the son of the managing director of the state owned Myanmar Oil Corporation as part of its technology transfer program.
We cannot stress enough that Canada's involvement through Petro-Canada brings great comfort to the Burmese military regime. I quote from the Bangkok Post of November 9, 1989: "At a time when many donors have adopted a wait and see attitude, Canada has continued its assistance to the economic and social development of Myanmar. Rear Admiral Wong Worn Kym said in Rangoon, 'A friend in need is a friend indeed'".
Is it not delightful to have Canada known as a friend indeed of the military dictators of Burma? There was a time before the government's privatization move when it would have been easy to instruct the Crown corporation to get out of Burma. As section 89(1) of the Financial Administration Act had it, and I quote: "The Governor in Council may, on the recommendation of the appropriate minister, give a directive to any parent Crown corporation if the Governor in Council is of the opinion that it is in the public interest to do so".
The thing to bear in mind is that it is still possible to do so even after privatization for, as is noted in the prospectus again of June 18, 1991: "The Government of Canada has stated that it will deal with its common shares as an investor and not as a manager, and that it does not intend to exercise the right to vote at meetings of shareholders although it reserves the right to do so".
The Crown has reserved the right to vote those shares. Therefore in the interest of making real the policy about which the Prime Minister has spoken it must vote those shares. It must vote those shares to cause Petro-Canada to cease its activity in Burma until such time as the legitimate democratic governance of that country is restored.
In pursuit of such a policy almost a year ago on November 22, 1990, I wrote to William Hopper, chairman of the board and chief executive officer of Petro-Canada. I quote from my letter: "I urge you to take the admittedly difficult step of winding down and thereafter suspending all of Petro-Canada's activities in Burma", now known by some as Myanmar, "as quickly as possibly. I further urge you to ensure the suspension of activity
October 22, 1991

prevails until such time as democracy is restored to that unhappy land".
Mr. Hopper kindly replied on December 6, stating in part that were the company to follow that advice "we would, however, have sacrificed a long-term investment opportunity in response to what we hope will be a short-term political problem". It is more than a shortterm political problem. It is a tragedy and a crime.
Also on that same day I wrote to the energy minister, the hon. member for Provencher, and to the then minister of external affairs, the right hon. member for Yellowhead, urging them to "convince your cabinet colleagues to vote the government's shares in Petro-Canada in such a way as to effect the company's withdrawal from all operations in Burma". Although I did not receive a reply from the then Secretary of State for External Affairs, I did receive a reply from the minister of energy in which he noted: "It would be contrary to the policy we have been following since 1984 and to the present course of privatization for the government to vote its shares in this point".
We have a new policy enunciated by the Prime Minister. I must conclude I would do so by urging them to follow that policy and forget the previous one.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all I want to underscore that the policy enunciated by the Prime Minister is not a new policy. It has been in existence as long as this government has been in office and, in part, when the previous government was in office. I note that the New Democratic Party has been playing a giant game of human rights hopscotch around the world, picking and choosing those regimes it wants to talk about and, among other things, the member for Victoria said that Mozambique ought to be getting more aid.
I would ask him: Does he know clearly what the human rights record is of Mozambique? Has Mozambique now passed the test for human rights in order to get more aid? If he knows, if he really knows, does he approve of the human rights record of Mozambique? While I am asking questions like that, since it changed the motion and crossed out the word "Gabon" in the
Supply
motion and added "Zaire", why rather than adding Zaire did it not add Cuba?
Cuba is not the most stellar example of democratic institutions. The caucus of the New Democratic Party ought to understand it very well. Enough of its members take their Christmas vacations in Cuba. They should come back informed. Why would they not talk about Cuba as being a country that ought to have its aid cut back because of its human rights abuses?
To take the point that the member for Edmonton East has just made regarding Burma, he would have the public understand that there has been no change in aid allocations regardless of regime. I want to outline for him that countries that saw Canadian assistance increase or resume for good human rights performance, improved democratic practices, or better governments are Benin in 1991 following democratic elections, Haiti in 1990 following President Aristide's election, the Philippines in 1986 following President Aquino's democratic election, and Uruguay in 1985 following President Sanguinetti's democratic election.
Some countries saw Canadian assistance decrease or cut off entirely because of human rights abuses or non-democratic practices: Haiti in 1991 in response to the coup-I hope members from the NDP caucus can remember that far back-China in 1989 as a result of the Tiananmen Square massacre, Myanmar in 1988 in response to the forceful repression and I will have more to add to that, and in 1987 in response to a coup bilateral aid was suspended as a result of the apartheid policy of the government in Fiji now. Assistance was suspended after an execution in Berchina Faso and resumed in 1991.
Members of the New Democratic Party would believe that once aid is in place it stays regardless of the regime. That is not true. The aid has been cut off, suspended in Burma. They should not mislead the Canadian public by letting it believe that aid has gone on in unrelenting consistency during this regime.

Madam Speaker, very briefly, the reason I did not deal with any of the instances raised by the hon. member is that I had but 10 minutes to speak and it took 10 minutes to go through and deal reasonably with the matter of Petro-Canada's activities in Burma. It is a fact that the federal government could

October 22, 1991
Supply
vote its shares in Petro-Canada and cause Petro-Canada to withdraw from Burma.
It is a fact that as long as the federal government does not do that Petro-Canada remains active in Burma and that gives direct aid and comfort to the military dictatorship in Burma. That is the matter I chose to deal with.
Just very briefly dealing with the question of Mozambique, if the hon. member wishes to imply that the human rights record of the Government of Mozambique is not spotless, I will agree with him. Compared to the abuses of the South Africa financed, so-called Renamo movement operating in Mozambique routinely, for example, decapitating people at whim, I would say that the real human rights abuses, the most dangerous and persistent human rights abuses in Mozambique, come not from its government but from the puppets of South Africa.

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to take part in this debate today on the motion brought before us by the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway.
In this motion the hon. member makes the remarkable contention that the human rights situation in Mexico is so deplorable that we must suspend our trade negotiations with that country and the United States. By making this claim, he has clearly decided to overlook the substantial progress Mexico has made in the human rights field. Beyond that, he has chosen to scorn the potential contained within a North American free trade agreement to build a better society in Mexico, a society better able to provide and protect the freedoms of its citizens.
I will return shortly to the important improvements that Mexico has made in its human rights record, but I would like to begin by talking briefly about the ways in which a closer economic association between Mexico and its two northern neighbours will contribute to the strengthening of political, legal and human rights.
Like governments everywhere in the last decade, Mexico has been part of the movement to throw off the shackles of government control and create a new economy in which market signals play a much more important role. The government of President Carlos Salinas has embarked on a major program of privatization and
deregulation that will create a more flexible economy better able to meet the needs of its citizens.
One of the inevitable results of this process is the removal from the close, continuous and suffocating control by government of so many aspects of daily economic life. Economic power in Mexico is being wrested from the hands of bureaucrats and is being returned to the marketplace where it belongs. As economic power is being distributed to more hands, so is political power.
It is no coincidence that in all the world's most advanced economies, in all the G-7 countries including our own, democratic institutions hold sway.
When free economic actors with diverse interests pursue their various objectives, a free political dialogue is the inevitable result. The ambitious program of the Salinas government to return power to the market is a force for pluralism, a force for greater political freedom.
This trend in Mexico will be reinforced by the proposed North American Free Trade Agreement. The agreement will help release at all levels of Mexican society even more entrepreneurial energies than those already put into play by domestic reforms. That will solidify the foundation of political reform but, beyond that, the trilateral agreement will also bring about a closer association among the people of the three countries.
There is no better way to strengthen human values than through the close and continuous exchange of ideas. Ideas are transmitted in many ways, and they are often transmitted through the marketplace.
As the three countries learn more and more about each other, their people will increasingly make comparisons among themselves and draw conclusions about their way of life. There is no greater force for political freedom and respect for human rights than in the power of example.
In a North America where the people have come to know each other better, few will care to be seen as lacking the appropriate regard for human rights. Looking ahead, it seems inevitable that a closer economic

association with Canada and the U.S. would have positive effects on Mexico's social and political institutions.
Free trade will generate a multiplicity of connections, institutional linkages, contacts and influences that will have a considerable impact on all levels of society, both theirs and ours. No doubt this will be a long-term process, but Mexico is moving in the right direction, away from the elitist and economic disparity toward a more open, fairer system.
Human rights regarding social, labour and environmental matters stand particularly to benefit. Historically Canada has encouraged all countries to be more open economically and politically in their relations with the international system.
Looking at Mexico in particular, free trade could offer the material incentives for achieving this goal. A prosperous Mexico joined with North American markets and technology would act as a positive element in the geopolitical dynamic of North American and the hemisphere at large.
Although the view from outside a country's borders is frequently incomplete or misinformed, no government is comfortable with international criticism of its domestic policies. In this regard, Mexican President Carlos Salinas has been deeply concerned about his own country's reputation of the political and human rights front since the inauguration of his administration in 1988.
He has realized that the trilateral negotiations have focused extraordinary attention on political developments in Mexico and he has been energetic in pursuing political reform.
I would like to remind the hon. members that President Salinas has publicly recognized on successive occasions that human rights violations in Mexico do pose a problem. To address the problem, however, President Salinas appointed a human rights commission in early June 1990 mandated to investigate and report on alleged human rights abuses.
The commission is headed by a Supreme Court judge with 11 prominent Mexicans. Since its establishment the commission has issued two reports, both demonstrating the commission's independence through the criticism of long-standing government practices.
Canada is encouraged by these developments which mark clear progress toward improving the promotion and
Supply
protection of human rights in Mexico. Other initiatives undertaken by the Mexican government include a major reform of the civil code in 1990 to prohibit admission in court of evidence obtained through torture.
These initiatives of the Mexican government point to an improvement in Mexico's human rights record. In the estimation of Canadian observers and Mexican activists, Mexico continues to move in the right direction. However, much remains to be done and Canada will continue to maintain close interest in this important question.
I can assure that Canada will continue to maintain our very constructive dialogue with Mexico on the human rights issue. I am pleased to inform my colleagues in the House that the deputy minister to the Mexican attorney general will visit Ottawa and Quebec next week for discussions on these very questions. Over-all then, Mexico's record is improving, albeit not overnight. As these positive trends continue there is no justification whatsoever for not continuing participation in the Canada-United States-Mexico free trade negotiations, as the motion before the House states. As Canadians observe the increasing globalization of issues, we are reminded once again that acting alone we can contribute only marginally to resolving the problems confronting us in the Americas and elsewhere. We must work together. That is why Canada became a member of the Organization of American States where we can work together with our hemispheric colleagues to address such pressing issues as human rights, democratic development, the environment, drugs and arms control.
As a full and active member of OAS, Canada is committed to the promotion and defence of human rights in the hemisphere, consistent with provisions of the OAS charter. To cite one example, the OAS unit for promotion of democracy, a Canadian initiative supported by Mexico and all other OAS members, has contributed to democratic development and political rights in the hemisphere through election monitoring missions. The current difficult situation in Haiti will further test the unit's capacity to protect human rights in the hemisphere.
I have spoken about the benefits of closer economic association generally and the progress Mexico has made on the human rights front. Let me focus now on the North American free trade negotiations specifically. We cannot overlook the importance of Canadian participation in these negotiations. Canada decided to participate

October 22, 1991
Supply
in the North American free trade negotiations because it is in the national interest to do so. Only by being at the negotiating table can we improve and secure greater access for Canadian goods and services and ensure that Canadian interests and concerns are properly and fully addressed. Moreover, only by participating in the negotiations can we ensure that Canadian companies share the same access as U.S. companies to all North American markets, thereby promoting job-creating investment at home here in Canada.
Madam Speaker, Canada's broad objectives in the NAFTA negotiations are; first, a barrier-free access to Mexico for Canadian goods and services, while developing tariff phase-out provisions and safeguard mechanisms which reflect Canadian import sensitivities; second, improved access to the U.S. market in such areas as financial services and government procurement; third, improved conditions under which Canadian businesses can make strategic alliances within North America to better compete with the Pacific Rim and the European communities; fourth, ensuring that Canada remains an attractive site for foreign and domestic investment; and fifth, the establishment of a fair and expeditious dispute settlement mechanism such as that which has served Canadian interests so well in the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.
Mexico is prepared to work with Canada to achieve a balanced comprehensive agreement in the interests of all three countries. This openness to substantial change is remarkable. It augers well for a positive change more generally throughout Mexican society. After decades of running a closed economy, Mexico saw the economic well-being that other countries had benefited from as a result of lower tariff and non-tariff barriers.
Since 1986 the average Mexican customs tariff has decreased from over 25 per cent to around 10 per cent and maximum rates have reduced from 100 per cent to 50 per cent. Import licences and border restrictions have also been radically reduced; moreover, the government of President Salinas has instituted sweeping tax reforms, thereby eliminating tax loopholes, promoting a regime of better enforcement and a broader tax base, and as a consequence increasing tax revenues dramatically. Mexico has also significantly liberalized its treatment of
foreign and private investment capital, especially as a result of new regulations approved in 1989.
A dynamic and determined Mexican administration is transforming the country into a modem, prosperous and globally competitive player in world markets. Indeed, the president of the World Bank has described Mexico's reforms as "one of the most ambitious, courageous and determined programs of economic reform and institutional change recently undertaken in any country".
Mexico is a country that is rejuvenating itself in creating the kind of vigorous economy that will benefit itself and its trading partners. There is no doubt that Mexico's reforms are working. The indicators of newfound economic buoyancy are numerous. Mexico's gross national product for example is expected to rise by 4.5 per cent to 5 per cent this year, up from 3.9 per cent in each year of 1990 and 1989 and much lower figures during the height of the debt crisis. These are remarkable figures when much of the world economy was experiencing slow down or recession.
It is also important to stress that Mexico has successfully dealt with its debt load. Its indebtedness is no longer an obstacle to business looking for new opportunities. Mexico's economic reform minded leadership has firmly taken matters in hand and is creating an economy with which Canadians can most certainly do business.
Canadian companies have the chance to market not only goods but needed services as well and very important in Mexico's push for productivity is the development of human resources. Canadian firms that offer products and services that help in the development of human resources are well received in Mexico. The fuller integration of Mexico into the North American economy should also provide greater stability for Mexico's economic, trade, monetary and fiscal reforms already undertaken to date.
Throughout increased trade and economic expansion Mexico hopes to continue to improve working conditions and living standards. Trade and economic growth will also generate more resources for the Mexican government to enforce existing laws. What many people do not realize is that Mexico's extensive labour legislation is protective of workers' rights. The problem lies in the fact

that the government simply does not have the resources necessary to properly enforce these regulations.
With the prosperity that increased trade will bring that will change for the better. A successful NAFTA will be of benefit for workers and business. In all three countries the primary purpose of negotiating such a deal is to increase trade. One-third of Canadian workers have jobs that are dependent on trade.
Increased trade creates jobs, increased trade creates prosperity for the country and for its workers, the same as is true in Mexico.
Free trade improves the economic and social conditions of our trading partners, but in the process of doing so, our partners become better customers and we become more competitive suppliers. This is the power of liberalized trade. By bringing down barriers in the North American economy, we can create more opportunities for still more Canadian business.
It is this promise of helping to build a more competitive Canadian economy that sustains us in our determination to win a balanced North American free trade agreement that will be beneficial to all three countries. It is precisely for this purpose that Canada is pursuing NAFTA negotiations. The NAFTA will make all three countries more prosperous through free trade. Prosperity in turn brings greater business openness and freedom for the whole population which can only encourage greater social change.
It is not by turning our backs on Mexico that Mexican society can continue to evolve positively. An inward looking closed society in Mexico is in no one's interest. We must work with Mexico actively seeking closer co-operation. This will encourage greater familiarity with the social attitudes and norms of fully democratic societies in its own way. This is what the North American free trade agreement is all about.
In closing, I say change and growth through co-operation. Only narrow minded isolationists want us to proceed otherwise.

Madam Speaker, as quoted in The Ottawa Citizen on September 18 of this year Amnesty International basically said it takes a strong stomach to read the report entitled "Mexico torture with impunity". It documents one horrendous case of abuse after another, most involving
Supply
Mexico's federal judicial police. People are kicked, beaten, pushed into water tanks, given electric shocks, burned with cigarettes, subject to mock executions. Some are nearly asphyxiated by tying plastic bags over their heads. Others are forced into bowls of excrement. Toe nails are ripped out. Mineral waters are forced into them. It just goes on and on and on. Children are subjected to this, as are women and teenagers. It is very difficult, in the face of about 100 members of the political opposition killed, hundreds of trade unionists killed, to suggest that Mexico has any commitment to a reform program and that any success even to that is small.
But that is not what concerns me about the debate today. I listened with care to the presentation by the speaker. The one thing that you can count on is the Conservative government. It will tell you what it believes. The previous speaker said: "I believe the Mexi-can-Canadian-American free trade agreement is a good deal and we will go ahead in spite of this documented information and hopefully it will get better."
The party on my other side, the Liberal Party, moves around this country saying: "This is no good and we should not support this kind of trade agreement until conditions are laid down." This motion is the statement of the NDP and it is one you can count on. I am so critically disappointed with the Liberal Party for amending the motion before us to eliminate stopping the negotiation of a trade agreement with Mexico, that in fact it matches their other presentation. I am sure the speaker from the Conservative Party will agree because he watched, with me, in this House as the Liberal Party said: "We do not accept an attack or a war by Canada on Iraq", and then turned around and voted in absolutely the opposite direction.
The Liberal Party stands up and says that it supports choice on the abortion issue for women in Canada and yet turns around and half the party votes the other way.
We have a critical situation here today. The Prime Minister's statement was correct, absolutely correct and supportable. We are asking for some action. A reasonable action is to discontinue these negotiations until Mexico gives us a firm commitment that they will turn it around and then, by all means. What we get is a situation today where the Liberals back right away from that and take the opposite tack where they are prepared to

October 22, 1991
Supply
involve themselves without condition of human rights and without protection for Canada in-
I know they are upset-and I am sure the previous speaker would agree-but the absolute contradiction in their position is just untenable. The Liberals now come out in support of that Canada-U.S.-Mexico trade agreement in spite of its shortcomings and harm to Canada, in spite of the human rights violations in that country.
I would like to reiterate once again that the Prime Minister's statement on human rights is supportable. It needs action to confirm and give meaning to that statement. I admire the party of the previous speaker in that they stand up and at least say exactly what they mean. I think we say exactly what we mean, but I am just sorely disappointed that the Liberals will not give a solid indication to the Canadian people. They have turned around and basically supported the approach of the Conservative government and are saying another thing to the electorate.

Madam Speaker, again we have just witnessed what has been referred to as the black and white policy of the NDP.
I was quite impressed with my colleague from Surrey-White Rock-South Langley who made two or three good points awhile ago, one of them being that the policy the Prime Minister talked about is not brand new. It has been going on for many years, indeed by the former Liberal government as well.
My colleague cited several very specific examples that our government certainly has been helping to monitor, where specific decisions were made to either cut off aid or reduce it and, in other cases, increase it. However, to think that we should turn our backs on a country like Mexico which under Salinas has veiy definitely made some progress and is moving in the right direction is wrong. There are so many examples around the world, as the hon. member knows, in these situations where improvement was achieved did not happen in a day or a month or a year.
I have been chairman of the Soviet Jury Committee for Canada for almost five years now. When I think back
to my first trip to the Soviet Union in 1986, only 914 Jews were allowed to leave that year. The world, including countries like Canada, had been criticizing the Soviet Union, as you know, directly and through the United Nations.
Thanks to Mr. Gorbachev and his leadership there are tremendous changes. I am just highlighting one specific example, but starting in 1987-88, the number of Jews allowed to leave jumped to 18,000. No one knows what last year's figures are. We think it is 250,000 people. There are many movements. Sometimes there are as many leaving in one day as had previously been allowed to leave in a whole year.
It is now on the road to a freer type society. It has decades to go before we could compare it to Canada. I subscribe to an incremental theory that leadership of the country is honestly trying to move in a democratic way and honestly trying to improve the human rights situation to drastically reduce the violations.
I think it is going to be encouraged to do more things like that if we are supportive of them. We should not back off totally but give credit where credit is due on these improvements.

Madam Speaker, I do not want to question what the hon. member says. We are all astounded and amazed by what has happened in this short period.
I would point out that the government under the Prime Minister in the G-7 meetings was unprepared to support the Soviet Union and said "it had a way to go even with aid to survive the winter". That is beginning to change because of the coup and other things, so it has moved forward.
I would point out that the Prime Minister was even unprepared at that point to give aid. Yet with what is a serious problem in Mexico, the Prime Minister is willing to integrate the economy of Canada with that country without any preconditions. I think the preconditions to negotiating an integration of our economy, with the result in changes in standards in this country and foregoing some of the sovereignty in this country, is a condition that makes profound commitments to the changes in human rights.
October 22, 1991

I certainly agree totally with what the previous speaker has said about the massive changes that have occurred. I would say that before we integrate with Mexico, it would be useful to get those commitments.

Mr. Speaker, with all due respect, I think the hon. member is giving us a misleading comparison. The doubt that the Prime Minister and other leaders had about further aid to the Soviet Union at that time, in my understanding, had absolutely nothing to do with human rights.
We had just been party as many countries had to the CSCE, the human rights conference in Moscow. It was the first time ever, so I think he is linking two separate things together. It is perhaps a little misleading.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to address this very important issue today that was raised by the Canadian delegation at the recent Commonwealth Conference.
Let me first congratulate my members on the left who have met with some recent successes. Let me caution also that this debate-I will come back to it-shows what has been happening in the west of Canada.
It shows that the Canadian voters and the Canadian citizens are no longer happy with the status quo. They want their governments to start to act with some purpose. I suggest that what has been happening on the Canadian landscape which ties into this debate is that Canadians do not want to see the members of Parliament or the Government of Canada discuss issues like this.
They certainly want to see their elected members of government come up with some concrete productive ways to alleviate this terrible problem that confronts everyone on the world scene. Having talked about their successes, I also have some difficulty with their motion. "Linkage" seems to be the prevalent word. In our discussions we heard about linkage in the gulf war and linkage in other areas. What we see here in the motion that is before this House is a principle of linkage. That means that in this debate today we are discussing the principles of aid connected with those of human rights.
If we go further into the motion, we see that economic issues are tied with those affecting human rights in different countries in the world.
Supply
I think there was a quote made by the Prime Minister recently that Canadians will not subsidize repression and the stifling of democracies in the world.
I am going to come back to that if I can in my closing remarks. I am having a problem with the concept of linkage that is causing me some concern.
I am going to pose a question. Although I do not have the answer I hope that the members of this House will give it consideration and see what we are doing with respect to human rights in many countries in this world.
Let me say that in pressing for human rights to become a priority item on the agenda, the Canadian people can indeed be proud because they have certainly stood high among all nations in the world.
It is pleasant to be on this side of the House with the current government treading this path. I think we can find its germination in the path formerly laid down by a great Canadian, Lester B. Pearson, truly in the Liberal tradition.
It would be nice before the debate ends today if someone on the other side of the House would give that truly great Canadian the credit he deserves. I believe it was during his tenure as Prime Minister that we developed the Pearson image that made Canada a leader among nations of the world when it came to compassion, empathy and respect for those who were not quite as privileged as ourselves. To be imitated in this type of policy is the greatest form of flattery.
I would like to emphasize the high regard in which Canada is viewed by the developing countries and certainly this position must continue. Reforms such as those described at the Commonwealth Conference must not be shunted aside. The government must insist that flagrant violations of human rights not be rewarded by initiatives of trade and massive allotments of foreign aid by Canadians.
Democracies such as ours, the middle powers with no axes to grind have the opportunity and indeed the responsibility to provide a leading role in improving human rights around the world. We can do this in many ways. To this date Canada and all previous governments have done very well in regard to establishing Canada's reputation, not only as a peacekeeper in the world but as a benevolent and caring nation. But we must improve on that stance.

October 22, 1991
Supply
As an example, the decision of the present government to trade with China following the horrifying events in Tiananmen Square told the world that Canada would proceed with that regime as if nothing had happened.
We imported from China more than $1.2 billion in 1989 and that figure rose to $1.4 billion in 1990, an increase of over 18 per cent.
While this trade effort was being conducted, Amnesty International, an organization I think we all respect, said that at least 1,000 people were killed by security forces to suppress pro-democratic processes. Thousands more were beaten and tortured. Dozens of protesters have been sentenced to death after unfair trials and there were reports of secret executions. Persistent reports of torture and detainees in Tibet have also been obtained by Amnesty International.
I could go on and read descriptions of the very questionable human rights records of countries receiving bilateral aid from Canada. Bilateral aid simply means that money is given by this government or some of its agencies directly to other countries. The facilities we have available to us through the United Nations are not invoked.
Many of the countries which are the chief recipients of bilateral aid from Canada are indulging in human rights abuses of the most chilling sort.
Some of the most glaring examples of bilateral aid received by countries for the year 1989 are Bangladesh with almost $90 million in aid. We all know about the allegations of torture and criminal suspects in custody, of extrajudicial executions by incompetent villagers and government security forces. I have reiterated what happened in China at Tiananmen Square yet they were the recipients of almost $40 million in aid from Canada. I look at Jamaica receiving almost $30 million and you know the unrest that is in that country and the deprivation of its human rights. Pakistan, Indonesia and many others really deserve some scrutiny with respect to aid vis-a-vis human rights.
There is a question that has permeated my mind throughout the debate and it is a fundamental problem to which I really do not have the answer. I certainly
would like to pose a question in the hope that as we go down this road we all start to give some consideration to a very important aspect.
We all know that regardless of the form of government, whether democratic, despotic, a benevolent or true dictatorship, all people in the world are controlled and every act of every government affects the people in that country and they do not have a great deal to say about it.
As an example I do not want to debate these issues here but we do know that the government of the day in Canada brought in the free trade agreement as soon as this House sat in 1988. This had a direct effect on almost everyone in this country. The free trade agreement whether it created jobs or lost jobs, had a definite effect on almost every Canadian particularly those in the manufacturing industry.
We will not say whether the imposition of the goods and services act was a good move -we on this side think it was not -but in any event we know that the actions of the government affected every person in this country with respect to a system of taxation.
If we go across to our friends in the United States we see that their involvement in the gulf war had a direct effect on every citizen in the United States with respect to how they conducted themselves.
What I am trying to point out is that every government by its actions affects on a day to day basis the people who live within that country who usually do not have a great deal to say about how or why it will affect their lives.
I think today of the people who live in underdeveloped countries and are denied human rights as I listen with intent to all of the very good debate within this House.
I think of the children of the world who really do not have any say-the children in Canada, children in the United States-in whether or how their country is going to be operated. They are at the whim of those that have control over them.
What are we doing when we link our economic aid? As I said at the outset, I am posing a question. What are we doing to these children when we link the economic aid with the human rights of their governments? The children in these under-developed areas do not have the

right to dictate or to be involved in the system of government, yet they are the recipients of its actions.
I am appalled, and I am sure we all are in this House, when we look at the children throughout the world on television in some of the African countries, Bangladesh, Ethiopia, and even in Bulgaria. We see children with distorted eyes, protruding eyes, distended stomachs, lacking the fundamental medical care that they need in order to even just sustain life. You cannot even say these children go to bed at night hungry because they most likely do not have a bed to go to.
What right do these young people have with respect to human rights and the linkage of aid. This is the question that I pose.
What I propose is something I would like this House to consider. We know that as we consider all of the problems that exist throughout the world, perhaps the worst problems are what is happening to the children of the world.
We know that poverty and debt are the enemies. We know our development policy should be designed to benefit these children. We know we should be assisting increased productivity, and we know we should be increasing the incomes of these people in order that they can provide for the necessities of life.
I would like to be the author of this thought, but I cannot take credit for it. I have been doing some reading. It really generates from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister when he was speaking about what Canada could do with respect to feeding the world. The parliamentary secretary is a very successful farmer from Saskatchewan. He is a very knowledgeable person about agriculture. I discussed this with my colleague who was a former minister of agriculture and it seems that what we should be doing, rather than linking the problems that we face with aid and the rights of people within these countries, is designing a policy within our country that would alleviate the hunger of the children of the world.
When you look at Canada and try to find a national purpose for our country, it seems we lack a national purpose. What a great thrill and what a great challenge it would be if Canada truly becomes the bread basket of the world, and we take all of these children that are so deprived. Within this country we have great assets. We
Supply
have three provinces, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba that can out-produce because of their technology, climate and the ability of its farmers to produce the best wheat in the world in great quantities., We have this facility within Canada.
We have unmatched facilities within this country to process this product, this grain, this food that we can grow in our western provinces. We have at our disposal without question through the port of Churchill, the port of Prince Rupert, the port of Vancouver, the port of Thunder Bay and the down river ports in Montreal the ability to ship this grain, this food, vital necessity of life to all countries in the world, those children of the world who are deprived of their fundamental human rights through no fault of their own. Canada has become the country that has taken on itself as its national purpose to be the bread basket of the world, feeding people in especially those areas that have no ability, no resources and no facilities to feed themselves.
How else could we extend human rights to every country in the world? How better would it be? What a feeling it would be of national purpose for Canadians to say: "We undertake this gigantic responsibility. We are going to do the very best we can".
I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that it may be the most basic challenge for all Canadians at this particular period of time in our lives to take this responsibility and say: "We are going to reach farther than any country has ever reached in order to provide a solution to this problem that is not going to go away unless we ourselves attempt to do it and we start by little bits and pieces".
I am satisfied in my mind we will emerge as a country that is well respected, looked upon throughout this world as not only one that had the empathy and the care to take up this important challenge, but the foremost country in the world with respect to guarding the human rights of those who could not guard themselves.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to my colleague, the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon, intently, I may say even hanging on every word because of his poignant reminder to us all about the bottom line here and that is people, the plight of

October 22, 1991
Supply
people all around this earth and particularly the children of this world and the difficulties that they are having.
I think it is very important as we near the end of this debate today that we not forget the victims of poverty, of disease, of oppression. I am very grateful to the member for bringing us around to considering those factors and considering the forgotten people of the earth.
Having said that, I know that the member has a very acute legal mind. I want to ask him to tune in that legal mind, if I may, by focusing on a problem that I have with the opposition motion put forward by our friend in the New Democratic Party, specifically using the word "linkage" which the hon. member began his speech with. I ask him to consider the terms of the motion and perhaps comment on the question that I pose.
The question is this: Does the hon. member find it logical that the opposition motion begins by taking note of the Prime Minister's comments that he is committed to the principle of linking government aid, and I stress government aid, to respect for human rights and says "and in light of documented violations of human rights in countries such as Mexico, China, Zaire", et cetera?
The motion reminds us of the Prime Minister's commitment to linking government aid to human rights and reminds us of certain alleged, in fact documented, violations of human rights in certain countries and then says: "We should stop negotiating with the countries of the United States and Mexico", not stop providing aid to Mexico, but stop negotiations with respect to an agreement that is not even in place. They are not saying: "Let's link government aid to human rights". They are saying "Let's link aid to negotiations", even speaking with another government, even discussing something with another government if there are documented instances of human rights violations. That is what they are saying. They are trying to bring in the free trade debate through the back door of human rights violations, on the backs of the very people who should be protected. I am wondering if my hon. friend considers this to be logical.

Madam Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague from Scarborough for the question with respect to my comments on the motion.
At the outset, I think I complimented my colleagues with respect to some successes and then discussed with
them the difficulty I have with the motion that is before the House today.
In answering my friend, I do not have any difficulty with the concept, nor do I have any difficulty with the intent of what we are trying to accomplish in this respect. My part of the debate contained aid and feeding the children of this world through the concept of human rights, but I had some difficulty technically with understanding what the motion meant.
I said at the outset that I had difficulty with the word "linkage". I could not see how we could equate linkage in human rights with linkage in economic aid, especially if we consider that the very people we are trying to assist in human rights may not have the opportunity to help themselves in the country in which they live. Let me explain that a little further. I am talking about the underprivileged. There are degrees of privilege and underprivilege. I am talking about the underprivileged people, the older, the elderly, the seniors, in deprived countries. I am talking about the children, those who cannot help themselves within the system of government in which they live. They are truly the underprivileged of an underprivileged class.
That is my concern. If we link the economic aid and the economic principles with helping those of the underprivileged in the underprivileged countries, what have we really done? What have we accomplished? We have just imposed more of a hardship on those who can no longer stand any more hardship.
I can appreciate the question and I am answering it to the best of my ability. I just have difficulty technically with understanding the motion that is before the House, particularly as it forms a linkage. Second, I don't know how we got from human rights to an economic issue like the free trade agreement. It does not make sense.

Madam Speaker, "Police torture still routine", Amnesty says in Mexico in September. I certainly understand the previous speaker's sympathy and support with it. "Mexico- Torture with Impunity" is the title of a report. It talks about Mexico's federal judicial police kicking, beating, pushing into water tanks, shocking, burning with cigarettes, subject to mock execution, asphyxiating with plastic bags-and on and on and on-toe nails ripped out. It asks: "Who are these victims?" These victims are
October 22, 1991

political activists, people involved in land disputes, human rights activists, trade unionists, lawyers, and children, particularly homeless teenagers, children of poor urban families, young rural migrants from the Mexican interior. They tell of beatings, whippings, electric shocks, asphyxiations and sexual abuse.
It is not as if we were considering providing aid. We could provide aid, not bilateral aid to Mexico but we could provide it through the Red Cross and other agencies where it doesn't sanctify or in any way support that government.
What we are talking about the government doing here is involving Canada with an equal partner, somebody that we would want to partially integrate our economy with and take those kinds of chances. Quite frankly, by eliminating the phrase "that this House urge the government to discontinue immediately Canadian participation with Canada, the United States and Mexico in a free trade negotiation", you have really sanctified the kind of activities that are going on. The majority of Canadians oppose this government because they do not accept what it is doing. They tell the truth. They stand up and say what they are-

Madam Speaker, during the previous debate on C-204, I had given my full support for the nuclear energy industry within this country and I outlined some of the benefits to Canada. These benefits are needed for our security and diversity of energy supplies. Also, nuclear energy is very important for environmental protection and industrial development.
Many of the areas I outlined would be in Hansard, but I did not get a chance to speak with regard to the
These investments are substantially lower than those made in other countries. Canada has extremely good economic viability within the nuclear area.
I also want to say with regard to the disposal and repository for nuclear waste that an independent export group was formed in 1977 and carried out a study on the long-term disposal. It laid down the basis for the criteria for nuclear fuel and the waste management program. It has been the responsibility of AECL and Ontario together.
With regard to storage and transportation, Ontario Hydro looks after this responsibility for waste demobilization and the disposal concept comes under the control of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited.
All the Canadian nuclear power plants are setting aside a portion of the mill rate, in the area of 1 per cent, to cover the costs of spent fuel disposal, which will probably come many years from now.
Having been in Sweden, West Germany and France for some time studying the disposal of low and high level nuclear waste, there is a consensus being brought forward that the deep geological disposal on land is the best

October 22, 1991

means to permanently isolate high level radioactive waste.
Countries with established nuclear power programs are at various stages of developing their disposal systems. Switzerland and Sweden have already completed extensive tests. In Canada we hope that next year some recommendations will be brought forward. These recommendations will have political discussion, input and debate. Where and when any disposal is made with regard to a certain location would come forth after political participation.
In conclusion, I just want to give my unequivocal support to the nuclear energy industry within Canada. We are not discussing nuclear weapons. We are discussing nuclear energy for the generation of electric power in Canada. It is an important investment for our country and I am just pleased that I had the opportunity to speak against Bill C-204.

Madam Speaker, let me begin by congratulating the member for Winnipeg Transcona on his recent appointment on top of his other responsibilities as the New Democrat's nuclear energy critic. I know he brings to this position extensive knowledge, keen interest and a solid commitment which has already resulted in the introduction of the laudable bill we are discussing here today.
This bill, an act to amend the Atomic Energy Control Act, seeks to end the development and export of nuclear substances, nuclear reactors and certain equipment and materials required to build nuclear reactors, starting on January 1, 1992 and lasting until December 31, 2041.
In the short time available today, the exceedingly short time available, I can only focus on one of the many reasons for supporting this bill to phase out nuclear energy in Canada. Madam Speaker, simply put, nuclear power is an economic failure. Canada cannot afford to keep pouring money down nuclear sinkholes, and what a lot of sinkholes there are.
For starters, nuclear power plants are extraordinarily expensive to build. Ontario's nuclear facility at Darlington, for example, was originally projected to cost under $4 billion. By last December, that projected cost had soared to $12.9 billion and, in February, 1991 that figure
Private Members' Business
stood at a whopping $13.3 billion. That is a lot of money by any standard.
It also cost a lot to protect workers' health and safety at all stages of production, starting right back at the mining of the uranium ore. Nuclear proponents cavil at these safety costs. The Canadian Nuclear Association in its October 9,1991 statement to the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources claimed that new, stricter radiation exposure limits proposed for uranium mines could, and I quote, "render underground uranium mining unviable."
Since these new safety standards reflect current scientific consensus about the risks of radiation exposure workers could, I suppose, be excused for worrying that the CNA is taking the insupportable position that the industry can only remain viable if workers are put in danger.
As for other mining costs, one need only go to Elliot Lake to see that it also costs a lot to clean up after uranium mining operations.
Nuclear reactors themselves cost more than expected to operate, and this costs consumers money directly on their power bills. Double digit rate increases are expected in Ontario for the next two years.
Canada's nuclear reactors have not lived up to promises about their efficiency. Many suffer maddening complications from so-called premature aging, ranging from damaged fuel bundles to burst pressure tubes. Recent evidence suggests that Ontario Hydro predictions that its nuclear plants will average 75 per cent efficiency in the next decade are overly optimistic. In 1989, hydro's reactors ran at only 72 per cent efficiency and in 1990 these reactors produced a dismal 62 per cent of the power they would have produced if they had run all year at full efficiency.
As Ontario Hydro chairman Mark Ellison stated, and I quote from the July 29, 1991 Financial Post "Our nuclear system is not operating the way it was supposed to operate." Sad, is it not, Madam Speaker, but unfortunately and expensively, true.
What then about accidents? Well, nuclear accidents do occur and when they occur they are catastrophic. No one can forget the Three Mile Island accident in 1979 and the devastating explosion at Chernobyl in 1986. Recently some Soviet scientists claimed that initially the extent of the devastation around Chernobyl was seriously under-

October 22, 1991
Private Members' Business
estimated. The most senior scientist at the Chernobyl station and the scientific director in charge of the 30 kilometre exclusion zone said in April, 1991 that the explosion killed up to 10,000 people.
He added that the government is currently providing medical care to an additional 300,000 people and that the Soviet Union has already spent nearly $20 billion trying to clean up after the accident.
Prominent Soviet scientist Yuri Koryakin estimated in the October 1990 issue of the U.S.S.R. Academy of Science publication Energy that the financial cost of the Chernobyl accident to his country alone could be over $400 billion by the year 2000. That is unforgiving, expensive technology.
Many CANDU proponents protest that such an accident could never happen here, but note: Just in case, the industry has protected itself from financial liability. In 1970, at the insistence of the industry, the federal government set a $75 million ceiling on the damage reactor operators would have to pay in the event of a serious nuclear accident.
Even if that operator were negligent, the irony is inescapable. Nuclear proponents loudly proclaim that nuclear power is safe, loiowing full well that in the event of a serious accident, thanks to the federal government and the Canadian taxpayer, the nuclear industry is virtually off the hook.
As for the long-term disposal of nuclear wastes, no one knows how much that will cost because it has never been done. We do know that simply conducting research on how to manage these wastes has been expensive. In a speech to the conference of the Canadian Energy Research Institute given on behalf of energy minister Jake Epp on June 4, 1990, Conservative member of Parliament, Marie Gibeau, estimated that in the past decade alone, government funded Atomic Energy of Canada Limited has spent $400 million. That is $40 million a year on research into long-term disposal of radioactive fuel waste.
The campaign for nuclear phase-out hit the nail on the head in a recent leaflet stating: "The cost of nuclear waste disposal, including disposal of defunct reactors themselves, are among the least certain and potentially largest of all nuclear costs". The leaflet added: "No full
size nuclear reactor anywhere in the world has yet been fully decommissioned".
Energy minister Jake Epp admitted in his September 1990 letter to my colleague, New Democratic environment critic, Jim Fulton, that: "Estimates of decommissioning costs of nuclear reactors vary widely", adding that the nine-mile point unit 1 reactor would cost: "about $100 million in 1990 dollars" to decommission.
I might be wrong, but I suspect Mr. Epp would come up with $100 million tomorrow for anyone who would guarantee the safe disposal of that reactor. Where does all this money come from, Madam Speaker? From Canadian taxpayers.
According to the April 1991 corporate plan and budget summary for Atomic Energy of Canada limited, the federal government has invested $4.5 billion in nuclear energy research and development over the past 40 years. That amounts to $110 million every year for 40 years.
The same AECL report reveals that more than half of the $303 million in expenditures in nuclear research and development planned by AECL for 1991-92 will be provided directly through parliamentary appropriation.
In 1995-96 alone, Canadian taxpayers are expected to fork over $197 million to AECL. Energy minister Jake Epp continues to champion a so-called market based energy economy even though after 40 years of generous government support, the nuclear industry still relies on tax dollars to stay afloat.
The government clearly has a responsibility to help create jobs and to spur the development of more environmentally benign energy sources in Canada. Unfortunately, the government grants large sums of money to nuclear and traditional fossil fuel sources, thereby stacking the financial deck against new cleaner options while slashing funding for these alternatives. The government then adds insult to injury by complaining that these alternatives cannot compete in the marketplace. In fact, since 1984 this government has cut its funding for energy alternatives and conservation by over 90 per cent. As a result the federal government will spend a mere $37 million this year on energy conservation and on wind, biomass, solar, all sources of alternate energy put together. That is less than the $38 million the government will
October 22, 1991

give the Atomic Energy Control Board just to regulate the nuclear industry.
It is hardly surprising that many countries have decided to stop throwing money at their nuclear industries. The recent experience in Britain offers one very graphic measure of the industry's financial status. In its misguided zeal to privatize its state electric utility, the Thatcher government discovered to its chagrin that it simply could not sell its nuclear plants. Private investors judged them to be uneconomic.
As the London Observer said in an editorial on November 12, 1989: "Privatization has proved that nuclear power is hopelessly uneconomic and saddled with decommissioning costs that no private company could accept without huge guarantees from the government".
The paper added a number of intriguing comments. Let me close with a quote from The Economist, a Conservative magazine, August 31, 1991: "It is hard not to believe that if the cash thrown at nuclear power had been put into almost any other technology, even hamster-powered fly-wheels, it would eventually have produced something commercially viable".
It is time we stopped pouring money down the nuclear sink hole.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona has any idea of the impact this bill could have on Canadians' health. Does he know how devastating it could be for thousands of Canadians who receive treatment involving diagnostic techniques or therapies that use radio-isotopes?
What role does nuclear energy play in medicine? Madam Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona could tell me that, technically speaking, most radio-isotopes are not prescribed substances. Therefore they are not affected by this bill under which the Atomic Energy Control Board could not issue new licences for the possession of prescribed substances, which would exclude most radio-isotopes used in medicine.
Private Members' Business
Let me show how such a statement lacks objectivity. Under the Atomic Energy Control Act, "prescribed substances" designates uranium, thorium, plutonium, neptunium, deuterium, their derivatives and compounds, and other substances that the Commission can by regulation classify as sources of atomic energy or consider necessary for the production, application and use of atomic energy.
Most radio-isotopes used in the health field do not fit this category. You may wonder what role nuclear energy plays in medicine, Madam Speaker. The fact is that it takes nuclear reactors to produce many radio-isotopes; these are the same reactors that the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona would take out of service over the next 50 years under his bill. For those requiring treatment, Madam Speaker, 50 years might as well be forever.
Cobalt-60, for example, is an artificial, man-made isotope. It is obtained by replacing stainless steel bars in a CANDU reactor with cobalt-59 bars. Irradiated in the reactor for about a year, these bars absorb neutrons and are changed into cobalt-60. Cobalt-60 is then taken out of the reactor for various medical purposes, in particular radiation therapy equipment and irradiation sterilizers.
Madam Speaker, we shall see the applications of radio-isotopes in medicine.
It is a pity that the public is seldom interested in the beneficial effects of radiation. Nevertheless, use of this technology for therapy, diagnosis and research is very widespread these days. Much use is made of irradiation to improve the quality of products and safety in various industries.
When radio-isotopes are administered in fairly small quantities to a patient for diagnostic purposes, it is possible to measure the concentration of this radioactive substance and to monitor its distribution with special detectors. Medical products that use radiation help to diagnose and treat various illnesses, especially cancer.
In fact, cancer can be detected in its early stages by bringing a sample of blood into contact with a radioactive chemical that reveals the presence and size of tumour markers, or substances that indicate the presence of cancer cells. Radiation can efficiently destroy such cells.

October 22, 1991
Private Members' Business
Irradiation techniques are also used to sterilize surgical or medical equipment, as well as blood for transfusion to patients whose immune system is very weak, especially the newborn.
Radiation can be used to study diseases and the internal workings of the body, to preserve food, to control food-borne illnesses and to disinfect waste, in particular municipal sewage and medical waste.
Let us now look at Canada's abilities in nuclear medicine. At the present time, Madam Speaker, the world's largest supplier of cobalt-60, the radio-isotope most used as a source of energy for commercial irradiation or cancer treatment, is Nordion International Inc., a Canadian company.
Most of the cobalt-60 sold by Nordion is in fact produced by Ontario Hydro under contract in CANDU nuclear reactors. Nordion is also the main supplier of other types of radio-isotopes made in reactors; these radio-isotopes are used throughout the world, especially for diagnostic purposes.
Canadian industry is in the forefront of research in nuclear medicine and has greatly contributed to improving the health of all the world's people. Madam Speaker, every year, more than 500,000 patients in over 80 countries receive treatments based on nuclear technology developed in Canada. Thanks to radiotherapy, millions of lives have been prolonged around the world.
The Canadian cobalt 60 therapy unit is used worldwide. Over 1,400 units have been installed abroad, which represents over 75 per cent of the market. In Canada alone, Madam Speaker, physicians make over 12 million diagnostics yearly using radioisotopes produced in this country. It is estimated that this figure exceeds 300 million world-wide. I would also like to talk about other health-related uses of radioisotopes.
That being said, Madam Speaker, I might add that radioisotopes have other than medical health-related applications as well. For instance, nuclear research has resulted in the development of new high-yield species of plants with greater disease resistance. Other agricultural applications include measuring of the soil moisture content in various regions to evaluate its capacity to meet water needs of specific crops.
Radioisotopes allow us to see how crops absorb nutrients and therefore to improve fertilizers. Finally, radioisotopes are used to monitor the flow of contaminated waterways and make sure that drinking water intakes are safe.
Irradiation can also be used to reduce or eliminate infestations of insects that are harmful to cultures, animals and human beings. A lot of male insects are sterilized by exposing them to radiations. Once let loose, these insects mate with females, but they cannot reproduce themselves. That technique enables us to eliminate harmful species over a period of a few seasons, in a more ordinate fashion that is also less harmful to the environment.
One must not forget the food irradiation sector. As we all know, the food we eat could be infected with bacteria and could therefore be spoiled and make us sick. In extreme cases, this could even lead to death. For these reasons, the scientists in the government and the food processing industry work relentlessly to find appropriate techniques to preserve food stocks without diminishing the nutritional value. It is now believed that irradiation techniques will enable us to better preserve food, while at the same time reducing the number of diseases linked to its consumption. Therefore, the food preservation sector could play a very important role, in Canada as well as in Third World countries. Madam Speaker, all these new applications are essential to maintaining the quality of food stocks for Canadians as well as for the populations of other countries.
One of the numerous advantages of nuclear energy lies in the fact that nuclear reactions do not produce any combustion residue that could pollute our environment and undermine our health. Madam Speaker, by going nuclear, Hydro Ontario has, in only the last 20 years, avoided the release in the atmosphere of over 7 million tons of acid gases, half a billion ton of carbon dioxide and 12 tons of ashes. Be that as it may, the present government has clearly demonstrated that it promotes the development of hydro-production techniques using renewable energies, namely solar energy, wind power or tidal dower.
