speechtext:
I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but her time is up.
October 22, 1991



On a point of order, the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona.

Madam Speaker, I think it is unfortunate that in Private Members' Business we continue to get from government backbenchers these speeches that are prepared by the Department of Energy or some other hack in Atomic Energy of Canada.

Madam Speaker, the time limitation does not permit us to deal specifically with the response the member for Louis-Hebert made in her intervention. She certainly spoke the language of the nuclear industry. She delivered the well-known themes that have been over the years presented to us by the proponents of nuclear industry.
Her scientific basis is very shaky. As I said, it is unfortunate that we cannot deal point by point with the points she has elaborated, as if they were final, scientifically proven and correct.
The debate today is on ending the development and exportation of prescribed items and substances that come under the Atomic Energy Control Act.
It is an important thought that the member for Winnipeg Transcona has put on paper. It is something for which he ought to be congratulated because it makes a very important contribution not only to the knowledge of this House but also in raising the awareness about the fact that in this country we do not really have an energy strategy that looks at the short, the medium and the long-term.
Therefore, the member for Winnipeg Transcona ought to be congratulated and supported. I would ask colleagues who have spoken against this bill or intend to speak against this bill not to be afraid of sending this bill to committee for a very thorough analysis and examination.
Inevitably it will raise issues that are much broader than the question of bringing to a halt the development and exportation of certain prescribed items. Obviously the member for Winnipeg Transcona had a broader thought in mind and I think he is achieving that objective.
Private Members' Business
We have in the last hours actually launched in this Chamber something that this government has unfortunately failed to do, namely a debate on a national energy strategy. This is what we are actually doing. By voting or speaking against this bill we are really saying that Canada does not need a national energy strategy, that we should just ignore it and sweep it under the carpet and hope for the best. For that reason alone, were it only for that reason, we ought to support this bill and vigorously so.
It is ironic also that two months after the member for Winnipeg Transcona tabled his bill, the minister of energy and the Minister for International Trade would announce a loan of up to $315 million to Romania for the construction of the Cernavoda power station almost as if to provoke feelings in this field.
Without going again, because of time limitation, into the merits, I think it would have been more honest and more appropriate to describe this $315 million not as a loan but as an outright grant considering the economic difficulties that Romania is likely to encounter for a long time before being able even to look at debts with Canada.
Let me make the point that what we have here today is in a mini form, an integrated debate on the economy and the ecology, an integrated debate actually that brings the economy, the ecology and the energy all into focus. It should actually not be a debate in which we become polarized between two opposed factions, the enlightened on the one hand and the regressive on the other, and not knowing exactly who is where, but a debate that really brings together as a mainstream concern the public interest.
What is the public interest? It is really to address the question of the urgent necessity of discussing a longterm, medium-term and short-term energy policy. This is what the member for Winnipeg Transcona has achieved.
Therefore, for this reason it will be good to have a study of this bill in committee, I submit, and it would be a pity to be afraid of having this kind of study in committee. The difficulty that we face, and this has already been demonstrated by a number of interventions, is that the fate of nuclear power is being discussed in a policy vacuum. Since there is no national energy strategy for the next five years or longer we cannot really do it.

October 22, 1991
Private Members' Business
Imagine, even the champion of deregulation, namely the United States of America, has a national energy strategy that was determined after extensive public consultations. We do not.
This debate has to take place against the background of one major concern and that is the necessity of developing integrated policies that would aim at the reduction of the global climate threats which are the object of scientific elaborations in recent years. I would like to refer to the existence of a very impeccable source, a publication entitled "Energy for a Habitable World" which is published by the Interaction Council. This council is composed of former prime ministers and heads of states and can only be accused of having one vested interest and that is the best future for the world.
I am glad to report that the former Prime Minister of Canada, Pierre Elliot Trudeau, is a member of the Interaction Council. A national energy strategy would of course consist of several elements. Very briefly, it would deal with the fact, as a premise, that the global climate change is a reality and would therefore aim at developing policies to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by 20 per cent by the year 2005 as already discussed and concurred in Toronto at the Climate Conference of 1988.
Second, it would have a serious commitment at least for a long-term 50 per cent reduction by the year 2025. Certainly it would have a strategy that would end in the short-term to conservation and increases in the efficiency of energy users, namely on the demand side, and conservation and increases in the efficiency of production, namely on the supply side.
In the medium-term you would want to have a shift in the fossil fuel mix from coal and oil to natural gas, taking advantage of their different carbon contents and their impact of course on CO2 emissions.
In the long term, Madam Speaker, you would want to see and I am sure we are heading in that direction a very powerful and important promotion and aggressive introduction of renewable sources of energy, renewable because they are the ones that are going to serve the purposes of humanity in the long term and that would be required on a large scale.
To do that of course we will need to make very early, now, at this stage, in this decade, a massive shift in our resources and in our research funds.
The strategy in these very sketchy aspects would have to be complemented by other initiatives. For instance you would have to bring back into the National Research Council the energy division which has been systematically dismantled since 1984 and give this division a task that would be commensurate to this particular challenge.
Finally, it is important that we also as a nation give leadership internationally to the development of certain agreements that are required for the control of emissions of all greenhouse gases and agree with other nations on a concerted action.
I would conclude by saying also that this debate allows us to raise the importance of harmonizing environmental objectives and concern with energy promises. Here you have an example where all of us I am sure have made speeches on sustainable development and have here an opportunity to practice what they have preached in their respective ridings, cities and the like.

Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure to take part in this debate on the consequences of Bill C-204 on Canada's participation in the NPT and safeguards program.
This proposed amendment to the Atomic Energy Control Act would throw into jeopardy the long years of determined efforts and accomplishments that have established Canada as one of the world's leaders in the field of nuclear non-proliferation.
It is quite clear that Canada's international stature on this matter was achieved by our participation in a domestic nuclear power program which included the full infrastructure that is required to support the construction and operation of Candu nuclear power stations in three Canadian provinces.
Canada is the world leader in the production and export of uranium and, as a result, has been a major factor in determining the operating principles of trade in this commodity. Canada has also engaged in the export of nuclear reactors and has learned by experience of the hazards that may result from inadequate controls.
October 22, 1991

This bill would immediately curtail any further activity in these sectors and would certainly have a drastic neutralizing effect on our continued participation in the non-proliferation theatre. The reputation that Canada has attained by its steadfast and expert participation in the world's nuclear community would be thrown to the winds by this arbitrary and irresponsible severance from the continued development of nuclear power. It would preclude any meaningful international influence over the course to be followed in the peaceful application of nuclear power and its attendant immeasurable benefits to mankind.
I should like to draw to the attention of the members the great achievements in leadership that Canada has demonstrated in the field of nuclear non-proliferation, all of which would be put at a high risk by any ill-conceived, whimsical action such as this.
Canada's non-proliferation and safeguards policy has two objectives: (1) to promote the emergence of a more effective and comprehensive international non-proliferation regime; and, (2) to assure Canadians and the international community that our nuclear exports will not be used for any nuclear explosive purpose.
Canada's policy promotes attainment of the first objective by emphasizing the key role of the NPT, which is the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. Second, by promoting reliance upon and improvements in the international Atomic Energy Agency safeguards system, by treating nuclear weapons and non-nuclear weapon states alike regarding Canadian nuclear exports and, finally, by working for new approaches covering the sensitive phases of the nuclear fuel cycle.
The second objective is served through the network of bilateral nuclear agreements that Canada has put into place with its nuclear partners. Those agreements provide assurance that Canada's nuclear exports are used solely for legitimate, peaceful nuclear energy production purposes.
At the same time, Canada, having formulated its non-proliferation and safeguard policy during the years after the Second World War until 1980, has recognized that it has gone as far as it can on its own in this field and that from this point on any further changes should be made on the basis of international agreement.
The Canadian objective is to persuade the international community to devise a more effective and comprehen-
Private Members' Business
sive international non-proliferation regime in which Canada and other suppliers might subsume their national requirements.
Whatever else, the second half of the 20th century will come to be symbolized by the unlocking of power in the atom, which will be seen as one of the half dozen or so most significant developments. This power was first demonstrated close to the mid point of the century. There is no turning back the clock.
It is common knowledge that energy can be released from splitting atoms both suddenly in an explosion and gradually in a nuclear reactor that has mechanisms controlling the rate of the chain reaction.
The question that has preoccupied many governments and many individuals since nuclear energy was first shown to be viable is how to harness the energy in the atom while preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
A great deal has been written about nuclear proliferation and nuclear non-proliferation since the first detonation of a nuclear explosive device in 1945. The high point in the history of non-proliferation is, of course, the Treaty on Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons which was written in 1968 to 1970. The establishment of the International Atomic Energy Agency in 1957 is also highly significant, especially since it is that international body that is responsible for onsite inspection and safeguard measures that assist the member states of the agency to demonstrate that no nuclear material is diverted to non-peaceful purposes from safeguarded nuclear facilities.
Besides these international efforts, many countries that supplied nuclear related materials have developed national policies of their own which apply to the export of such nuclear items.
The essential determinant of a proliferation is the degree of political incentive or disincentive which countries face. Thus, while diversion of nuclear items from the civilian nuclear fuel cycle is one possible technical route to the development of nuclear explosive devices, it is not the only nor the most efficient route.
A political decision to proliferate would be better served by installing facilities dedicated solely to that objective. Controls on the diversion of nuclear items from civilian facilities are necessary but it is clear that if a country has sufficient political incentive, such controls by

Private Members' Business
themselves would not stop that country. Any industrialized country and many developing countries could develop a nuclear explosive capability if they so decided. A general political commitment by a country not to proliferate is therefore as important as the specific controls that prevent diversion.
Canada was one of three states that participated in the November 1945 agreed declaration on atomic energy. Throughout the years that followed Canada has played an active and significant role in efforts to define an international regime which would serve the twin principles set forth in the declaration. Canada participated both in the drafting of the International Atomic Energy Agency statute between April of 1955 and October of 1956 and in the preparatory commission appointed to make arrangements for the first sessions of the International Atomic Energy Agency's general conference and of its board of governors.
Canada has had continuous representation on the board of governors since the founding of the IAEA and has strongly supported the agency's efforts on nuclear safeguards. Canadian representatives were also involved in the negotiations of the treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.
Canada's uranium exports from 1945 until 1974 were carried out under a nuclear co-operation agreement which made the export subject to peaceful uses commitment and to acceptance by the importing country of bilateral verification measures by Canada, or increasingly through the International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards that they had put in place.
From 1945 through until 1965, Canada also exported uranium to the United States and to the United Kingdom for use in their nuclear weapons program. These export sales were carried out as part of Canada's defence relations with those two countries. That policy was ended in June, 1965 when former Prime Minister Pearson announced in the House of Commons that "as one part of its policy to promote the use of Canadian uranium for peaceful purposes, the government has decided that export permits will be granted or commitments to issue export permits will be given with respect to the sale of
uranium covered by contracts entered into from now on, but only if the uranium is to be used for peaceful purposes. Before such sales to any destination are authorized, the Government of Canada will require an agreement with the government of the importing coun-tiy to ensure with appropriate verification and control that uranium is to be used for peaceful purposes only".
So with the announcement of this policy all Canadian uranium exports became subject to the "peaceful uses" provision.
I can see that the Speaker is indicating that my time is almost up. I would conclude by saying that in the riding of Cambridge the firm of Babcock and Wilcox has been quite active in this particular industry and I know that the company and the workers at that particular company and the community of Cambridge would certainly want me to stand here today and oppose this legislation.

Madam Speaker, I rise in support of this very worthy bill. I want to first commend the member for Winnipeg Transcona for bringing the bill forward.
I would like to associate myself with the remarks made by the distinguished member for Davenport who spoke earlier. Had there been more time available tonight, we would have had another contribution in support of the bill namely from the member for Broadview-Greenwood who would like to see the bill go to second reading so that we could have a thorough examination of the nuclear industry.
How about Winnipeg North?

Yes, and I could say that the member for Winnipeg North also supports the bill.
This is an important debate for this is a very major issue and this is the place, the Parliament of Canada, where major issues of this kind should be debated.
I joined the debate for many reasons, one of which is out of respect for the many concerned citizens. The people who support a bill like this and who are concerned about the nuclear industry are not odd-balls. These are good people and responsible people. They have studied the issue very thoroughly. Their questions are pertinent and their concerns are valid.
October 22, 1991

At last count, about 170 organizations support nuclear phase-out. In my province there are six well-known organizations: the Concerned Citizens' Committee of Manitoba, Manitoba Uranium Action Coalition, Project Peacemakers, Veterans Against Nuclear Arms, Winnipeg Co-Ordinating Committee for Disarmament, and World Federalists, the Winnipeg chapter.
The words in the bill are quite sweeping. They call for a nuclear-free Canada, the cessation of all nuclear development and the phase-out of existing nuclear facilities at the end of their current life.
I would suggest that let us not focus entirely on the wording of the bill. Let us focus on the necessity of having a debate and a thorough examination of the nuclear industry in Canada. That is what I want from this particular exercise in Parliament.
To hear opponents of the bill tell it, any debate of this kind will bring the nuclear industry crashing down. Moreover, they would like us to believe that speaking in favour of a bill like this is akin to something unpatriotic. I say we should get serious because there is nothing further from the truth.
The nuclear industry is a huge industry in this country with thousands of employees. It has friends in very high places, starting with the federal government in Ottawa. It is anything but feeble and it can take care of itself. Let us have a debate because there is concern and that concern is growing.
In the 10 years ending in 1988 support for nuclear expansion dropped from 46 per cent of Canadians to only 16 per cent. A similar poll carried out by Decima in 1989 came up with a similar finding.
You might ask yourself the question: Is nuclear phaseout something far-fetched? I do not think it is. For example, there has been no new nuclear reactor in North America in the past 10 years. After Chernobyl, the Philippines closed its only plant. Several European countries-Sweden, Austria and Italy-have agreed to a nuclear phase-out and three plants have closed in Britain. Nuclear phase-out is something that is not far-fetched.
Relating to other concerns, things can go and have gone wrong with nuclear power plants around the world. We all know about Chernobyl in the Soviet Union. There, thousands of people died in the immediate area
Private Members' Business
around the plant which was transformed for a long, long time; perhaps forever.
We all remember Three Mile Island right on this North American continent. We thank God that there has not been something even worse than Chernobyl. We always think about a horrible, horrible meltdown, something that does not happen. Let us hope it never does.
Nothing as serious as Chernobyl or Three Mile Island has occurred in Canada. Our Candu reactor has according to world standards a pretty good record so far, but it is not perfect. There was a rupture of a pressure tube at Pickering, Ontario about eight years ago, in 1983.
The fear of accidents is one thing, but there are other concerns as well. There is radioactive pollution. Some countries, not Canada, have reduced permissible levels of radiation exposure for both workers and the general public. Nuclear power is dirty. It is dirty. The problems relating to waste, how to get rid of bad waste, are nightmarish.
Let me point out that over 17,000 tonnes of nuclear fuel bundles are currently in storage at reactor sites in New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario, 17,000 tonnes of nuclear fuel bundles.
Radioactive substances from nuclear reactors are among the most toxic materials known to mankind. Spent nuclear fuel cannot be handled by human hands. It remains toxic for hundreds of thousands of years.
These are real problems and we cannot wish them away. That is why I believe that a thorough examination by this House would be very much in order.
While we are at it, we could look at the whole question of economics as it relates to the nuclear industry. The question of economics has been touched on in previous speeches, but just let me raise the question.
Are taxpayers getting a good return on their dollars which have been sunk into the nuclear industry? Billions of dollars have been sunk by the public into the nuclear industry.
I think a review is in order. It has been promised in the past. It was promised, I believe, by a former Prime Minister in 1979. It was again promised in about 1984 and it was promised somewhat later, in the late 1980s. Those promises have not materialized in any review of the nuclear industry.

October 22, 1991
Private Members' Business
I say we should take this bill and send it to committee. Let us have a thorough review and let us address the concerns of very concerned Canadians.
